#5512. New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

A new wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.

Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.

REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an important role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for new treatments.

"This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," said Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.

"Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up new possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.

Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster

The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.

In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.

These improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.

Unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.

The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.

Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health

The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.

Among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.

Brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.

"REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being."

These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.

A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.

A New Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD

Building on the initial findings, the research team plans to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.

Beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a new way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.

"Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," said Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need."

The team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.

If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable new tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.

Other members of the research team include William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli, and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

#5511. D-Matrix bets stacked DRAM can solve inference’s memory bandwidth problem

As artificial intelligence workloads shift to inference, memory bandwidth decides whether hardware generates tokens quickly or sits idle. D-Matrix Corp. is answering with Raptor, a second-generation chip stacking 3D DRAM beneath its compute logic.

AI infrastructure has become a systems game, and winners combine memory, interconnect and software into cohesive designs, according to Satyam Srivastava (pictured), fellow at d-Matrix.

“It’s no longer a chip problem. Chip plays a part of it. Memory bandwidth is a fundamental advantage that has to be solved,” Srivastava said. “The next is energy efficiency. The next is interconnect efficiency. The next is software cohesiveness.”

Srivastava spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed d-Matrix’s Raptor chip and its stacked 3D DRAM, inference memory bandwidth and the shift toward heterogeneous computing. (* Disclosure below.)

D-Matrix proves each risky technology on a test chip first. Jayhawk proved die-to-die connectivity, and Jayhawk II validated digital in-memory computing. The Corsair accelerator combined both and entered full production earlier this year, Srivastava explained.

“Fast forward, we have the Pavehawk chip, test chip, which is proving out 3D DRAM stacked underneath the logic die, which serves as the core technology for Raptor, which is our second-generation chip coming out next year,” Srivastava said.

Stacking keeps the distributed memory architecture intact but moves memory cells onto a separate layer rather than consuming logic die area. Data travels a short distance and never crosses an interposer. That puts 3D DRAM in a new tier between SRAM and high-bandwidth memory, Srivastava said.

“So you’re getting 10 times higher energy efficiency compared to HBM, 10 times higher bandwidth compared to HBM, where it sits in between SRAM and HBM in terms of capacity,” Srivastava said.

Pairing a Corsair-based server with an existing Hopper GPU fleet can raise utilization from about 20% to as much as 80%, meaning more tokens per dollar, Srivastava noted. D-Matrix has also adopted NVLink Fusion rackscale infrastructure from Nvidia Corp. to connect its accelerators to Nvidia’s AI factories.

“For us, it unlocks the opportunity to participate in a very established ecosystem, the world’s most popular AI factory. We get access to a very hardened design of an MGX rack,” Srivastava said.

The partnership points toward heterogeneous computing, where software orchestrates GPUs, CPUs and accelerators such as Raptor as one system, with the cluster as the unit of computing, Srivastava explained.

“So think of a chip, but that chip is an entire cluster and it has many different hardware units,” Srivastava said. “Some are GPUs, some are CPUs, some are ASIC accelerators, and you can use whichever one you like to serve the needs of the workload the best.”

#5510. Why Do Empty-Nest Boomers Own So Many Homes in Top School Districts?

The best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put. But helping free up housing in these districts isn't as simple as getting older people to move, a new study argues.

The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry.

The Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts. But it pinned that on affordability challenges. Higher-income households of all types compete for housing in the best-performing school districts.

This is a conundrum for neighborhoods. Seniors are thus left in neighborhoods paying premiums for school districts they don't use. Meanwhile young families who'd like move into the district face limited options for homes there.

Of course, many seniors want to age in place in homes that they've lived in for decades. But others looking to downsize are "locked in" due to high mortgage rates. That can leave them in homes that they can't afford or, worse, in homes that pose safety risks for aging people.

"These findings suggest that policies aimed solely at encouraging older households to downsize are unlikely to substantially improve access to quality school districts," the paper says.

Low housing turnover in these districts drives up prices. The higher-rated public school districts are, on average, 49% more expensive, and homes there move faster, Realtor.com® data shows. But in some of the nation's top school districts—including in Dallas, Los Angeles, and San Fransisco—homes can sell for three times the price of surrounding metros.

Using data from the American Community Survey, the Cleveland Fed found that households over 65 occupy a disproportionate share of the housing stock in the best-performing school districts. While these account for 26.2% of all households nationally, they make up as much as 28.7% of households in the least affordable areas.

Meanwhile households with children, which make up about 31.2% of U.S. households, occupy 30.1% of housing in the best school districts and 40% of the housing stock in the lowest-quality districts. The same doesn't ring true for one-person households, which tend to be more evenly distributed.

Older homeowners move at about the same rate across all school districts—about 6.9% a year. About 81% of older adults in the best school districts own their homes. To the Cleveland Fed, that shows older households aren't limiting turnover of housing stock in high-quality and high-cost districts.

"While older households occupy a modestly larger share of housing in these expensive, high-quality areas, they do not appear to limit turnover," the paper states. "These patterns suggest that the challenge of accessing high-quality school districts is driven by a combination of income sorting and competition from multiple household types rather than solely by empty-nesters’ aging in place."

Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu says a few issues are affecting seniors as they consider their futures. They include capital gains taxes they'd incur on homes that have appreciated in value. They also include the kinds of taxes they'd incur when they move to a new place. Then there are the social considerations.

"Right-sized, single-level, accessible homes near family and doctors are scarce," Xu says. "Moving also means leaving behind the neighbors and community that owners have built over decades. For many longtime owners, there are few good places to go."

Buyers can still find deals in some of these good markets, Realtor.com found, if they look carefully. But in some good districts, there simply aren't a lot of homes changing hands.

Xu adds that she's surprised that young professionals without children can also compete for housing in these expensive districts. Jobs, urban amenities, and investment opportunity for the real estate tend to make these areas attractive.

"Even if more seniors moved, the homes they left would likely go to higher-income buyers, because this is a sorting story. The districts wouldn’t become much more affordable," Xu says. "The more direct solution is building more homes in and near high-demand districts. Adding right-sized options could also give older owners who want to move somewhere to go, but supply is what would ease pressure on prices."

To Arick Morton, CEO of NIC MAP, the frozen market points to a need for more housing oriented toward seniors. Earlier this year, his group said the nation needs to add 1 million new senior housing units by 2040. That $1 trillion homebuilding frenzy would meet the moment 10 million baby boomers pass age 80.

"People stay at home much longer than they did previously," Morton said. "Of course folks stay at home as long as they can and then movie into senior housing when the need is there."

But when there isn't enough senior housing or they don't have good alternatives to downsize, those seniors end up displaced when age or an accident means they require more intensive care needs.

"The best policy options are those that help expedite the construction of senior housing," Morton said. "We don't have enough capacity to create a dent in that logjam."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5509. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5508. Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

Researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the new findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks

The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

However, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

"Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk."

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

Wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen said.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health

To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several important limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

Alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

The researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an important distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

For now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

Materials provided by American College of Cardiology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5507. Inside the $1.1 Million ‘Barbie Dream House’ That Started as a Goth Mansion Before Going Under Contract

A real-life Barbie dream house is turning heads in Hudson, WI, where an eye-catching pink Victorian has gone under contract after hitting the market for $1.1 million in June 2026.

With its pink walkway, bubble gum–colored staircase, and vibrant interior, this seven-bedroom, 5,189-square-foot home is anything but ordinary.

But behind its playful Barbie-inspired appearance is a spacious historical residence built in 1900 that is packed with character, original details, and incredible versatility.

“An everyday buyer interested in a classic Victorian home might think this is a bit much,” says listing agent Jennifer R. Martin of Edina Realty Inc. “It has a lot of great qualities. I would say to anyone not to let the color deter you. Painting is easy, and it’s not that expensive to make changes.”

Currently a successful short-term rental, the home is near the St. Croix River and could be used for multigenerational living or converted into a single-family home.

“The sizing alone of the house is incredible,” Martin says. “It’s enormous and goes on forever. It has two separate kitchens, so it could also be turned into a duplex.”

It is part of a collection of rose-hued homes operated by Fleetwood Rentals, which hosts everything from birthday parties to bachelorette weekends.

“The seller’s clientele is looking for a party weekend destination,” she notes. “It’s one block from the riverfront and two blocks away from downtown.”

Located 30 minutes from the Minneapolis/St. Paul airport, the property last changed hands for $614,000 in 2020. It offers “outstanding income potential,” the listing states.

“When the seller bought it, right away she had it painted in dark charcoal,” Martin says. “Her vision at that time was to have a Goth mansion that would be similar to Disney’s Haunted Mansion. It was right around the time the 'Barbie' movie was coming out, so she decided to take advantage of that.”

The multilevel home also has formal and casual dining spaces and expansive gathering areas. Original details include woodwork, built-in cabinetry, vaulted ceilings, and dual staircases.

"I envisioned the next buyer to be either another Airbnb owner or a large family who would un-pinkify it," Martin says with a laugh. "It's a great house with a lot of great qualities. I told potential buyers not to let the color deter you."

The living room has pink walls, drapes, and couches. The formal dining room has built-in cabinetry and a fireplace. The light-filled kitchen, with an enormous breakfast bar, is a surprise with its white cabinetry and a copper farmhouse sink.

The bubble gum–painted grand staircase leads to the colorful sleeping quarters. Four bedrooms are on the second level and three more are on the third floor. The primary suite has a walk-in closet, a soaking tub, a separate glass shower, and a dual-sink vanity.

Other highlights include a home theater, a hot tub, a 14-foot swim spa, and a patio designed for entertaining. The fenced lot comes with a private patio, a two-car garage, and a driveway with parking for 12 vehicles.

The property is conveniently located near boutique shopping, riverfront parks, and the marina.

"Hudson is a riverfront town with tons of history," Martin says. "People love to come here for bachelorette parties and places to go out to dinner. It also has a lot of charming, fun shops."

#5506. AI inference servers shrink to fit the air-cooled racks enterprises already run

Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own.

As AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera.

“Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija said. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.”

Botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. (* Disclosure below.)

Axelera’s Europa chip has been shipping since September. Ahead of SC26, the company unveiled Titania, a third-generation architecture that scales the design up to a 400-watt chip. The resulting six-kilowatt server is built to perform like leading data center GPUs while fitting into the existing 20- to 30-kilowatt air-cooled racks of an ordinary enterprise data center, Botija explained.

“Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre GPU is a pretty big deal,” he said. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.”

For enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the company’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage.

“Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija said. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a company.”

#5505. Mastering Digital Marketing - How to Grow Your Business Online

Having a solid digital marketing strategy is essential if you want to succeed as a business owner in the modern day. Effective digital marketing lets you get more eyes on your business and ensure consistent growth.

Because digital marketing trends are forever changing, it’s important to stay on top of your brand’s strategy. Doing so ensures that you stand out above your competitors and gain the recognition that your brand deserves.

If you’re unsure how to master your digital marketing strategy, consider working with an expert company that can help you figure out which direction to go. A professional agency, such as Scorpion Digital Marketing Agency, can support your online efforts to maximize your success.

If you don’t want to outsource your digital marketing processes, try these top tips below to maintain an effective digital marketing strategy and boost your business growth.

Your website is where most of your new audience will find your business and your existing customers will shop for your new products and services. If you create a strong first impression through your website, you can gain credibility and authority in your industry.

Make sure to regularly update your website content so it’s accurate and on-trend. Doing so also signals to Google that your website is authoritative and credible, increasing your rankings on search engine results pages (SERPs).

The higher your rankings, the higher your visibility, meaning you can expand your reach with minimal effort. When updating your content, use plenty of industry-relevant keywords and key phrases to ensure your target audience finds your site.

With a strong social media strategy, you can significantly expand your reach and gain recognition as a trustworthy brand. Regularly posting content enables you to provide consistent value to your audience while displaying your expertise.

You can create posts highlighting the benefits of your products or the quality of your services. You can share positive testimonials and reviews from happy customers to build your credibility.

Social media platforms allow you to connect directly with your target audience too. You can answer queries and concerns in your DMs and show the human side of your brand.

Video marketing is becoming increasingly effective. Over four-fifths of consumer internet traffic comes from videos, so it's the perfect way to expand your reach and drive more traffic to your website.

Whether you use live or pre-filmed video content, you can capture your target audience's attention and provide helpful information in an engaging way. You can share demonstrations of how to use your products or explain your services in more detail to persuade consumers to check out your brand.

Optimize your videos for search engines by including keywords and phrases in your video titles and descriptions. Doing so increases your rankings on SERPs and puts your brand in front of as many people as possible.

#5504. Senate Passes Controversial Permitting Bill Aimed at Speeding Construction and Lowering Costs

A bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for major infrastructure projects could have implications for both housing and energy costs.

The Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act. Much of that was aimed at big energy infrastructure, but it also has implications for housing and even data centers.

Senate committee leaders Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill. It's since been attached to a larger and more popular bill, but lawmakers have been debating and tweaking it for several weeks.

The latest version released this month updated language to assuage concerns that it would weaken environmental protections and rights of Native American groups. The bill has been popular but divisive: While the speed would boost green energy like wind and solar power, plus electric infrastructure that lowers costs, it could also speed along fossil fuel investments, like natural gas pipelines, and nuclear power.

"Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs," Lee said on the floor before the vote. The bill could make "everything you buy" less expensive in the long run.

But several housing advocates have cheered the bill, saying it would make it easier to build affordable housing and invest in local communities. They include the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, the Niskanen Center, Associated Builders and Contractors, and the National Community Development Association.

"America’s housing shortage demands solutions that make it easier and more affordable to build," National Association of Realtors® Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn said. NAR "supports streamlining permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction, and limit housing supply."

A White House policy paper estimates federal permitting requirements for major infrastructure take 4.2 years to complete—and produce 1,700 pages of paperwork. It expects reforms to increase the GDP by $82 billion to $164 billion and produce $14 billion to $28 billion in tax revenue.

It also said permitting reform could cut electric bills by $178 to $251 a year for the average household. President Donald Trump urged the bill's passage in a post on Truth Social, calling it "a BIG WIN."

"This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs," the president posted.

"We can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs," Whitehouse said.

A number of groups opposed to the bill argued that some of the protections it removes would endanger protections for Native American groups and hamstring environmental preservation.

The Association on American Indian Affairs said the bill would "threaten Native sovereignty and the protections that safeguard our country's cultural and historic heritage." The Endangered Species Coalition says it would weaken protections. Both continued to oppose the bill even as it was amended.

The House would need to vote on the bill next, and members have already began debating its merits.

"Even as amended, it undermines Tribal sovereignty, environmental laws, and locks in dangerous projects," Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-NM) said in an X post. "This is NOT the deal, NOT the time, and NOT what the American people asked for."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) cast the bill as a way for Republicans to use the remaining weeks of their majority to improve affordability for Americans.

"One of the biggest things we can do to address affordability for the long term is to ensure a reliable and affordable energy supply," Thune said. “And that starts with ensuring that energy projects don’t face unnecessary permitting barriers."

The federal permitting process, he later said, "has unfortunately gone far beyond these reasonable expectations.

“And that’s due in large part to senseless delays caused by cascading litigation from environmental groups and by agencies determined to study a project to death," Thune said. “We’ve seen those delays happen to everything from water projects to broadband deployment to affordable energy and improving roads and bridges."

A poll by moderate think tank Third Way found bipartisan support for the tenets of the bill. About 62% of respondents named lowering utility bills as a top concern, and 57% keeping the power grid reliable.

“It’s more important than ever to pass permitting reform this year. The overwhelming support for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act reflects the Senate’s commitment to addressing the nation's energy affordability challenges."

The bill was also host to Congress' latest effort to rein in data center developments proliferating throughout the country. One amendment by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) would have banned data centers on public lands. Republicans blocked it.

"There is enormous concern that this bill puts the pedal to the floor on data centers across the country," Wyden said on the floor.

Following Democrats' gains in the House after the 2026 midterms, a number of left-leaning groups have called for a hesitant Congress to formulate more laws involving data centers. Among them, the Chamber of Progress called for federal AI safety standards and requirements for data centers to cover their own costs.

A recent study by the Wharton School indicates that data centers have indeed increased industrial electricity prices in the nation. But it also said that residential customers absorbed relatively little of that price gain.

But that doesn't mean they don't affect communities. A group of Senate Democrats, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, released a report pinning other costs on them. It also criticized the tax incentives.

"This investigation finds the data center industry is bulldozing local communities and using their economic resources to play states and local communities against one another, creating a race to the bottom in which state and local policymakers feel they have no choice but to accede to the data centers’ demands—and leaving ordinary citizens stuck with the bills," they said in a joint statement.

Voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. Virginia spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. Ohio lost $2 billion in foregone revenue from its incentive in two years alone.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5503. Jon Hamm and Wife Anna Osceola Have Welcomed Their First Baby—Inside the ‘Mad Men’ Star’s Bachelor Pad Turned Family Home

Jon Hamm and Anna Osceola are officially parents! The "Your Friends & Neighbors" co-stars welcomed their first child together.

The new bundle of joy is a boy, according to a People magazine source.

The couple, who met on the set of "Mad Men," first sparked speculation that they were expecting after Osceola, 38, was seen with a baby bump during a trip to the Hamptons—with sources quickly confirming to People magazine that Hamm, 55, and his spouse were happily preparing to welcome a child.

The actor—who tied the knot to Osceola in an intimate cliffside ceremony in California in 2023—broke his silence on those rumors during an appearance on “Late Night With Seth Meyers," telling Meyers that he was "very excited and deeply terrified" about becoming a dad.

“I think I’m doing it right," he said, adding that those feelings shouldn't ever “go away.”

He then poked fun at his age, teasing, "When your kid is 70, you’ll be like, ‘I did it!’ When I’m 152.”

Back when rumors began surfacing that the couple was expecting, an unnamed insider told People, “Jon’s incredibly excited. This is something he and Anna have wanted and hoped for. He’s not thinking about his age or what anyone else has to say about it. He’s just really happy.”

The source added that Hamm is "happy, settled, and ready" for the next stage of his life, while a different insider told Us Weekly that the couple was "trying to relax a bit but are enjoying making plans for the baby."

While the process of nesting can look entirely different from one family to the next, the news about Hamm and Osceola's new addition does raise a question about whether the couple will raise the baby in the actor's longtime $4 million Los Feliz pad, which he purchased in 2017, before he was officially linked with his now-wife.

Though the home served as a bachelor pad for Hamm for several years, it has since become a marital residence for the couple and could now evolve once again—this time, into a family dwelling.

Certainly the four-bedroom, 3,600-square-foot home boasts plenty of room for a family of three. There's a spacious kitchen equipped with top-of-the-line appliances and a spacious pantry.

The 4.5 bathrooms feature spa-worthy furnishings, while the comfortable family room opens up to a stunning backyard patio complete with a built-in grill station, fire pit, and saltwater pool.

The property’s midcentury aesthetic makes it the kind of place one might picture the actor’s most notable on-screen character, Don Draper, residing, with wood paneling and asymmetrical design choices that ooze character while maintaining a peaceful environment.

The gated property is located at the end of a charming cul-de-sac in the Los Angeles neighborhood, which many big names in Hollywood have called home over the years, including Brad Pitt, Kristen Wiig, and Aubrey Plaza.

It’s not the first time Hamm has invested in the area, purchasing a 3,100-square-foot Los Feliz abode for $900,000 in 2002 with his then-partner, actress Jennifer Westfeldt. The duo parted ways in 2015 after spending 18 years together.

During his previous relationship, Hamm was not sold on the concept of fatherhood.

“I see my friends who have children and I’m like, ‘Dude, how are you even upright, much less here at work at 6 a.m.?” he candidly said to Us in 2012.

However, he’s changed his tune since beginning a life with Osceola and is now “over the moon” at the thought of enjoying a new life as a dad, according to an Us Weekly source.

“Jon has always wanted to be a dad with Anna,” the source continued. “Having a family was something that was really important to both of them from the beginning.

"They’ve talked about this chapter for a long time and were always on the same page about wanting children, so for it to be actually happening now feels incredibly special.”

The Emmy-winning performer has opened up about his desire to have a family with his wife, telling The Hollywood Reporter that, due to his parents’ divorce during his childhood, he “didn’t look at marriage as a thing,” but was hopeful for his own union to turn into a growing family.

“I will be the old dad, but so it goes,” he said in 2024, then 53 years old. “It could be a good thing. We’ll see.”

Hamm and Osceola first crossed paths in 2015, when filming the finale episode of “Mad Men” in Big Sur, CA.

Romance rumors swirled in 2017, but their relationship was not officially confirmed until 2020. The couple made their public red carpet debut at the Vanity Fair Oscars Party in 2022.

Hamm eventually popped the question. “I just knew at a certain point I wanted to be with this person,” he shared with The Hollywood Reporter in 2023. “But when I proposed, I was terrified. I was like, ‘What am I doing?’”

The couple tied the knot in July 2023, with their sentimental wedding celebration serving as a thoughtful nod to their “Mad Men” roots.

The ceremony was held at Anderson Canyon, the Big Sur spot where they first met when filming the show’s final episode. Surrounded by loved ones and lush florals, they exchanged vows alongside the Pacific Ocean.

#5502. Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.28% Rate

Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac.

Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.

So what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

At today's 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,354. This reflects a $40 monthly increase from the previous week’s payment of $2,314.

Compared to the 6.26% average from November 2025, which required a $2,120 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $234 more a month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,839.

This reflects a $48 increase from last week's monthly cost of $2,791. Compared to the 6.26% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,558, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $281 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $145 in relief.

The long-term financial picture shows how this abrupt reversal affects total borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.28% rate will pay a total of $847,328 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage.

While this week's jump erased much of the ground gained over the past month, this total still represents a contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630.

By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $43,302 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.28% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,022,090 for principal and interest.

If that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $52,233 for FHA buyers.

#5501. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5500. What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly said he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”

After listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The company made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress said the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

She explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

Asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The company’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the company held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress announced plans to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

For information technology buyers, nothing changes about what you’ve ordered or planned over the next 18 to 24 months. Don’t pause a deployment because of a leadership headline. The advice I gave in August still applies: Welcome Nvidia’s simplification and hedge the dependency.

One of the more interesting comments on the call came from Jones, not Kress. In describing the CEO search, which will consider both internal and external candidates, he said the board “appreciates that we’re living in a world where advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are driving major changes in our marketplace. Our new CEO will need to navigate those waters carefully.”

That was paired with immediate action. On the morning of earnings, the board created a standing national security and export control oversight committee of three directors that will retain outside experts. Kress disclosed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China and noted that the U.S. Commerce Department issued new export controls this week, which the company “still has some time to study.”

Huang was a product visionary who also served as the industry’s chief diplomat. The board is now signaling that fluency in Washington is a core requirement, on par with technical vision.

For IT leaders at multinationals, export policy is now a deployment variable. The new Commerce rule is intended to block remote access to advanced chips via data centers in third countries, so the location of your capacity and who can access it are now compliance questions. Bring your compliance team into AI infrastructure planning early.

With demand still far ahead of supply, who gets Nvidia systems matters more than what they cost. Kress laid out the criteria more clearly than I’ve heard before. First are land, power and shell, meaning whether a customer’s facility is ready to receive and use the gear in the quarter it ships. Second is capital. Third, for customers that aren’t investment-grade, is proof of off-take, or evidence that someone has committed to use the capacity.

“All are getting the same pricing,” Kress said. “That is super important for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute.”

Those same factors were incorporated into the guidance. Kress said the outlook “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The reality is that the AI bottleneck has shifted from the chip to the building, the grid and the balance sheet. Nvidia is serving as the industry’s underwriter, determining who is ready.

The lesson for enterprise buyers is that readiness is the currency. If you want on-premises systems, secure power, cooling and funding before requesting allocation. If you can’t, buy capacity from a provider that has already cleared this hurdle. In my view, this also helps explain why sovereign AI is growing so quickly for Nvidia. Those projects often arrive with land and power already in place.

Over the past year, Nvidia has used its balance sheet to seed the ecosystem through guarantees, investments, and commitments to neoclouds and AI labs. Though  neoclouds remain important, Kress brought a different tone to this audience. She said Nvidia will “continue to be disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and that it is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” as other sources of capital become available. Asked about vendor financing, she acknowledged that “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter.”

Two notable details emerged during the call. When Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon pressed on what he read as new disclosure language about neocloud commitments, Kress explained that Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only after a partner has raised its own debt and equity, built the facility and installed the compute. If the project stalls, the guarantee lapses.

“Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said. Even so, spelling it out clarifies Nvidia’s participation in neoclouds. When asked about uses of capital beyond the share buyback, which she said Nvidia still plans to complete, she put suppliers first: “The top priority is going to be our suppliers.” Prepayments to expand capacity come before customer financing, which will be reserved for “very strong customers.”

This was a critical piece of information for investors. I’ve previously compared vendor-financed neoclouds to the CLECs of the internet era, where the financing organization was left holding the bag. A CFO-led Nvidia appears to see the same risk. The result is a shakeout in which well-capitalized neoclouds with contracted demand grow stronger, while thinly funded ones struggle to secure systems. This should offer some comfort to investors that circular financing has been de-risked.

The flip side is that someone still must fund the buildout outside the hyperscalers. Kress pointed to infrastructure capital partners establishing financing platforms. Whether that money arrives as fast as Nvidia steps back is what to watch for.

My advice to IT buyers is to ask, before signing a multiyear deal with a neocloud, how it’s financed, how much capacity is committed and where it stands in Nvidia’s allocation queue. Those were niche questions a year ago. They should be standard due diligence now.

The demand story has shifted from training models to running agents, broadening what customers need from Nvidia. Citing OpenRouter data, Kress said agentic workloads now account for roughly 80% of tokens. Falling token prices are driving more usage, keeping GPU rental rates climbing.

The CPU growth story shouldn’t surprise anyone. In May, I wrote that agentic AI opens a massive new spigot for Nvidia on the CPU side. This quarter, demand outpaced supply. “Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply,” Kress said, noting that Nvidia’s Vera CPU is now adopted by CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and Open AI. Agents spend much of their time calling tools, running code and moving data, which is general-purpose work. A CPU shortage amid a GPU boom shows how quickly the workload is changing.

Nvidia is also filling in the layers above and around the hardware. The agent safety platform pairs OpenShell, which limits what agents can access, with Sentry, which runs on BlueField data processing units and monitors agent behavior in silicon. In my view, the biggest barrier to deploying agents in production is control, not model quality.

The network is part of this, too. Kress said co-packaged optics is in volume production, and Lambda’s deployment, announced at this week’s SC26 conference, is the first large-scale proof point. Nvidia is a formidable networking vendor, though buyers mixing accelerators will still want to weigh a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing chip.

For IT buyers, plan CPU capacity for agent workloads now, and insist that agent controls reside outside the model, in infrastructure you can audit.

The question of who the new CEO will be might not be just about Nvidia but about the entire industry. If the board goes internal, Ian Buck seems to be the frontrunner. Externally, the names most bandied about are Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su, Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, or we could see Manuvir Das make a comeback and return to the company.

Most industry watchers describe Nvidia as a chip company, a view that is about a decade out of date. Nvidia’s value comes from the full systems it has built around its silicon. Each is a stack tailored to an industry: hardware, libraries, frameworks, pretrained models, simulation and developer tools, all tuned to work together.

The next CEO must treat silicon as a key layer of an open, secure, agentic enterprise stack. Enterprises won’t buy GPUs. They’ll buy outcomes: agents that run safely on governed data across clouds, on-premises and at the edge. Whoever runs Nvidia next must sell that outcome, play well within an ecosystem Nvidia doesn’t fully control, and make security a core part of the platform. Here are three dark-horse candidates to consider:

Matt Garman. The Amazon Web Services Inc. CEO has led the world’s largest cloud through the shift to AI. He knows what it takes to turn infrastructure into consumable services at enormous scale. Garman also lives the open-stack approach: AWS offers model choice, runs its own Trainium chips alongside Nvidia’s, and sells to enterprises that want flexibility rather than lock-in. He would bring operational discipline and a deep feel for the customer. The question is whether Nvidia’s biggest customer-turned-competitor can credibly lead the supplier.

Jeetu Patel, Cisco Systems Inc.’s president and chief product officer, is the best storyteller in enterprise tech after Huang himself. He has spent the past few years rebuilding Cisco’s portfolio around secure AI infrastructure, integrating networking, security and observability into a single platform. That is exactly the “open, secure, agentic” stack Nvidia must deliver. Patel thinks in platforms, moves quickly,and has been personally using AI agents to shape his product views. He also has deep enterprise credibility, which Nvidia needs more than additional credibility with hyperscalers.

Charlie Giancarlo, CEO of Everpure (formerly Pure Storage), may be the most underrated name here. He built networking businesses at Cisco, spent time in private equity, and has repositioned Pure as a data management company. Storage revenue is growing thanks to hyperscaler wins. Giancarlo understands that agentic AI depends on data and that the data layer and the network are where enterprise AI succeeds or fails. He is a systems thinker who has led a platform transition before.

Two final points on the CEO hire: For some reason, there is a tremendous amount of industry chatter that Jensen Huang was the only person at Nvidia with key relationships with suppliers, partners, and other ecosystem providers. I know for a fact that is not true. Nvidia’s leadership, which includes Buck, Deb Shoquist (executive vice president of operations), Nico Caprez (vice president of global AI development), Gilad Shainer and Kevin Deierling (networking leadership), Kress and others, all have deep relationships with the ecosystem.

Also, I wouldn’t expect the board to make a snap decision about its next CEO. The roadmap is baked beyond Feynman, and the company can continue for a couple of years, if needed. This is an important hire; the board should take its time and ensure it’s the right person.

This call confirmed what many industry watchers, including me, have long believed: The moat was built in layers, and those layers held. Supply is constrained, the roadmap is set and customers are still asking for more than Nvidia can build.

Kress closed the call by saying, “We’ve got this.” On execution, I believe her. Kress is a steady hand right now, and the discipline she brings to capital allocation should make the AI buildout healthier. The bets that created Nvidia’s position, though, were placed years before the market arrived. Post-Jensen, Nvidia will continue to perform as it did; as Robbins put it, no one is bigger than the industry.

My advice to IT buyers is to stick with current plans and closely monitor the CEO search. Since Nvidia’s roadmap is baked through Feynman and beyond, it can ride momentum for the next two years or longer.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5499. Sector Snapshot: Investors Turn Up The Volume On Voice AI

Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work.

Companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology.

The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation.

The funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession.

The numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data shows. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025.

The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents.

The biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI, which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based company is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners.

San Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners, completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital-led financing in April. The company provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models.

Customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV, at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels.

Meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners, at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation.

Among companies focused on AI-generated speech, New York-based ElevenLabs announced a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The company is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing.

Beijing-based ModelBest, which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July.

Voice AI companies have also begun delivering exits. In January, Deepgram acquired OfOne, which automates restaurant and drive-thru orders.

In September, Inworld acquired Ultravox, a developer of conversational voice AI technology.

The sector also saw an IPO. Neosapience, the South Korean company behind synthetic voice platform Typecast, listed on the KOSDAQ on Sept. 21.

Looking ahead, additional acquisitions are in the pipeline. Automation Anywhere agreed to acquire Boost.ai, an enterprise voice and chat AI provider, in October. And Deepgram announced plans to acquire Daily, creator of the Pipecat voice-agent framework.

More recently, Five9 agreed to acquire Level AI for $325 million in cash, adding technology that analyzes customer conversations, assists contact-center workers and automates voice and digital interactions. The Level AI transaction is expected to close by year’s end.

Overall, the space is booming, and it doesn’t look like interest in voice AI will die anytime soon. Tom Hulme, managing partner and head of Europe at GV, told Crunchbase News in 2025 that one of the most exciting trends he believes is underway in the growth of voice AI is that “we’re returning to humanity’s most natural form of communication.”

After decades of adapting ourselves to technology, “technology is finally adapting to us,” he said.
