#5498. The Houses That Made New Orleans—and the Rising Cost of Keeping Them Standing

The World Monuments Fund's 2026 Irreplaceable America list recognizes the kind of architecture that has come to define the country—landmarks that serve as reminders of who we are and where we came from.

But one place was so emblematic of the country's past, present, and future that no single building could serve as a symbol of the whole.

New Orleans is the only entire city among the 10 places to receive the designation.

“New Orleans itself is irreplaceable—not just one building, one district or one monument, but the entire living city,” says Kristin Gisleson Palmer, executive director of the Preservation Resource Center of New Orleans when the title was announced.

Yet the buildings that earned the city that recognition now face a mounting threat: the cost of protecting them.

New Orleans has the second-highest homeowners insurance costs relative to property values among the nation's 100 largest metro areas, according to research from Realtor.com®. Now, as storms intensify and insurance costs rise, the city's historic homes are becoming more expensive to protect and preserve.

On a recent walking tour through Bayou St. John, Heather Veneziano—director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program, who helped spearhead the city's nomination—began not with a building, but with the ground beneath our feet.

The bayou that gives the neighborhood its name connects to Lake Pontchartrain, a brackish estuary fed by rivers and linked to the Gulf of Mexico. The slower-moving waters served Indigenous communities as a transportation route before European colonization.

Alongside that access, nearby natural ridges offered comparatively high ground in a landscape shaped by water, making the area an appealing, if imperfect, place to settle.

But higher ground didn't always mean dry ground. And the European settlers who followed knew the water would eventually return, and they built their homes accordingly.

“You have to build for place,” Veneziano tells Realtor.com.

At the Pitot House, a Creole colonial country house built in 1799, she pointed to the elevated living quarters as an example. The ground level, she said, could be used for storage during dry seasons, while allowing floodwater to enter below the principal rooms during wet ones.

“You lived, I think, with the knowledge that water is going to be a thing you can't fight against,” Veneziano said.

That understanding shaped the building from the ground up. Its broad roof and galleries offered shelter from the elements, while its timber framing incorporated cypress, a locally abundant wood prized for its resistance to decay and insects.

Residents adapted that approach across generations, raising homes as new neighborhoods and architectural forms developed, according to FEMA's history of building elevation in New Orleans.

But even the most carefully adapted homes can't eliminate the danger.

Today, an estimated 88.9% of residential property value in the New Orleans–Metairie metro faces severe or extreme flood risk, according to the 2025 Housing and Climate Risk Report from Realtor.com.

As New Orleans grew, new residents brought their own architectural traditions, transforming both the appearance of its neighborhoods and the ways people lived within them.

The Creole townhouse, with shops beneath upper-floor residences and courtyards tucked behind masonry facades, became a defining feature of the French Quarter.

Interestingly, its appearance was partly shaped by disaster. After fires destroyed much of the city in 1788 and 1794, Spanish authorities favored more fire-resistant construction, helping establish the brick, stucco, and ironwork associated with the neighborhood today.

New Orleans' celebrated architecture was also built on slavery.

Behind the ornate facades, enslaved people lived in courtyard quarters and worked in the homes they helped construct. Enslaved craftspeople helped construct the homes themselves, while the city's wealth was deeply tied to their forced labor.

Yet within this slaveholding society, free Black New Orleanians also established themselves as builders and property owners. Architectural historian Tara A. Dudley has documented how the Dolliole and Soulié families shaped the city's housing and built wealth through real estate, despite laws restricting Black economic independence.

Following the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, Anglo-American settlers introduced different architectural preferences. Wealthy merchants built double-gallery houses Uptown, their stacked porches and classical columns reflecting fortunes tied to shipping, cotton, and enslaved peoples.

The craftsmanship that distinguished these homes also presents a modern financial challenge.

Rami Sneineh, a licensed insurance producer and owner of Insurance Navy Brokers, says replacing handmade windows, woodwork, or plaster may require scarce materials and specialized craftspeople.

“If your home sustained significant damage, it could take months to source similar materials and you’d likely need to hire specialized craftsmen to restore those one-of-a-kind details,” he says.

An older home worth $400,000, he offers as a hypothetical example, might cost $700,000 to reconstruct with comparable details.

But not every architectural tradition emerged from wealth.

The shotgun house, which spread through working-class neighborhoods during the 19th century, arranged narrow rooms one behind another. Its origins are debated, but historians have identified possible African and Caribbean influences. Double shotguns accommodated two households beneath one roof, making efficient use of narrow lots.

And as drainage technology opened lower-lying areas to development, raised-basement houses appeared in neighborhoods such as Broadmoor and Mid-City. Their main living quarters sat a full story above the ground, carrying the tradition of elevation into the 20th century.

Yet the pumping systems that enabled the city's expansion also contributed to land subsidence, according to the Historic New Orleans Collection.

The homes remained elevated, but their protection increasingly depended on an engineered system of drainage, pumps, and levees—whose vulnerabilities became devastatingly apparent during Hurricane Katrina.

As we walked through Bayou St. John, the distant sound of a marching band practicing for upcoming Mardi Gras parades drifted across the neighborhood. Veneziano paused to listen, reflecting on the communities hidden behind and whithin the structures that surrounded us.

“The architecture is the setting for those relationships,” she said. “And people's voices are told through the built environment in which they live.”

Today, New Orleans has 26 historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places, covering more than 45,000 properties and roughly 40% of its urbanized area.

But preserving the appearance of those neighborhoods doesn't always preserve the communities within them.

During our walk, Veneziano pointed out double shotguns converted into single-family homes, a trend she said accelerated after Hurricane Katrina. The exteriors might remain recognizable even as two residences become one.

“It's taking away affordable housing for the rental population because there's not as many rental units anymore,” she said.

The lost rental unit also means losing a potential source of income that could help an owner maintain an aging structure.

And for the homeowners who do remain, those costs are rising on many fronts.

Single-family homes in the area carry an estimated annual homeowners insurance premium of $8,328, according to research from Realtor.com—equivalent to 3.6% of its median market value, and the second-highest burden among the 100 largest metropolitan areas.

Those estimates don't even account for the specialized demands of restoring historic architecture or purchasing separate flood coverage.

Even insured owners can face substantial out of pocket expenses. Sneineh notes that a 5% hurricane deductible on a home insured for $600,000 leaves an owner responsible for $30,000 before the insurer covers eligible damage.

“Properties that were previously affordable to purchase may now be unaffordable to insure,” says Mujahid Merchant, an independent researcher in climate risk and mortgage credit.

When private coverage becomes unavailable, homeowners may turn to Louisiana Citizens, the state's insurer of last resort, which is required to charge higher rates than qualifying private insurers.

And if a mortgaged home loses required coverage, its lender may purchase more expensive insurance and charge the owner. Merchant warns that the resulting increase in monthly payments can contribute to delinquency or foreclosure.

Yet some of the solutions draw on the same practical ingenuity that shaped these homes in the first place.

“Contrary to popular belief, you can strengthen your historic home’s roof without changing its historic look,” Sneineh says.

Louisiana's Fortify Homes Program offers eligible owners grants of up to $10,000 to strengthen roofs against hurricane winds. A state report found that median recipients saved $1,250 a year, or 22%, on insurance premiums. New Orleans also provides an expedited review process for qualifying roof replacements in local historic districts.

But even as owners find new ways to protect their homes from the elements, keeping those buildings affordable presents a different challenge.

After Hurricane Katrina, thousands of New Orleanians left for cities such as Houston and Atlanta. Not everyone returned.

Veneziano described the familiarity of living near former teachers, relatives, and neighbors whose lives have intertwined for generations—connections that can't simply be reconstructed in another place.

“You can't take what you have anywhere and put it somewhere else,” she said. “Places don't matter without people."

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5496. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5495. Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

Enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating new requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure. While much of the early AI investment centered on access to powerful GPUs, organizations moving AI applications and agents into production are discovering that accelerators are only one part of the equation.

Agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure. That requires more than bare-metal GPU capacity. It calls for a complete cloud platform that combines compute, networking, storage, security and the services needed to manage applications at scale.

That shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them. Infrastructure providers increasingly need to support the full application lifecycle rather than simply supply specialized hardware.

During a live interview at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty spoke with Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer at Vultr, about the changing requirements of enterprise AI infrastructure, the return of CPU-based computing, data sovereignty and the growing role of platform engineering.

“They need a full cloud platform,” Cochrane said. “They need cloud compute, specialized AI compute, networking, storage and an open ecosystem.”

Vultr entered the cloud market in 2014 with a developer-focused platform built around performance, cost efficiency and accessibility. Since then, the company has expanded into AI infrastructure, offering both traditional cloud services and specialized GPU resources.

Cochrane said Vultr took a deliberate approach to the AI infrastructure market, prioritizing enterprise workload and platform-engineering requirements rather than focusing exclusively on GPU availability.

“We’ve always said that we’re the tortoise in AI infrastructure,” he said.

That approach reflects a broader change in how enterprises are approaching AI. Early infrastructure demand largely came from hyperscalers, AI research organizations and startups building large-scale models. Those customers needed access to GPU clusters, often through bare-metal infrastructure.

The next phase is different. Enterprises are looking to use AI agents to streamline operations, improve customer experiences and create new revenue opportunities. Those applications must work alongside existing enterprise systems, comply with security requirements and integrate with established network and application architectures.

Bare-metal GPU infrastructure alone does not address those needs. Cochrane identified complexity and a lack of specialized skills as major obstacles to enterprise AI adoption. Organizations may have access to powerful accelerators, but they still need the surrounding infrastructure and services to build, deploy and operate applications.

Vultr’s strategy is to provide a more integrated environment, including traditional cloud compute, GPU infrastructure, networking, storage and access to cloud-native projects. Cochrane said the platform supports more than 60 Cloud Native Computing Foundation projects that customers can deploy directly.

The goal is to reduce the work required to assemble an AI environment. Rather than making enterprises integrate every component themselves, providers can offer preconfigured services and composable infrastructure that developers can deploy as needed.

That distinction is becoming important as AI moves beyond experimentation. Enterprises need infrastructure that supports production applications, not just model training and inference.

The growing focus on GPUs has sometimes obscured the role of traditional computing resources in AI architectures. But agentic AI is expanding the range of workloads that infrastructure providers must support.

An AI agent does more than send a prompt to a model and receive a response. It may execute scripts, interact with repositories, run builds, access databases and invoke external tools. Those activities require compute resources beyond the GPU.

“Not all workloads need to be on a GPU,” Cochrane said.

CPUs remain essential for databases, application code and data pipelines. They can also support smaller, optimized open-source models and inference workloads that do not require dedicated accelerators.

Another emerging requirement is the environment in which agents execute tasks. As agents gain the ability to run code and interact with systems, enterprises need secure sandboxes that isolate those activities from production environments and sensitive resources.

Cochrane pointed to work underway in the cloud-native ecosystem around safe and secure agent sandboxes as an indication of how infrastructure requirements are changing.

This creates a more complex infrastructure model. GPUs may handle demanding model reasoning and inference, while CPUs support the applications, pipelines and execution environments surrounding those models.

For organizations, the implication is that enterprise AI infrastructure decisions should account for the entire agentic workflow. Buying GPU capacity without considering the compute, storage, networking and isolation requirements around it can create another infrastructure silo. A full-stack approach gives platform teams more flexibility to match resources to individual workloads while maintaining a consistent operational environment.

As enterprises expand AI deployments across regions, data sovereignty is becoming more than a question of where information is stored.

Organizations operating in regulated industries or under national data requirements need to understand where data resides, which services can access it and what happens if infrastructure outside a particular region becomes unavailable.

Cochrane described Vultr’s regional architecture as an isolation model in which each of its 34 global data center regions operates independently. According to him, data within a region remains resident there and is not accessed by Vultr services outside that region.

The distinction extends beyond data residency to application operations. Cochrane used France as an example. An application running in a French region should continue operating even if Vultr’s global control plane and its other regions become unavailable.

“If the rest of the world went dark, your production application in France? It just runs,” he said.

That approach is intended to reduce dependencies on global services that could otherwise affect regional application availability. It also gives organizations a clearer boundary for managing sensitive workloads and maintaining operational continuity.

For enterprises, this is an important architectural consideration. A cloud provider may offer regional data storage, but that does not necessarily mean every service required to operate an application is isolated within the same geography.

As AI applications become more deeply integrated into business operations, organizations will need to evaluate sovereignty across the full application stack, including data, compute, management services and operational dependencies.

The cost of running AI applications is becoming another major consideration as organizations move from pilots to sustained production workloads.

Inference costs can increase quickly when agents repeatedly call models, retrieve information and execute multi-step workflows. As usage grows, enterprises must balance model performance, throughput and infrastructure expense.

Cochrane believes some organizations will increasingly turn to open-source models that can be adapted to their own data and operated on infrastructure they control. Rather than relying entirely on large commercial models for every task, enterprises can post-train specialized models using proprietary information and deploy them for operational workloads where that approach makes sense.

He described an example involving a platform engineering organization that reduced inference costs by 80% by post-training an open-source model and running it on its own infrastructure. The example illustrates a potential economic advantage, although results will depend on the workload, model, infrastructure and operational requirements involved.

The broader point is that organizations are beginning to evaluate the economics of enterprise AI infrastructure across the entire stack. Model selection matters, but so do infrastructure utilization, throughput, data movement and the cost of operating agents over time.

For some workloads, owning more of the infrastructure and model lifecycle may provide better cost control than depending entirely on external inference services.

That does not mean every enterprise should build and operate its own models. It does suggest that organizations need more flexibility to choose where models run and how workloads are distributed.

The changing infrastructure requirements of agentic AI are also expanding the responsibilities of platform engineering teams.

Cochrane expects platform engineers to become central to enterprise AI adoption, working more closely with business units to understand which agents and preconfigured application environments are needed across the organization.

That moves platform engineering beyond infrastructure provisioning and developer enablement. Teams will increasingly need to help define the building blocks that allow developers to deploy governed AI applications without having to assemble every component independently.

Cochrane also sees an opportunity for the cloud-native community to evolve how it shares infrastructure patterns. The CNCF ecosystem has helped developers adopt individual open-source projects across networking, storage, observability and other infrastructure categories. But as architectures become more complex, organizations need guidance on how those components fit together.

Cochrane predicted the emergence of marketplaces where developers can share opinionated, prebuilt stacks for specific workload types. Instead of selecting and configuring individual components, teams could start with a tested architecture and adapt it to their requirements. That could help reduce the complexity of building agentic applications while encouraging more consistent deployment practices.

He also expects consolidation in the neocloud market. Providers focused primarily on bare-metal GPU capacity may face pressure as enterprises demand broader cloud capabilities. Those able to expand into full public cloud platforms could be better positioned to serve production workloads.

Vultr’s existing cloud platform gives it a foundation for that transition, Cochrane said, with its investments in both traditional compute and specialized AI infrastructure.

Enterprise AI is changing the definition of cloud infrastructure. GPUs remain important, but agentic applications require a broader foundation that includes CPUs, secure execution environments, networking, storage, data sovereignty and integrated cloud-native services.

That creates an opportunity for providers that can deliver more than specialized accelerator capacity. It also puts platform engineering teams in a more strategic position as enterprises work to standardize how AI applications are built, deployed and governed.

The next phase of the neocloud market may therefore be determined less by who can offer the most GPU capacity and more by who can provide the complete environment enterprises need to run AI in production.

As Cochrane’s comments suggest, the infrastructure challenge is no longer simply making AI compute available. It is making the entire system around AI practical to operate at enterprise scale.

#5494. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

Buyers rarely get low rates and strong negotiating power at the same time, and today’s market is handing you the leverage. Connect with a local real estate agent to find homes where sellers may be open to covering a rate buydown or closing costs, so you can see if today’s market can work for your budget.

#5493. The Key Numbers I’m Watching As Anthropic Makes Its IPO Debut

Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The company says revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero.

The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing.

Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments.

I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns.

OpenAI’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users.

By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1, the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record.

Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it says it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology.

Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets:

Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn-led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion.

Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google, Amazon, Spark Capital, Menlo Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow.

The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension.

The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services.

That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses.

Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption.

Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company says it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. Anthropic points to its launch of Mythos as an example of that balance.

As Anthropic debuts tomorrow, I’ll be watching how well it balances AI’s promise with the risks its own filing lays out.

#5492. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

#5491. Angelina Jolie Feels ‘at Home’ in Cambodia as She Expands Business Overseas—Inside Her Plans To Be a ‘Bit Nomadic’ After Ditching Los Angeles

Angelina Jolie is ushering in a new era after quitting Los Angeles.

In the wake of selling the $24.75 million California estate she snapped up less than a year after filing for divorce from Brad Pitt in 2017, the actress has revealed plans to enjoy more time overseas and less time tied down to a singular location.

Jolie recently visited Cambodia, where local outlets reported she met with religious leaders. The “Maleficent” star reportedly “paid her respects and presented religious offerings” to Samdech Preah Maha Sumeatheathibodi Am Limheng, supreme patriarch of the Mohanikay Buddhist order.

She also visited a traditional crafts village on Cambodia's Koh Dach, which is known as Silk Island, to observe local artisans.

The mom of six detailed her special connection to the country during earlier travels to the Philippines, where she spoke on a Nov. 11 panel alongside Cambodian filmmaker Rithy Panh.

“I found this place and the people to be so warm and so open, and I couldn’t believe their spirits were so strong after all they have suffered,” Jolie said of Cambodia. “You go to certain places, and you just feel at home.”

According to People magazine, the actress plans to expand her creative collective, Atelier Jolie, with a residency in Cambodia in 2017.

The effort will be a partnership between Panh’s Bophana Center and the Maddox Foundation, which Jolie founded in 2003 and named for her eldest child, Maddox Jolie, whom she adopted from Battambang, Cambodia, in 2002.

According to the Atelier Jolie website, the business is focused on “the discovery of art, craft and design work from cultures around the world.” She founded the certified B Corporation business in 2023, with a headquarters in Manhattan’s NoHo neighborhood, which serves as a retail store, art space, and cultural center.

Jolie spoke about her plans for the future in a September 2026 interview with L’Officiel, noting that she plans to spend more time “out of the States.”

“The hope for the atelier was always to be global,” she said. “The idea would be to visit the different locations around the world and meet local artists and makers.”

She noted a desire to expand the atelier to Brazil, as well as “get back to doing more hands-on work” with the Maddox Foundation in Cambodia.

She also expressed a desire to live a life that’s less tied down to one specific locale.

“I don’t really plan to have a base,” Jolie admitted. “I’d like to have a home base for my family, a place where some of the mom stuff and the family photos are. And then I’d like to be a bit nomadic for a while.”

The star also noted that she has a home in Cambodia, which “will also be a residency a few months out of the year for the Khmer culture.”

Jolie’s appreciation for the Southeast Asian country began when she first visited to film the 2001 movie “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider.” She returned a year later to adopt her son and has since spent lots of time traveling back and forth with her family.

In 2017, she directed “First They Killed My Father,” a Khmer-language biographical thriller based on a memoir of the same name by Cambodian human rights activist Loung Ung.

In a People magazine interview, Jolie revealed Maddox—who was 15 at the time—was deeply involved in the creation of the film and helped with research.

Jole revealed her son spent “over four months” in the country at that time, “really reading, listening, learning, and absorbing all things about his culture and his country, including the very, very dark parts.”

Although Jolie was born and raised in Los Angeles, she has long expressed her desire to leave the city.

“I grew up in this town. I am here because I have to be here from a divorce,” she told The Hollywood Reporter in 2024. She explained that once her youngest children—twins Knox Leon and Vivienne Marcheline—turned 18, she’d be “able to leave.”

The milestone birthday passed this July, paving the way for a new chapter for Jolie.

“It’s the end of a certain time for me,” she told L’Officiel weeks later.

Jolie made moves quickly, putting her idyllic Los Angeles compound on the market for $29.9 million in May, seemingly in anticipation of Knox and Vivienne’s 18th.

The six-bedroom, 10-bathroom abode found a buyer in September, selling for $24.75 million. Jolie had originally purchased the home for $24.5 million in 2017, and it served as her primary residence for nearly a decade.

While Jolie plans to spend the bulk of her time jet-setting, she hasn’t said goodbye to the United States for good, and has reportedly purchased a Connecticut mansion, according to Page Six Hollywood.

#5489. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? #5488. Dow and S&P 500 Plunge Into Correction as Tech Sell-Off Deepens

The major stock indexes extended their losses on Friday, as the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 briefly plunged into correction territory, defined as a 10% decline from their last peak.

By the closing bell, the S&P 500 had fallen 265 points, or 3.70%, while the Dow Jones dropped 949 points, or 1.93%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.28%, wiping out its gains for the year.

The sell-off, driven by a wipeout in tech and AI stocks, comes a day after Anthropic raised a staggering $81.34 billion during its IPO on Thursday, lifting the company's valuation to $1.414 trillion.

Anthropic shares were down 12% on Friday, giving back most of their gains after jumping 17% in their debut session.

Sevens Report Research's Tom Essaye said Thursday's sell-off primarily hit the tech sector, but added that "weakness is extending this morning and, like yesterday, pulling the broad market lower (although there was no new negative news overnight in the tech sector)."

Concerns over inflation, a potential U.S. government shutdown in December, and continued conflict in the Middle East have kept some investors on edge. That, coupled with a recent spate of tech outages—including the FAA outage last Friday and the Microsoft outage last Thursday—have created a sense of unease among tech investors.

AI investors were already feeling wary—as the burgeoning AI industry matures, it has yet to reach profitability. Anthropic reported $33.24 billion in revenue in the first three quarters of this year, but a $104 billion net loss for the same period.

One sector that is seemingly bucking the downward trend is real estate, which is performing better than the overall S&P 500. The S&P 500 Real Estate Sector is up 6.95% since the beginning of the year, while the overall S&P is up 3.15%.

Housing stocks—especially those of major homebuilders—have shown relative strength this month due to continued institutional investment from firms such as Berkshire Hathaway.

Despite headwinds for homebuilders, there are reasons for optimism following the midterm elections and the passage of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which passed with bipartisan support in July.

#5487. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. But you can start making a plan.The earlier you figure out what needs to be done, the more time you'll have to do it right. #5486. Medical AI startup Boltz raises $110M to speed up small molecule research

Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.

Bessemer led the Series A investment. Boltz stated on Wednesday that the fund was joined by a large group of new and returning backers. The consortium included Greycroft, Andreessen Horowitz, Amplify Partners, F-Prime Capital, Hummingbird and others.

Small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it. As a result, researchers start drug discovery projects by looking for molecules that have a high binding affinity with pathogens. They often review hundreds of thousands of candidate molecules per project. The process can take months and often costs millions of dollars.

Boltz offers an AI model called BoltzMol-1 that speeds up the workflow. It generates binding affinity data by reviewing only a few dozen, particularly promising molecules instead of the hundreds of thousands usually needed. The fewer molecules need to be studied, the less time the analysis takes.

Binding affinity evaluations don’t yield drug discoveries right away. Instead, they produce data points called small molecule hits. Those are essentially faint clues that help researchers pinpoint the area where they should focus their efforts.

Boltz staffers asked BoltzMol-1 to look for small molecule hits across 10 “challenging and therapeutically-relevant targets.” Targets are biological building blocks that play a role in disease processes. According to the company, the model found small molecule hits for six of the targets.

Scientists can adapt BoltzMol-1 to project-specific constraints. If a research team has access to a relatively limited number of compounds, it could configure the model to only consider small molecules that can be made from those compounds. When material procurement is not an obstacle, BoltzMol-1 evaluates a much larger number of candidates.

The company also offers a second model called BoltzProt-1. It can generate tens of thousands of protein designs based on data gleaned from small molecule hits. Additionally, BoltzProt-1 automatically reviews each protein to determine if it could be used to develop a new drug.

Usually, AI models evaluate protein designs based on rubrics that provide only an indirect view of their effectiveness. BoltzProt-1 uses more direct metrics. The company says that BoltzProt-1’s protein evaluation mechanism demonstrated “higher success” than several competing models during internal tests.

Boltz sells its algorithms via an application programming interface that is billed based on token usage. According to the company, customers’ token consumption has grown by a factor of 50 since BoltzMol-1 and BoltzProt-1 launched in June. Boltz counts six of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies as clients.

The company will use its new funding to grow its headcount and procure more computing infrastructure. The extra hardware should make it easier for Boltz to keep up with leading AI labs such as newly public Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group. Over the past year, both companies have introduced models that are highly adapted to biology research tasks.

Boltz has already started training a new generation of molecule design algorithms. The company says that they are “showing substantial improvements” over its current models.

#5485. A Fixer-Upper Could Be Your Path To Homeownership

When the homes you love keep landing outside your budget, it may be time to look at the ones other buyers skip.

A fixer-upper won’t be the right call for everyone. Plenty of buyers want a home that’s ready on move-in day. But homes that need some updating could get you in the door for a lot less.

More buyers are starting to realize it too. And Danielle Hale, Chief Economist at Realtor.com, explains why:

“Fixer-uppers give buyers a way to break into the housing market at a time when affordability is still stretched thin. For those with the vision. . . fixer-uppers provide both a starting point in the market and the chance to create a home that’s truly their own.”

If that sounds like you, here’s why a fixer-upper could be worth a closer look.

Because these homes need work, they tend to have a lower asking price up front. According to AmeriSave, fixer-uppers usually sell for 20% to 30% less than what they’re worth on the market.

Here’s what that could look like. KCM applied a 25% discount – the middle of that range – to the median home price from the National Association of Realtors (NAR). This is an example, not the average price of a fixer-upper. But it shows the savings could top $100,000 (see graph below):

That’s a big difference up front and it could be what gets you into a home today. And odds are you don’t have to tackle all the repairs at once – you can space them out over time as it works for you.

Just remember repair costs can add up quickly and eat into those savings if you don’t plan ahead. So, before you make an offer, get estimates from a contractor and set a repair budget you’re comfortable with. There are even some loan types designed to help pay for the work.

With a renovation loan, you can roll the cost of the work into your mortgage, so you don’t have to cover it all out of pocket once you move in. Here are a few options from FHA, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the VA (see visual below):

Each program has its own rules, and not every lender offers all of them. So, talk to a trusted lender to see which options are available to you and which make sense for how you plan to tackle updates and repairs over time.

Some cities even offer tax breaks to buyers who renovate a fixer-upper and raise its value. These programs vary by location, so check with your city or a tax professional to see what’s available where you want to live.

If you want to check for more information yourself, go to your local county or city official dot-gov website. Then, use the search bar and look for: [City or County Name] AND “home rehabilitation” OR “property tax incentive” OR “housing repair”

A local agent can also help you find fixer-uppers in the neighborhoods you have your heart set on.

If move-in-ready homes keep coming in over budget, a home that needs some TLC could be your way in. #5484. Their HOA Approved Their Backyard Fences. Now They’re Being Told To Tear Them Down.

Almost six years ago, Laura Burns-Sierra hired Home Depot to install a fence around her property in the Cypress Mill community near Tampa, FL. She submitted the plans to her homeowners association, received written approval and had the fence professionally installed.

Now, another organization says the fence has to come down.

"We couldn't do anything, any construction, any fences, nothing, without HOA approval," Burns-Sierra tells Realtor.com®. "I followed the procedures to the T."

Burns-Sierra is among a group of homeowners in the Sun City Center neighborhood caught in an unusual dispute between their HOA and the Cypress Mill Community Development District, or CDD. The latter says fences installed within drainage easements are interfering with its ability to maintain the community's stormwater infrastructure and now need to be removed.

The conflict has left residents facing hundreds or even thousands of dollars in unexpected expenses—and raises an important question for homeowners everywhere:

Is an HOA's written approval enough to protect you when another governing body has authority over your property?

At the center of the dispute is a distinction many homeowners may not realize exists.

An HOA generally oversees community standards, including architectural approvals, landscaping, and fence design. A CDD, meanwhile, is a special-purpose local government that can be responsible for infrastructure such as roads, drainage systems, and stormwater ponds.

In Cypress Mill, those responsibilities overlap on portions of homeowners' properties designated as drainage easements.

Jonathan Ellis, a Florida attorney experienced in HOA law—but is not involved in the dispute directly—tells Realtor.com that HOA approval doesn't necessarily authorize a homeowner to build within an easement.

"The HOA is telling you we don't have an objection to the fence," Ellis explains. "That doesn't mean now you can build the fence and don't worry about federal law, municipal law, or requirements of the CDD."

In other words, the HOA may have properly approved the fences under its own rules without resolving whether they complied with the district's separate requirements.

Ellis says the similar names of the HOA and CDD can add to the confusion, particularly for homeowners who aren't familiar with the distinction between the two organizations.

Burns-Sierra says the community's drainage ponds had been maintained for years without her fence becoming an issue.

She had her fence installed in May 2021, after receiving written approval from the HOA. About five years later, around Sept. 1, 2026, she and other residents received notice that the structure encroached on a drainage easement and would have to be removed by Sept. 18.

Burns-Sierra says maintenance contractors eventually arrived outside her home prepared to remove her fence and sought $625 for the work.

She refused, saying she wanted time to investigate the district's authority and understand why a fence that had been approved years earlier was suddenly unacceptable.

"I am not going to pay you no money to tear down my fence," she recalls telling the workers.

Neighbor Victor Abreu faced a similar predicament, although his circumstances were different.

Abreu tells Realtor.com that he received written HOA approval to install a gate connecting his home to an existing fence belonging to his neighbor.

When the CDD subsequently demanded that the structures obstructing the drainage easement be removed or relocated, Victor complied.

On Oct. 19 he paid a contractor $1,000 to install a new section of fencing closer to his house, losing part of a garden he estimates had cost approximately $1,500.

Victor says he believes communication broke down between the two organizations.

"I would blame both of them," he says. "I would say 50-50."

The Cypress Mill CDD maintains that the drainage easements are essential to the neighborhood's stormwater management system.

In a written response to Realtor.com, district counsel Whitney A. Sousa said the ponds and drainage areas are subject to environmental permits and oversight, including requirements administered by the Southwest Florida Water Management District.

The district has a legal responsibility to ensure contractors can inspect, maintain, and repair the system.

Mason Leon, the CDD’s on-site manager, tells Realtor.com that the fencing situation eventually made one pond inaccessible to the district's aquatic maintenance contractor through authorized access routes.

According to Sousa, the issue was brought before the CDD board on Aug. 13, 2026. A subsequent review identified 11 properties with fences or other structures encroaching on drainage easements.

The district determined that the encroachments must be removed to preserve access for maintenance equipment, vehicles, and contractors.

Importantly, Sousa acknowledged that better coordination between the HOA and CDD might have prevented the dispute.

"Ideally, these easements would have been identified during the HOA's review process, and the CDD would have been contacted before the fences were approved or installed," she wrote.

The district plans to work with the HOA to clarify approval requirements going forward.

For homeowners already affected, however, the district expects them to cover the costs of removing or relocating their fences.

Sousa said residents requesting additional time have received extensions. The district does not believe those expenses should be spread across the neighborhood through CDD assessments.

Although residents are understandably frustrated, Ellis cautions against assuming the HOA is legally responsible simply because it approved their projects.

"Normally it's the unit owner that's responsible," he says, referring to securing all necessary permissions before construction.

He explains that an HOA's approval generally addresses its own governing documents, including covenants, conditions, and restrictions. It doesn't eliminate the need to comply with separate drainage easements, building regulations, or other legal requirements.

Contractors may also have a role in identifying restrictions before beginning work.

Ellis notes that some communities permit fences within easements on the condition that homeowners remove them when access is needed.

The Cypress Mill CDD, however, has determined that all identified encroachments must be removed.

For homeowners like Burns-Sierra and Abreu, the distinction between an HOA's authority and the district's legal responsibilities has proved expensive.

The dispute offers a cautionary lesson for anyone purchasing a home or planning an outdoor renovation.

Ellis recommends determining which organizations have authority over a property before undertaking improvements.

"Homebuyers want to make sure when they're buying a home that they know of each of the entities that has a say over their property," he says.

That means checking recorded plats, property surveys, and easement documents before installing fences, patios, pools, or other improvements. Homeowners should also determine whether approvals are required from an HOA, CDD, municipality, county, or utility provider.

And when multiple organizations are involved, written approval from one shouldn't be mistaken for permission from all of them.

#5483. 3 Housing Questions That Might Come Up at Your Next Family Dinner

This time of year usually means more time spent with family and friends. And in recent years, when everyone gets together, the conversation has a way of drifting to housing.

Your uncle is sure home prices are about to crash. Your cousin heard foreclosures are surging. And someone across the table brings up the word “recession.”

If you’ve wondered about any of this yourself, that makes sense. There’s a lot of noise out there. So let’s look at what the data actually shows, so you’ll have real answers the next time it comes up.

Let’s start with your uncle’s crash prediction. The short answer is no. Experts project home prices will keep climbing nationally in 2027.

On average, forecasters expect prices to rise about 1.4% next year (see graph below). That’s slower than the big jumps of a few years ago, but it’s still growth, not a crash.

Prices are dipping in some markets, though. It just depends on where you live. Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), explains why:

“Price declines are occurring mainly in southern states, where there has been robust new home construction in recent years. Given the region’s faster job growth, these price drops should be viewed as temporary and as a second-chance opportunity for those previously priced out of the market.”

So, the dips that are fueling all the social media chatter are limited to select areas, and experts think they’ll be short-lived. It doesn’t mean a crash is looming.

If you’re thinking about moving, look at the numbers for your area.

Then your cousin chimes in about foreclosures. They’ve ticked up lately, but here’s some important context. That’s compared to very low levels. They’re still below where they were before the pandemic, according to ATTOM.

So, why doesn’t today look like 2008? Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . we have had many recessions post-WWII but only one foreclosure crisis. That foreclosure crisis started with a massive credit boom from 2002-2005, and then a credit bust. . . none of that is happening now . . .“

Today’s homeowners also have something a lot of people didn’t have back then – equity. In every state, the average homeowner with a mortgage has more than $100,000 of it, according to Cotality (see map below):

If a homeowner hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house instead of facing foreclosure.

While someone in your family may be convinced a recession is coming, experts don’t agree. The average forecast from The Wall Street Journal’s survey of economists puts the odds at about 24%, so most experts aren’t expecting one. And that’s a good thing.

But even if one hits, history shows a recession doesn’t mean home prices will automatically fall. In 5 of the last 6 recessions, prices actually went up, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) (see graph below):

The one exception was 2008, the only one of these recessions that started in the housing market itself.

So, the next time your uncle predicts a crash or your cousin brings up 2008, you’ll know prices aren’t crashing, foreclosures are still low, and a recession doesn’t automatically spell trouble for housing. If a move in 2027 is on your mind, connect with a local real estate agent to look at what prices are doing in your neighborhood so you can plan with real local numbers, not scary headlines.

#5482. 3 Things Sellers Need To Know About Pricing Today

If you’re getting ready to sell your house, you’ve probably heard how important it is to price it right. And that’s especially true right now.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from and they’re feeling pinched by today’s mortgage rates. That makes them more selective. And that means having the right pricing strategy matters more than ever.

That starts with understanding these three things. Because, with the right approach, you can still put your house in a great position to sell.

It’s natural to look at what your neighbor’s house sold for and think yours should sell for something similar. And those comparable sales (or comps) absolutely matter. But they only tell part of the story. Here’s why.

Buyers aren’t shopping against what sold three or even six months ago. They’re comparing your house to what’s available right now.

That’s why your agent will look at more than just recent sales. They’ll also consider the houses currently for sale, what’s going under contract, and how your house stacks up against those options to find the right price for your house.

The goal isn’t necessarily to price lower than everyone else. It’s to make sure buyers see the value in choosing your house over the competition.

As Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com explains:

“Pricing to today’s demand is helping homes move and keeping more transactions alive in a high-rate environment.”

Understanding how your house compares to what’s available today can help you feel more confident in your asking price.

Getting your asking price right puts you in a stronger position from the start. But when an offer comes in, remember that price is only one part of the equation.

Today’s buyers may still negotiate on things like money toward closing costs or repairs, even when a house is priced well – and that’s not necessarily a commentary on your price, it’s just the norm for negotiation in today’s market.

According to Redfin, 44.7% of home sales involve seller concessions. That’s just under half. And 15.8% had both a price reduction and a concession.

Now, that doesn’t mean you have to agree to everything a buyer asks for. But sometimes offering a closing-cost credit or helping with a mortgage rate buydown could be what seals the deal. Other times, holding firm is the better move. Your agent will help you decide.

The best advice? Look at the whole offer, including what you’ll actually walk away with, to decide what’s right for you.

Even with a competitive price, some houses take longer to sell than others. And if yours isn’t getting the attention or offers you expected, that doesn’t mean your sale is off track. It just means it’s time to take a closer look at what’s happening.

Your agent can help you use buyer feedback and local market activity to figure out what adjustments, if any, could make a difference.

Are buyers seeing your listing online but not scheduling showings? Maybe the photos or presentation aren’t doing your house justice.

Are people touring but not making offers? It could be the condition, the price, or how your house compares to others they’ve seen.

And if buyers are making offers, but the terms aren’t working for you, that may call for a different negotiation strategy altogether.

While you may worry that means you have to drop your price, that’s not always true. A price cut can help, but only if it addresses what’s keeping buyers from making a move.

That’s why feedback, local competition, and an agent who knows how to interpret both are so important.

Selling successfully today isn't about finding one magic number and hoping everything falls into place. It's about starting with a competitive price, understanding what buyers expect, and being willing to adjust your strategy when needed.Want to know what it'll take to sell your house in today's market? #5481. Intuit sells Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68B, less than a third of what it paid

Financial software company Intuit Inc. today announced that it has agreed to sell its Mailchimp email marketing business to Italian technology holding company Bending Spoons S.p.A. for about $3.68 billion.

Coming five years after Intuit agreed to acquire Mailchimp for $12 billion, the sale price is less than a third of what the company paid. The 2021 purchase was the largest in Intuit’s history at the time.

Although Bending Spoons describes the transaction as all-cash, Intuit will reinvest $368 million of its proceeds in newly issued Bending Spoons shares. That leaves Intuit with $3.31 billion in cash from the sale, according to the companies. Included in the deal is The Rocket Science Group LLC, the legal entity behind Mailchimp. Closing is expected in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.

Selling Mailchimp is said to sharpen Intuit’s focus on the artificial intelligence-native tools it has built to help businesses win new customers, manage their pipeline and grow. Once the deal closes, Intuit intends to use the cash proceeds to buy back its own shares before the end of fiscal 2027.

Jack Tam, a senior vice president at Intuit, said the company is confident Bending Spoons “will lead Mailchimp to continued success in this next chapter.”

Growth at Mailchimp has stalled in recent quarters. Revenue from the business fell 1% to $313 million in the quarter ended Oct. 31. Intuit’s full-year guidance has Mailchimp revenue coming in flat to down 1%. In November 2024, Chief Financial Officer Sandeep Aujla told analysts that Intuit was seeing higher churn from smaller Mailchimp customers.

“Mailchimp is a powerful brand, built over two decades of reshaping the email marketing category and redefining how companies grow their audiences,” said Luca Ferrari, co-founder and chief executive of Bending Spoons. “We’re honored to welcome it to Bending Spoons and excited about what we can accomplish together.”

Ferrari added that Bending Spoons plans to invest substantially in Mailchimp after closing. According to Bending Spoons, the transformation of a business it acquires is typically deep, entailing reorganized teams, overhauled technology and redesigned user interfaces.

Founded in 2013, Bending Spoons has built a portfolio of digital businesses that includes AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Tractive, Vimeo and WeTransfer. Since listing on the Nasdaq in July, the company has also completed acquisitions of Airtable Inc. for $1.285 billion and whiteboard platform Miro for $1.355 billion.

Intuit announced the sale alongside its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results. For the quarter, it reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.91, up 56% from $1.87 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $4.35 billion, up 12% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting adjusted earnings of $2.70 per share on revenue of $4.31 billion.

For its fiscal second quarter, Intuit expects adjusted earnings per share of $3.17 to $3.22 on revenue of $4.93 billion to $4.95 billion. Intuit lowered its full-year revenue guidance to between $23.08 billion and $23.37 billion.

Behind the cut is Credit Karma, the company’s personal finance and credit score service, which is now forecast to grow 3% to 7% this fiscal year, down from 11% to 13% previously. Intuit reiterated its full-year adjusted earnings guidance of $22.88 to $23.12 per share. None of the guidance includes the effect of the Mailchimp sale.

Intuit shares fell more than 10% in after-hours trading.
