#5438. Inside the $7 Million Historic Georgia Estate Straight Out of ‘Practical Magic’

Tucked away along Pine Log Creek in Fairmount, GA, sits a nearly 71-acre historic estate that feels less like a residential listing and more like a Hollywood set.

Known as Yarborough Mill, the $7 million property features a restored late-1800s Queen Anne Victorian—a 4,500-square-foot former grist mill and plenty of period charm.

"It looks like something that belongs in 'Practical Magic'," says listing agent Logan Fitts with Mountain Sotheby's International Realty. “It is definitely the most historic property I've had the chance to work with, and with that it is just so unique.”

The property has several structures, but the highlights are the former grist mill and a late 1800s Queen Anne Victorian.

“Everything's original, but it's all been restored because it was not in perfect condition when [the sellers] bought it. It's a complete restore project and everything is true to period,” Fitts explains.

“The exterior of the main house, the colors she chose, the roof tiles, the architecture, and the landscaping. Everything there was intentional.”

The Victorian home has some Georgian features and has five bedrooms and three full bathrooms.

“It looks like it could be in The Gilded Age or something like that. There are a total of eight fireplaces in the house. There's parlors, there's dens and small living rooms, and little nooks and crannies throughout the house,” he says, adding the kitchen is updated appliance-wise, but still has character.

“[There are] stained glass windows throughout, and pressed tin ceilings throughout. It’s insanely intricate.”

But it’s another room that caught Fitts’ eye.

“They have an old solarium on the lower level that they turned into the coolest bathroom that I've ever seen,” he says.

“You have to be in there to really see it. If you’re entertaining in the house, anyone what visits or goes to that bathroom is just totally wowed. It just it feels like you're in a solarium, but it is a bathroom.”

This home has been the seller’s primary residence, with a three-bedroom and three-bathroom cottage for guests and others, especially during events. The seller has operated a small wedding business on the property.

“She's done it herself. It has been more of a passion for her. It's a wedding venue for small groups and the guest cottage is used as a bridal suite.”

The groom’s suite and game area are above the barn, and the 4,500-square foot former grist mill is the event space.

Fitts says most of the wedding ceremonies happen along the waterfront along Pine Log Creek, which creates a stunning backdrop.

“You pull up to a gate and [after] the gate opens, you go down this long winding driveway with rows of trees and the river that winds through the entire property to your right,” he explains. “Then you turn in up the bluff a little bit, and then it kind of opens up to what you would see in the olden days, like its own little village town.”

An old general store and smokehouse are also on the property. Fitts says the sellers saw a for sale listing in the newspaper at least 15 years ago, drove up to see it, fell in love with it, and then restored it.

“I was impressed with the story behind it [and] the amount of love that went into owning the property,” he says, adding there are two kinds of buyers who would be perfect for this estate.

“It could be a visionary entrepreneur that really wants to lean into making this a hospitality-based venue, spa, bed and breakfast, a true sanctuary. There's potential for growth,” Fitts explains, adding the buyer could build other structures throughout the orchard and make the main home a gathering space.

“It could be somebody's true entrepreneurial dream or it could just be someone that truly loves historical properties that wants to preserve what is there, love it with their family or for themselves, and just cherish it for what it is.”

#5437. Enterprise AI hits a wall of power and cooling, not GPU supply

Enterprises racing to build AI factories and push edge inference into the field are learning that buying graphics processing units is the easy part. Power, cooling and network throughput now decide whether those costly systems produce intelligence or sit idle.

Those physical limits shaped much of the high-performance computing and AI conversation at SC26, where commercial AI infrastructure increasingly shares the floor with scientific computing. Rack densities that once topped out at about 10 kilowatts are now on a path toward a megawatt, a step change that forces enterprises to look both above and below the traditional network, storage and compute layers, according to Jack Hogan (pictured), senior vice president of advanced growth technologies at SHI International Corp.

“When we look at the full stack, we recognize that customers are getting tripped up. They can go get the GPUs, but they can’t power them. They can’t cool them,” Hogan said. “These are not cheap systems either. Procuring the infrastructure is just the start.”

Hogan spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed edge inference and how power, networking, model choice and business outcomes are reshaping the way enterprises build and run AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)

The economics of AI infrastructure are shifting along with the hardware. Enterprises once sized deployments by the rack unit or the rack, but entire data centers now operate as a single system with shared memory, and every GPU must be kept fed to justify its cost. That change has altered how SHI measures success, Hogan explained.

“Now we’re talking about row and now data center scale. … We’re measuring that now in megawatts,” Hogan said. “So the megawatt now starts to become a measurement that people start to grasp and understand. How many flops can you get through that megawatt? How fast can you process your tokens?”

SHI’s role spans the full life cycle of these systems. Drawing on 37 years in the industry, the company builds customized racks in its integration facilities around the globe and runs pre-site assessments so systems can be powered on as soon as they arrive. In a recent New Jersey project, SHI is hosting and operating the customer’s system in its own data center. Location matters at the edge, too, where workloads such as video input generate data that must be processed in place, Hogan noted.

“You can’t backhaul that. The networks are not necessarily the right way to move that,” Hogan said. “We’re creating the scenario of both the mega hyperscaler as well as the edge inference and be able to tie those two things together.”

Busy GPUs are not necessarily productive ones. SHI starts every engagement by asking customers what they are trying to achieve, then works backward to the right model, whether that means frontier intelligence or a small language model running on an edge device. Silicon follows the same logic, with GPUs, newer CPUs, inference-specific chips and neural processing units validated in the company’s AI and Cyber Lab.

“It’s not about the cost of the token or reducing the number of tokens or even finding cheaper tokens. It’s about optimizing and ensuring that those tokens are turning into business value,” Hogan said.

#5436. Inside a Secluded Cabin Hidden Right Beneath Big Sur’s Iconic Landmark

A secluded retreat tucked beneath one of California’s most photographed landmarks in Big Sur has come on the market for $3.65 million.

The home at 39320 Coast Road sits in Bixby Canyon and is one of only seven residences behind a private gate.

“Millions recognize Bixby Bridge, yet very few will ever experience the landscape beneath it,” says listing agent Michael Hornig of the Strock Team at eXp Realty.

The canyon also comes with a literary history: In 1960, Jack Kerouac retreated to a cabin here owned by Lawrence Ferlinghetti, the poet and co-founder of City Lights Bookstore. His time in the canyon formed the basis for his 1962 novel, “Big Sur.” While this is not the original Kerouac cabin, it shares the same setting.

According to Hornig, the canyon has also been home to the film director Sam Peckinpah and the Disney illustrator Ron Dias.

“There’s an extraordinary feeling about this canyon,” Hornig says. “You’re surrounded by a landscape that inspired some of America’s most influential writers, and remarkably, much of that atmosphere of solitude and wilderness remains intact today.”

Built in 1984, the single-level home has three bedrooms, two full bathrooms, and 1,489 square feet of living space. Vaulted, open-beam ceilings, hardwood floors, and three wood-burning stoves characterize the interiors, as do large windows that frame the surrounding redwoods. A wraparound porch overlooks the forest.

“Luxury doesn’t always have to be expressed through scale or elaborate architecture,” Hornig says. “Here, the luxury is the relationship between the home and its surroundings.”

The property covers two parcels: a 0.79-acre residential lot and an adjacent 0.33-acre creekside lot. It is move-in ready, with a private well, septic system, and electricity. There is also a fenced backyard, storage shed, pasture space and parking for 10 vehicles, including EV charging.

Owners share access to a privately held canyon enclave of more than 140 acres. There, a creekside trail winds through redwoods and ferns to a secluded beach beneath the bridge.

“You can walk from your front door through a redwood forest, follow the creek toward the Pacific, and emerge beneath one of the most recognizable bridges in the world,” Hornig says.

Next to the property, Brazil Ranch adds about 1,200 acres of U.S. Forest Service land for hiking, hunting, and recreation. The historic Old Coast Road offers miles of biking, horseback riding, and backcountry exploration. Highway 1 is about five minutes away. Carmel, Monterey, and Big Sur’s restaurants and state parks are about 20 minutes away.

“To me, the greatest luxury here is the privilege of belonging to a landscape that most people will only ever admire from a distance,” Hornig says. "It's this contrast between one of California’s most recognizable landmarks and the hidden residential community beneath it."

#5435. Etherscan Warns of Support System Access Attempts as Security Scares Hit Crypto and Banks

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning users after detecting attempts to gain unauthorized access to its customer support system. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

The warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

Meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

So what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

Etherscan disclosed earlier today that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The company is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

Security Notice: Reminder Regarding Etherscan Support CommunicationsEarlier today, we detected attempts to gain unauthorized access to our customer support and ticketing system (Freshworks).We are currently investigating the situation and taking precautionary measures.In…

The concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal users’ crypto and money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

But Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and said it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

Crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

Lighter said its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

Another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

These incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

Traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank said customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

Deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Deutsche Bank said security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Still, the leak could have wider geopolitical repercussions.

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

The Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto company.

Neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

Crypto users have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan investigating attempted unauthorized access, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies dealing with security incidents.

#5434. Anthropic goes public, but is it too late to save the AI trade?

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

Anthropic came through with its initial public offering Thursday, but did it just signal a top in the AI trade?

The artificial intelligence model maker’s IPO went almost picture-perfectly, really, producing a 17% pop that wasn’t so high that it left an excessive amount of money on the table but high enough to call it a success. But it seemed to take some of the air out of AI stocks. Continued worries over AI spending and prospects, as well as factors such as a likely interest-rate hike, dragged down the entire market, including other AI names from Google, Microsoft and Meta to AMD, Broadcom and Nvidia. Asian stocks too.

And on Friday it got even worse, as the Nasdaq crashed 5.6%. Bye-bye, $4 trillion. No doubt Anthropic stock will be at least as volatile as other AI stocks — today it fell 9% — but it can live with that alongside the more than $90 billion now in its bank account. Now all eyes turn to OpenAI, which finds itself chasing after Anthropic in more ways than one, with plans to go public sometime in next year.

Nvidia posted its usual better-than-expected earnings this week, which didn’t help its stock much but indicates, along with interim CEO Colette Kress’ bullish comments during the earnings call, that it’s going to be fine for some time to come in disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang’s absence.

Meantime, Huang said he’s open to returning — but that’s not only appallingly premature at best, the board appears adamant it’s not going to happen. The supposed friends clamoring for his return are just reinforcing their selfish, clueless nature, the attitude that has plunged tech into such low esteem that auto salespeople and journalists have more company now. Maybe those guys on X (always guys) approve of behavior like this.

What’s with all the outages all over the place? That’s what everyone’s asking, and we looked into what’s behind them all. It doesn’t seem to be the obvious thing — cybersecurity attacks — or really any single cause. Perhaps it’s a lot of 20th century technologies that just aren’t ready for the AI-driven speed of the 21st century, making everything less reliable. Or: All those AI-driven fixes to vulnerabilities are getting done so fast they’re breaking things along the way. Still, is it only a coincidence that the U.S. cyber director just got canned this week?

Palo Alto Networks remains one of the most acquisitive cybersecurity companies out there, once again laying out a tidy sum this week, buying AI startup Applied Compute $4.5 billion. It’s a sure bet consolidation will accelerate as AI enables more and much faster attacks. Indeed, late Friday came a report that an equally acquisitive CrowdStrike is looking to buy Zscaler, which has been a consistent acquirer itself.

Next week’s significant earnings reports include Dell, HP, Nutanix, Workday and Zoom. And then we can all take a brief respite for Thanksgiving before gearing up for AWS re:Invent the following week in Las Vegas, with its blizzard of news. SiliconANGLE, theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with news, analysis and interviews.

#5433. Four Open Real Estate Founding CEOs, CMLS CEO to Kick Off RISMedia’s 7th Annual Rocking in the New Year

From massive consolidation to pre-marketing and private listing policies to MLS lawsuits, to say 2026 was a tumultuous year in real estate is an understatement.

One of the most notable developments in the industry came late in the year–the launch of Open Real Estate (OpenRE), a national data-sharing platform that aims to streamline listing data distribution. Founded by the CEOs of AGNT (parent company of eXp Realty and NextHome), HomeServices of America, Keller Williams and Real REMAX Group, the platform has grown to include four additional participating members and has received letters of support from another 826 firms nationwide ahead of its official launch in 2027.

OpenRE’s founding CEOs–Leo Pareja, Chris Kelly, Chris Czarnecki and Tamir Polig–are set to take the virtual stage at RISMedia’s 7th Annual Real Estate’s Rocking in the New Year, to discuss the vision behind their ambitious collaboration and detail why the pledge to keep housing markets open, transparent and accessible is especially critical right now.

The all-day virtual event, titled “Own Your Success in 2027,” will take place on Thursday, Jan. 7 from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. EST. Registration is open and available here. The event is free for RISMedia Premier members.

The conversation will also explore the importance of data distribution, consumer choice and complementary rulemaking amid a “deteriorating” public marketplace.

Keynote: Buckle Up! The Road Ahead in 2027

Immediately following the kickoff session, Jessie Edgerton, CEO of the Council of Multiple Listing Services (CMLS), will share her views on the Open Real Estate discussion and deliver this year’s keynote address, “Buckle Up! The Road Ahead in 2027. The keynote theme centers around the industry’s rapidly evolving landscape, with legal challenges, regulatory changes and emerging issues poised to shape the year ahead. Edgerton will talk about what may be coming around the corner, and which developments could have the greatest impact on the business of real estate.

RISMedia’s 7th Annual Rocking in the New Year virtual conference brings together the industry’s brightest minds, freshest ideas and most innovative strategies to help you take control, win more business and carve your own path to success in 2027. This year 50 industry leaders will be speaking in 15 sessions over a range of timely topics. Here are just some of the sessions on deck:

–Inside the Situation Room: How Brokers Are Strategizing for 2027 with Wendy Forsythe, Chief Operating Officer, eXp Realty; and Michele Harrington, CEO, First Team Real Estate

–Economic Outlook 2027: The Potential Paths for the Economy and How to Prepare with Dr. Lisa Sturtevant, chief economist, Bright MLS

–Building the AI Coach: How Agentic AI Is Changing Real Estate with Mel Robbins, digital marketing manager, Northrop Realty; Creig Northrop, CEO and founder, Northrop Realty; Todd Denman, founder and principal Realtor®, eXp Realty-The Denman Group; and Marki Lemons Ryhal, chief artificial intelligence officer (CAIO), ReMarkiTable, LLC

–Surviving—and Thriving—Amid Consolidation with Christina Pappas, president, The Keyes Company/Illustrated Properties; Dean deTonnancourt, broker/owner and CEO, REMAX Revolution; and Sandra Rathe, broker associate, speaker, coach, author, The Sandra Rathe Team, Real Broker, LLC

#5432. Rare 25-Foot-Wide Carnegie Hill Townhouse With a Private Carriage House Lists for $11.95 Million

A 25-foot-wide townhouse with a carriage house has just hit the market for $11.95 million in Manhattan’s Carnegie Hill.

Built in 1899, the five-bedroom residence underwent a “no-expense-spared” reconstruction and features 13 newly renovated rooms, each with individually zoned heating and cooling.

“It is certainly very rare for a listing like this townhouse with a carriage house to come on the market in uptown Manhattan,” said listing agent Daniella G. Schlisser of Brown Harris Stevens. “I don’t recall ever seeing something like this here.”

The 7,700-square-foot interior was entirely gutted and rebuilt with new structural steel, plumbing, electrical, and commercial-grade mechanical systems.

“It has incredible sun and light, which is incredibly unusual for a townhouse,” Schlisser said. “The home is flooded with direct sunlight facing the back and it also gets sun to the north in the front.”

The six-story dwelling features a garden level that leads to a limestone gallery with custom paneling. There is a separately accessed commercial space offering “continued retail or office use” that could also be transformed into additional living space. French doors open to a bluestone-decked garden with a built-in grill.

“There is a phenomenal amount of space and light, and being a 25-foot-wide townhouse is also rare,” she noted.

A parlor level boasts a living room with a fireplace and herringbone floors. The nearby formal dining room was designed for grand-scale entertaining. Also on this level is a garden-facing eat-in kitchen with a breakfast bar, granite countertops, custom cabinetry, and high-end appliances.

The third floor has two en-suite bedrooms and a den with coffered ceilings, a wood-burning fireplace, and access to a private terrace overlooking the carriage house.

Two king-sized bedroom suites with custom "study" areas are on the fourth floor.

A lavish primary suite spans the entire fifth floor. It features a south-facing sitting room that opens to a private terrace, a windowed dressing room, and a spa-inspired bathroom with a skylight, soaking tub, and a double vanity.

The sixth floor boasts a “skylit” fitness and wellness room along with a roof terrace “awaiting the next owner’s finishing touch.”

Schlisser said every prospective buyer she has shown the home to is interested in living there full-time.

“Carnegie Hill is a wonderful neighborhood,” she said. “Culturally and educationally, everything is there and the most frequented museums are there as well as some of the best private schools in Manhattan.”

The detached carriage house has cathedral ceilings, vertical-grain Douglas fir paneling, and a sleeping loft that could be used for guest accommodations or additional recreation space.

“I think the next buyer will be someone who is looking for space and proximity to schools,” Schlisser added. “The style is all new but very much a pre-war style. Everything has been done with incredible care. It’s really beautiful.”

#5431. Mortgage Mix: MBA Petitions Senators for ‘Take Care of America’s Veterans Act’ Changes; Newrez Widens Inventory

Editor’s Note: The Mortgage Mix is RISMedia’s highlight reel of need-to-know mortgage-industry happenings. Watch for it every other Friday afternoon.

The numbers: Despite mortgage rates’ downward trend for the past few weeks, the latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® reveals that the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage increased sharply to 7.28%, up seven basis points from the previous survey’s result of 7.11%.

The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage also increased to 6.66%, up from last week’s 6.45%. Both the 30-year and 15-year rates are more than a full percentage point higher than those from the same period last year.

What does this mean: Economists generally attributed the spike in rates to inflation-related pressures, stemming from global conflicts and the rise in overall prices caused by it.

Realtor.com® Senior Economist Anthony Smith referenced the October Consumer Price Index (CPI) report as his basis for why the market expects another rate hike in the upcoming Federal Reserve December meeting.

“The October CPI report came in above expectations on both the headline and core measures, cementing market expectations for a December rate hike and giving the 10-year little room to fall,” he said.

The CPI report saw an all-items index increase of 0.4%, which is a slight decrease from September’s increase of 0.6%, but was still described as “hotter than expected,” by Navy Federal Chief Economist Heather Long.

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh kept his cards close to his chest at his Nov. 16 speech and did not reveal whether a rate hike is on the table, but Fed Governor Michelle Bowman did note her disappointment at the central bank’s progress towards lowering inflation.

She stated that inflation has “proven to be more persistent than (she) had anticipated,” and pointed to the Middle East conflict, Trump Administration-imposed tariffs and “AI-related price pressures” as the main cause, in her speech to the Council on Foreign Relations.

How is the market reacting: As a byproduct of the spike in mortgage rates, the volume of mortgage applications decreased in the latest Market Composite Index from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA).

The MBA reported that mortgage application activity decreased 2.3% on a seasonally adjusted basis, with MBA Vice President and Deputy Chief Economist, Joel Kan emphasizing that “renewed affordability challenges from elevated mortgage rates have pushed prospective homebuyers to the sidelines.”

Overall, the third quarter of 2026 saw a significant decline in mortgage and lending activity. ATTOM reported that purchase and refinance mortgage originations were down 12% in Q3, and were down 15% compared to last year’s data.

MBA writes to Congress: On Nov. 18, the MBA sent a letter to four members of the Senate—John Thune, Jerry Moran, Charles Schumer and Richard Blumenthal—in the hopes of altering the “Take Care of America’s Veterans Act,” after its passing in the House of Representatives, and prior to the Senate’s vote on the bill.

Also known as H.R. 9237, the act is a legislative package that includes more than 60 proposals to modify compensation programs for veterans, including extending entitlements to remarried surviving spouses and establishing a supplemental monthly allowance for certain disabled veterans.

The MBA noted in its letter that they “fully support the laudable goals of this legislation” but that it cannot fully support the bill in its current form, specifically pointing out the VA Home Loan program funding fee increases.

Within the Veteran’s Act, it includes modifications to the VA Home Loan Program that would turn the Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan (IRRRL) from 0.50% to 1.42%, and turn loan assumption from 0.50% into 1.00%.

“The funding fee offsets in (The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act), if enacted, would have an inverse and negative impact on veteran homeowners and homebuyers (and other eligible servicemembers) who rely on their earned VA Home Loan benefit to achieve the American Dream of homeownership,” the MBA stated.

Newrez launches Personal Loans: The residential mortgage lender and servicer, Newrez, now offers Personal Loans for all eligible Newrez homeowners.

According to a release, Newrez Personal Loans are available through a partnership with Upgrade—a financial technology company that offers consumer credit products—and are issued by Upgrade’s bank partner, Cross River Bank.

“Our relationship with homeowners doesn’t begin and end with a mortgage,” Newrez CCO Leslie Gillin stated.

The release notes that the new offer expands the financial tools available to eligible Newrez homeowners, providing access to funds for a variety of financial needs. These include debt consolidation, home improvements and unexpected expenses.

Rental demand rises: Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report revealed that demand for single-family homes has risen.

Within the report, consumers noted that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly cost of owning a home, prior to saving for a down payment. “For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.”

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5430. This Renovated 1949 Santa Monica Home Looks Like a Movie Set—And It Just Hit the Market for $6.9 Million

A five-bedroom modern retreat nestled on a tree-lined street in Santa Monica, CA has just hit the market for $6,898,000.

Built in 1949, the 4,746-square-foot residence was renovated in 2022 and now features a sun-soaked open floor plan with curated finishes, designer lighting, and walls of windows.

“I love all of the light that comes into the home,” said listing agent Shelton Wilder of Christie’s International Real Estate Southern California. “It has beautiful skylights throughout and it’s located on the side of the street that gets so much natural sunlight. It looks like a movie set.”

Designed for grand-scale entertaining and everyday living, the thoughtful layout offers a lavish primary sanctuary separate from a second-story guest wing that could also be used for extended family.

“The primary suite is so private and very luxurious,” Wilder noted. “It was the primary residence for the sellers, who have owned it for five years. I think the next buyer will use it as a primary as well. It was so special for the sellers who have three kids. It could also be someone with older kids who want to stay there while visiting.”

A sleek chef’s kitchen has two refrigerators, double ovens, custom cabinetry, a breakfast bar, and a built-in coffee machine. Glass doors from the dining area open to the private backyard with an outdoor shower and a brand-new heated pool and spa.

Architectural details include a sunken sitting room with built-in seating, a living room with a fireplace, and a primary suite with access to two offices, one of which opens to a rooftop deck designed for soaking in the sweeping canyon views.

“Santa Monica Canyon is a magical place to live,” she said. “You can walk to the beach; Montana Avenue is very close for shopping and restaurants; and Canyon Elementary School is just a few minutes away as well.”

A bonus playroom could double as a family room, and a commercial-grade fitness center occupies the lower level.

“It’s very rare for a house like this with this amount of square footage, two offices, a pool, and a gym to come up in this area,” Wilder added.

#5429. Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

Agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it. Open-source efforts such as Upbound Inc.’s Modelplane route inference across clouds, but many enterprises want the models on hardware they control.

That shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure. Oxide Computer Co., which raised $445 million in October to expand rack production, built its business on the idea that enterprises at scale will want to own their computers, according to Bryan Cantrill (pictured), co-founder and chief technology officer at Oxide.

“Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it. You get to a certain scale, as it turns out, you want to own your own computer,” Cantrill said.

Cantrill spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed renting versus owning compute, why agentic workloads are moving on-prem and multi-tenancy for isolating those workloads.

Agentic workloads are driving an explosion in compute demand, and much of it is CPU-heavy work that enterprises would rather own than rent. Economics remains the main reason to bring it in-house, but where models live is a close second, Cantrill explained. That makes the model plane as much a data governance decision as an infrastructure one.

“There is a real enterprise drive towards open-weight models, and I think you’re going to see more and more of that as people want to run the models on-prem and allow their data to not actually leave,” Cantrill said.

Security is the other half. Oxide stripped the UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controller out of its rack to shrink the attack surface, and built public cloud-grade multi-tenancy in from the start. Those early design choices give enterprises a perimeter for isolating agentic workloads, according to Cantrill.

“I think multi-tenancy means you’ve got potentially adversarial tenants that are going to be on the same resource,” Cantrill said. “They’re going to be sharing the same computer, sharing the same network, and they need to do that … without violating the confidentiality, without breaching one another.”

The same racks can take on legacy virtualization workloads from customers unhappy with pricing changes at Broadcom Inc.’s VMware business. That lets enterprises run old and new applications on one general-purpose platform, Cantrill noted.

“You want all that flexibility that you get from elastic compute, but you need it for economic reasons, security reasons, latency reasons,” Cantrill said of the case for on-premises cloud computing. “You need it in your own data center. You want to control your fate.”

#5428. President Woodrow Wilson’s Historic Princeton Home Lists for $5.85 Million After a 7-Year Restoration

The home where Woodrow Wilson lives as a professor before becoming president has hit the market in Princeton, NJ for $5.85 million.

The Tudor Revival at 82 Library Place was built in 1896 for Wilson and he lived there with his wife, Ellen, and their three children until 1902, when he became president of Princeton University and moved on campus.

The home was first listed in May 2025 for $6.5 million.

“Wilson and his wife had a lot of input in the design and finishes chosen for the home, which included double stained-glass doors from the Sears catalog,” says listing agent Barbara Blackwell of Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty.

The estate is one of only two working homes in the U.S. designed and built by a president, the other being Monticello, according to the listing.

Blackwell says the house has had 19 owners since the Wilsons, including Princeton University itself, which used the home as faculty housing during the Great Depression.

The current owners spent seven years restoring the property with architect Ron Berlin and Baxter Construction. The award-winning project brought back the original beams and woodwork and re-glassed the leaded windows. It also gave the home a distinct sense of presidential charm, making it easy to imagine Wilson tucked among its interiors.

The work also restored the stucco and timber exterior, added a cedar shake roof and a generator, and updated all mechanical systems.

The three-story home includes seven bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. Wilson once taught students in the spacious foyer, which opens to a wood-paneled library the current owners added. Stained-glass pocket doors lead to a dining room with a commissioned mural of campus landmarks.

The kitchen pairs restored original cabinetry with new matching pieces. It also has a copper drainboard sink, a working dumbwaiter, and a double Wolf range. Nearby, a new glass-roofed sunroom with a wet bar overlooks the grounds.

“The sunroom is a perfect blends interior and exterior with views of the gardens and flowering trees,” Blackwell says.

Of the four bedrooms on the second floor, one is a soundproofed primary suite with a coffee bar and a radiant-heated marble bathroom that opens onto a balcony. The skylit third floor contains three more bedrooms, a bathroom, laundry and a cedar walk-in closet.

Outside, the recently redesigned gardens surround two patios, a fountain and a koi pond. The 0.74-acre lot also has a circular driveway lined with boxwoods, an office in a former porte cochere and a restored, oversized two-car garage in the same Tudor style as the house.

The property is in Princeton’s Western Section and backs up to the current home of the university’s president. Nassau Street’s shops and restaurants are a short walk away.

“This home represents a substantial piece of history with all the modern conveniences of a new home,” Blackwell says. The owner’s collection of Wilson books and memorabilia can be bought separately.

#5427. Consumer Sentiment Jumps After Election Results

While the economy and housing still face hurdles, consumers are feeling more confident following November’s election results, according to the latest Index of Consumer Sentiment from the University of Michigan.

Consumer sentiment took a leap upward, climbing 7.3% to 51.5 in November due to “substantial post-election gains in both short- and long-run expected business conditions,” as noted by Surveys of Consumers Director Joanne Hsu. Responses were collected from Oct. 20 through Nov. 16.

“Consumers appear to anticipate potential changes to public policy under a divided government to come,” continued Hsu. “Accordingly, the expectations index surged for independents, who swung to the left in the midterms, and increased more moderately for Democrats. Expectations fell for Republicans, who may not favor a slowdown of the White House policy agenda.”

Voters have expressed expectations for the “blue wave” that swept the election to make meaningful changes when it comes to inflation and housing affordability, an undertaking that many Democrats who ran (and won) included in their campaign promises.

Sentiment is also slightly higher (1%) from one year ago, when it was at 51. Hsu noted, though, that sentiment is still “subdued” by 9% from where it was in February, prior to the start of the conflict in Iran.

The index of Current Economic Conditions also saw a monthly boost of 5.8% to 49.4, but was still down 3.3% year-over-year.

Hsu noted that some respite in gas prices during the survey period improved finances for low- and middle-wealth consumers, but “those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline in personal finances, consistent with continued AI-related agitation in stock markets.”

The forward-looking Index of Consumer Expectations saw the largest monthly leap, shooting up 8.4% to 52.9. Year-over-year, the index is up 3.7%.

Median year-ahead inflation expectations shifted downward from 4.7% last month to 3.7% this month, but remained above the 3.4% recorded in February, pre-Iranian conflict. Long-run inflation expectations also decreased slightly, from 3.5% in October to 3.3%. These expectations, however, remained above the 2.8% to 3.2% range seen back in 2024.

Hsu noted that despite consumer expectations “softening,” they “continue to report overwhelmingly that inflation—rather than unemployment—will cause greater hardship for consumers in the next one or two years.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5426. XRP Price Was Worth Less Than a Penny When GTA 5 Launched: Could GTA 6 See It Hit $100?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP price was trading below one cent when Grand Theft Auto V arrived in September 2013. Thirteen years later, Rockstar is preparing to release GTA 6, while XRP has grown into one of the largest cryptos. XRP is a financial giant today.

The comparison is striking. On September 17, 2013, the day GTA V launched, XRP was trading at $0.009613. Today, XRP trades near $0.95, representing a price gain of almost 100 times from that launch-day price.

But can XRP deliver another extraordinary rally as GTA 6 arrives? A $100 price target would turn a relatively small crypto investment into a fortune, but it would also require XRP to reach a market valuation never seen before in the crypto industry.

When GTA V introduced players to Los Santos in 2013, XRP was still largely flying under the radar. Its price sat below one cent, and its market cap was ranging around $75 million. Then the following years changed everything.

XRP broke above $0.10 in May 2017 before accelerating during the historic crypto bull market. By December 2017, the token had crossed $1 and continued climbing toward its January 2018 all-time high of $3.84.

That is an extraordinary transformation from its GTA V launch-day price. A $1,000 investment at $0.009613 would have purchased more than 100,000 XRP. At $3.84, that position would have been worth nearly $400,000. Something that only crypto can do.

However, XRP’s journey was far from smooth. The token endured successive bear markets, regulatory uncertainty, and the SEC’s lawsuit against Ripple in December 2020. Its recovery eventually pushed XRP back toward record territory in 2025, when it reached $3.65.

Now, XRP is trading around $0.95, substantially below its previous peaks. Will another major recovery begin before GTA 6 is released?

Rockstar’s GTA 6 arrives more than 13 years after GTA V, creating an interesting milestone for XRP investors. XRP has experienced multiple market cycles during the same period, transforming from a sub-penny asset into a major digital currency.

XRP currently has 63.5 billion tokens in circulation. At $100 per token, its market capitalization would reach $6.35 trillion. That would put XRP among the most valuable financial assets in the world, exceeding the market capitalization of most publicly traded companies.

The bullish argument rests on XRP’s potential to capture a much larger share of institutional payments, cross-border settlements, and digital asset liquidity. Ripple has spent years building financial infrastructure around the XRP Ledger, while institutional interest in crypto investment products continues to develop.

A stronger crypto market could also provide the liquidity needed for another substantial XRP rally. But XRP would need considerably more capital, adoption, and sustained demand to justify a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.

The historical comparison remains fascinating. XRP went from less than a penny when GTA V launched to several dollars during subsequent crypto cycles. Few people back then would have believed XRP could get to where it is now.

#5425. AI deals shrink to as little as 30 days as the data layer sets the pace

Artificial intelligence has turned data infrastructure from a back-office purchase into the bottleneck that decides how fast GPUs pay off. As hyperscalers, neoclouds and enterprises race to expand their data layers, the way that infrastructure gets bought is changing just as fast.

The storage industry’s longtime performance specialist sees that shift as its opening. DataDirect Networks Inc. built its reputation on scale and speed, and those traits now carry more weight in AI infrastructure, according to Kevin Delane (pictured), president and chief revenue officer of DDN.

“When you look at the data layer, performance in the data layer drives value. So yes, it has to be simple, it has to be reliable. Those are table stakes, but performance drives business value,” Delane said.

Delane spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure sales cycles have grown more complex and faster, DDN’s tighter ecosystem work with partners such as Nvidia Corp. and Super Micro Computer Inc., and the company’s hiring for a direct, results-driven culture. (* Disclosure below.)

The way companies buy AI infrastructure has changed along with the technology. Deals at neocloud providers no longer go to a single enterprise buyer. They now involve the off-taker renting the capacity, the cloud operator and the integration software layer, Delane explained. Timelines have shrunk just as sharply, from six months to a year for a traditional enterprise sale to as little as 30 days.

“The sales cycle is more complex for sure. The speed is insane,” Delane said. “Sometimes these things are 30 days and you have to be ready to turn things around and really work with your customers and partners quickly.”

DDN is answering with tighter ecosystem work. Its decade-long partnership with Nvidia anchors the strategy, and joint offerings with Super Micro, such as the Enterprise AI HyperPOD, aim to replace a data center buildout with a ready-to-run AI stack. At SC26, DDN also introduced software-defined EXAScaler deployment to give enterprise AI customers more choice of hardware.

“It takes the complexity out of it, allows an enterprise to set up an AI pod within 3 hours,” Delane said.

The performance case holds up in the public cloud too. On Google LLC’s Google Cloud, customers using DDN’s Managed Lustre service saw 70% better training performance and a 40% gain in overall GPU efficiency, Delane noted.

DDN is growing threefold this year while adding only a few salespeople, leaning its hiring toward technical and implementation staff who can get customers up and running faster. Delane looks for grit and a fit with a direct, results-driven culture.

“If people can fit that culture, want to come in, want to grow this company to multiple billions, we have a place for them,” Delane said.

#5424. A Legacy Built on Trust and Community

Long Companies, a member of Leading Real Estate Companies of the World®

Favorite part of your job: Helping agents find opportunities and ways to navigate through them

Motto or work philosophy that you live by: Be curious. We apply our own filters and biases when we think we know the answers, so when faced with a challenge, I get really curious about why things are happening, what people need, what has changed and how we can align around that.

What is the biggest challenge currently facing your brokerage?

Rather than looking at things as challenges, I view them as opportunities—and while I believe there’s an opportunity in everything that happens, it’s about navigating that. Right now we have a market that’s starting to soften a little bit and regulate, so the question is: what do people need, and how do we deliver that?

From an industry standpoint, it feels as though a lot of brokerages and brokerage models appear to be chasing one another, but I’m more focused on quality experiences. And that begins with quality agents and staff.

I also believe the human part of this is really important in real estate. We’ve seen time and again that people want to work with a human, so doubling down on that experience is critical as we deal with a changing market.

Long Realty has reached an incredible 100-year milestone. What has contributed to the company’s success and longevity?

Having survived World Wars, recessions, depressions and pandemics, the company is adaptable and resilient. Communication is key when it comes to educating our agents so they can take that information to the consumer. We don’t make decisions blindly, and people can get behind what we’re doing, as we’ve built up a level of trust over the years.

The other thing I would point to is that we’re community focused. In addition to our own foundation that gives millions of dollars to local nonprofits, we’re also engaged in community activities, causes and sponsorships.

We’ve spent a long time building out our brand. More than just a logo, it’s the way people feel about us. A big part of my job is being a steward of the brand, ensuring that we’re doing things that align with how we want to be known.

What leadership practices have been most important in building and sustaining Long Realty’s success?

For me, it’s about empowering the people I work with. Not only do you need to work together to establish your vision, but you also need to have buy-in and ensure that people are passionate about it. And that begins with having great people who fit the culture. I find that most people want to do a great job and feel fulfilled, so how do we help our staff and our agents do amazing things? It can’t be about one person. It’s a collective, and we’re here to help the collective be better.

How do the partnerships you enjoy as a LeadingRE network member impact your business?

While we have the HomeServices network and our sister companies that we work with, layering on an organization like LeadingRE expands our capabilities and footprint. Through LeadingRE, we’ve built a lot of relationships with brokers around the country and the world, which has allowed us to service more people. We’re also members of Luxury Portfolio, which is important given the fact that Long Realty has nearly 40% market share on the million-dollar-plus side in our community. The members match our culture, and we feel comfortable referring and working with these folks.

For more information, please visit https://www.leadingre.com.

Paige Tepping is RISMedia’s senior managing editor.

#5423. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5422. ‘Momentum is the cure of all fear’: Mauricio and Alexia Umansky talk ‘Special Forces’

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

It’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

At the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio said the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He said he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

Alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Alexia: I had zero plans on talking about that while we were there. Before we go into the course, they make you talk to some psychologists … they do ask you before the show, “What’s the worst thing that you’ve ever been through?”

And I remember thinking, like, “Are we gonna go there? … That would be so inappropriate. Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she said to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

And each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a big hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

#5421. Inference pushes AI to smaller sites, making the data layer the deciding factor

Inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off. As GPU costs climb and component shortages persist, the architecture behind AI is shifting from a handful of massive facilities toward a distributed web of smaller sites.

That shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation. Turning data into insight at an acceptable cost now depends on a resilient, secure data engine built for GPU efficiency, according to Alex Bouzari (pictured), co-founder and chief executive officer of DataDirect Networks Inc.

“As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari said. “Costs are skyrocketing. GPUs are becoming more and more powerful, but also more and more expensive.”

Bouzari spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how inference, cost pressure and shortages are reshaping AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)

The first wave of AI buildouts concentrated GPUs in large, power-hungry facilities. Inference changes that math because it needs to run close to users and their data, Bouzari explained. Communities are also pushing back on giant monolithic data centers, he added.

“Now, what is happening with inference, you need to supplement that with smaller footprints. Let’s call them data centers, 1 megawatt, 2 megawatt, 5 megawatts. And those need to reside where the action is taking place, where the autonomous driving is happening, where physical AI is happening, where the sensor data is,” Bouzari said.

Connecting small pods back to large AI factories requires a different approach to data. DDN is building a software layer that spans many types of hardware, a direction reflected in its recent move to free its EXAScaler file system from DDN’s own hardware. The goal is to squeeze more use out of very expensive gear, according to Bouzari.

“It is a software layer that needs to accommodate the different types of hardware because, look, the costs being so high, people want to be able to maximize the utilization over an extended period of time, just like it was in high-performance computing,” Bouzari said.

The scale of spending has changed dramatically. A couple hundred million dollars once funded the world’s fastest supercomputer but now buys 15 to 20 racks of equipment, Bouzari noted. Shortages of GPUs, memory and solid-state drives are colliding with tighter budget scrutiny.

“On the one hand, you have budgetary constraints and the need to extract as much value as you can from your investment,” Bouzari said. “On the other hand, you have the shortages. And so a data layer that can do a lot more with a lot less infrastructure, the smaller footprint is extremely valuable.”

That thinking extends into the enterprise. DDN’s Enterprise AI HyperPOD packages CPUs, GPUs, networking and storage into a rack that can drop into existing corporate sites with available power. Keeping the pod on-premises also gives companies tighter control over their data, Bouzari explained.

“I think we’re entering an era where we will see a blossoming of smaller footprint pods being deployed in enterprises globally,” Bouzari said.

Bouzari framed the AI data layer as the counterpart to accelerated compute, with Nvidia Corp. supplying the processing and DDN supplying the data. As inference and agents take over, the data side carries more weight, he said: “You need both to make it successful. But the data engine, I think, is becoming increasingly important as inference and agentic is really becoming the predominant way to utilize AI and get value out of it.”

#5420. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.
