#5386. Homebuilders’ $30B buying spree has cooled; now it’s all execution

Homebuilding’s consolidation wave produced 200 plus transactions and $30B plus in announced value since 2010. As incentives rise and margins shrink, returns hinge on integrating people, land pipelines, systems, and operating models.  AI Summary

For the better part of 15 years, U.S. homebuilding has been on a mergers-and-acquisitions buying spree. Since 2010, more than 200 homebuilder transactions have conservatively totaled more than $30 billion in announced deal value, based on just seven of the largest acquisitions and excluding scores of private-company transactions whose purchase prices were never disclosed.

The buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway‘s $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry‘s approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year’s largest deals. More recent transactions included Daiwa House subsidiary Stanley Martin‘s July acquisition of Holiday Builders, Dream Finders Homes‘ August acquisition of Beazer Homes, and Century Communities’ October purchase of HistoryMaker Homes.

Yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry’s competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted. Weak demand, costly sales incentives, shrinking margins, and uncertainty over land and home values are forcing acquirers to reconsider not only which businesses are worth buying but also how the companies they already own should operate.

“We’re not busy now,” one deeply experienced homebuilding M&A dealmaker told me recently. “This is no time to be trying to take a seller to market for acquisition. Nothing’s happening.”

That assessment does not mean homebuilding consolidation has ended. It’s still “morning time in America” for homebuilding’s inevitable grind toward concentration of fewer, ever larger, more industrialized homebuilding giants.

My source’s observation suggests that the economics of bringing new sellers to market have become harder, even as the largest and best-capitalized acquirers continue pursuing strategic combinations.

Business and investment models in homebuilding can look remarkably good when demand, prices, and asset values are rising. The real test comes when the cycle turns, gravity takes hold, and assumptions that worked on the way up begin to break down. That’s when the industry’s outliers distinguish themselves, not simply through stronger balance sheets, but by how well their people work together, how quickly they adapt their processes, how effectively they serve customers, and how consistently they outperform competitors when business conditions get messy.

That is the test now confronting the companies assembled through homebuilding’s extraordinary consolidation era. Have their acquisitions produced merely bigger enterprises, or have they developed the leadership, operating discipline, local knowledge, and capacity to improve that will make them fundamentally better homebuilders with greater connectivity to and attainability for America’s economically bifurcated households?

The answer will increasingly depend on what happens inside the enterprises they’ve acquired. The challenge is to capture the value of their land positions while developing the people, operating systems, technologies, and organizational capabilities needed to replenish those positions, improve profitability, and serve customers more efficiently in a difficult market likely to extend into 2027 and potentially 2028.

That is where the next, and perhaps most demanding, phase of homebuilding consolidation begins.

Homebuilding acquisitions are distinct from many other corporate combinations because the value of the acquired business is inseparable from its land positions and the people capable of turning those positions – sustainably and repeatedly – into profitable homes.

An attractive acquisition may bring years of controlled lots, entitled development opportunities, established relationships with landowners and municipalities, and access to markets that would take an outsider years to enter. It may also include an experienced management team, trusted trade relationships, established brands and the organizational knowledge and local intel needed to perpetuate the business beyond its current land pipeline.

Those assets are related, but they are not interchangeable. When one goes missing, the others quickly fall out of balance. The value of the land depends on its location, basis, development requirements, timing, and the demand for homes that can be built on it profitably. Realizing that value depends on decisions about product, construction costs, sales strategy, purchasing, development sequencing, and capital allocation.

An acquirer that buys a good land portfolio but loses the ability to develop and replenish it efficiently may find that the acquisition’s original promise was a mere blip. An acquirer that preserves an admired local management organization without improving its operating economics may find that the business remains well regarded yet increasingly uncompetitive.

Successful acquisitions require balancing those two realities. The objective is to capture the value of the acquired land and operating platform as a launching pad for building the leadership, relationships, systems, and financial discipline needed to extend that profitability long after the original inventory has been delivered.

That balance of 100% binding capabilities becomes harder to hold together when market conditions weaken.

For years, one of the most attractive features of selling to Berkshire Hathaway’s Clayton Properties Group or one of the major Japan-based acquirers was the prospect of continuity.

Many regional builders joined larger, well-capitalized ownership organizations while retaining key elements of their identities, management teams, local relationships, and operating independence. That approach appealed to owners seeking liquidity or a succession solution without losing the character of the companies they had built.

It also made strategic sense. Local knowledge, land relationships, management experience, customer trust, and an almost irreplicable entrepreneurial fire and come-what-may resiliency were among the assets the buyers sought to acquire.

But serving as a benevolent, deep-pocketed, and patient capital-access channel for a local autonomy confederation across an expanding collection of businesses comes at a cost. Separate purchasing organizations, technology systems, back-office functions, product-development practices, and management structures can limit the benefits of larger ownership. When sales are strong and margins are healthy, those costs may be easier to absorb. When sales slow, incentives rise, and profitability contracts, the economics become less forgiving.

The pressure to coordinate operations, consolidate functions, standardize selected processes, and reduce unnecessary overhead intensifies. So do difficult decisions about regional leadership, divisional responsibilities, and the roles of managers at the divisional and neighborhood level who helped make the acquired businesses successful in the first place.

Those decisions can be disruptive, especially for employees and former owners who believed their companies would continue operating as they had before the acquisition and, in some cases, had enjoyed a solid few-year runway of exactly that. Some will regard the changes as evidence that the new parent does not understand the business it acquired. Others will see them as necessary steps toward strengthening the combined organization.

Eliminating management positions or consolidating administrative functions does not, by itself, demonstrate operational improvement. Nor does a departure from established practices necessarily indicate that an acquirer has made a strategic mistake or an unforced error.

The relevant test is whether the changes improve the organization’s ability to develop land, build homes, serve customers, maintain valuable relationships and generate returns that stakeholders and owners can count on as durable. That is a more useful standard than judging an acquisition by how many legacy executives remain in place or by how many familiar operating practices survive.

An important distinction exists among the companies driving the latest phase of consolidation. Daiwa House, Sekisui House, Sumitomo Forestry, and Berkshire Hathaway operate with strategic planning horizons and ownership structures that can offer greater flexibility than the quarter-to-quarter performance pressures faced by many publicly traded U.S. homebuilders.

The Japanese companies are publicly traded, and Berkshire Hathaway is accountable to its shareholders. None is insulated from financial performance requirements. But their diversified businesses, substantial resources, and long-term commitments to housing and related industries can allow them to invest in capabilities whose returns may take years to materialize.

So far, that difference has played out as an “acquirer-of-choice” factor as homebuilding firm sellers considered how firms organize and develop the businesses they acquire.

A longer-term ownership philosophy does not require codifying every management position or maintaining every regional operating structure indefinitely. In fact, patient capital may be most valuable when it enables an organization to undertake difficult transformations without expecting every investment to deliver an immediate earnings benefit.

The challenge is to distinguish costs that can be eliminated from capabilities that need strengthening.

Japan-based companies also have another potentially important advantage. Their experience with industrialized construction, standardized components, manufacturing systems, production engineering and deeply vertical integration extends well beyond what is typical of conventional American site-built homebuilding.

Clayton also brings experience in manufactured housing, factory-based production, and vertically integrated housing-related businesses. Its expanding site-built platform, particularly following the Taylor Morrison acquisition, creates opportunities to combine capabilities that have historically operated in unrelated realms of the residential construction business.

None of this means that industrialized methods developed elsewhere can simply be transplanted into American site-built construction. Differences in building codes, product preferences, transportation, trade labor, land development, and construction practices remain unsolved obstacles.

The industry has not yet demonstrated that these capabilities can be deployed broadly enough to transform the economics of conventional site-built housing. Still, the long-term strategic opportunity is hard to refute.

A collection of independently operated regional builders can provide market presence, land access, local expertise and “trust capital.” A more coordinated enterprise may also provide the common systems, product architecture, production volumes, and organizational learning needed to adapt industrialized methods across multiple markets.

As ambitions go, that’s far bigger than reducing SG&A. It also raises a question that applies to every major acquirer: Which capabilities should remain local, which should be shared across the enterprise, and which should be fundamentally reengineered into the holistic, interoperable system modern homebuilding organizations seem to need?

Homebuilding has long featured an argument over whether privately held regional builders are inherently better businesses than their larger public competitors. The case for private builders emphasizes their closeness to customers, knowledge of local land markets, relationships with municipalities and trades, and the loyalty and committed engagement of talented employees who have worked together for years.

Those advantages are real in many companies. They can influence everything from land acquisition opportunities to construction execution and customer referrals. But private ownership does not guarantee those qualities, just as public or institutional ownership does not necessarily diminish them.

A privately held company can become inefficient, undercapitalized, or resistant to change. A large enterprise can cultivate strong local leadership, build trusted community relationships, and adopt operating practices that improve the customer experience.

The more useful distinction concerns the quality of the operating organization, a characteristic we’ve talked about as homebuilding’s “outlier” factor.

Does it put decisions in the hands of people with the knowledge to make them? Does it give those people the resources, information, and accountability to perform effectively? Can it identify successful practices and extend their benefits beyond the division where they originated?

Answers to those questions reveal more than public or private ownership labels. They also help explain why the integration decisions now confronting the major consolidators are so difficult. An organization can destroy valuable local capabilities by centralizing too much. It can also waste substantial resources and miss opportunities to improve by centralizing too little.

Integration is knowing the difference. Some acquirers are good integrators. That doesn’t mean people swept up in them, or spat out due to them, agree.

For decades, scale in homebuilding has largely meant more closings, more communities, more controlled lots, greater geographic reach, and increased purchasing power that leads to market-share advantages. Those advantages remain as a bulwark of near-flywheel-like value creation. Larger builders can spread fixed costs across more homes, negotiate favorable supplier arrangements, diversify market exposure, and access capital on terms that smaller competitors may struggle to match.

Still, everyone who’s done well in the business can attest that size alone does not explain why some organizations consistently outperform others.

A more meaningful definition of scale includes an enterprise’s ability to combine capital, land, local knowledge, talent, technology, and relationships into an operating system that continuously improves performance. In that sense, homebuilding was AI before AI was cool because its best operators knew and practiced “recursive learning” as a core skill set.

That means acquiring land at bases that support acceptable returns under realistic demand assumptions. It also means developing products that customers value without unnecessary design, material, or construction complexity.

It means coordinating suppliers and trades to reduce delays, rework, and waste. It also means developing managers who can exercise sound judgment locally while drawing on the organization’s broader capabilities. It also means using information gathered across markets to make better decisions throughout the enterprise.

A builder operating in 20 markets should have opportunities to learn from 20 distinct sets of customers, land conditions, construction challenges, and operating practices. But those opportunities yield little advantage if the information remains trapped within individual divisions or if the organization lacks the discipline to identify and transfer improvements.

This is where AI-powered data systems and other technology capabilities could change the economics of scale. Better demand forecasting, more accurate construction scheduling, earlier detection of cost overruns, improved land underwriting, and more systematic comparisons of product performance could help organizations spot problems sooner and make decisions faster.

AI could help reveal patterns that managers would otherwise struggle to recognize in large volumes of operational data. It could also make institutional knowledge more accessible to those making daily decisions about land, purchasing, construction, and sales.

But value will not come from installing technology alone. Companies will need reliable data, consistent definitions, disciplined operating processes, and managers who can distinguish useful insights from misleading conclusions. They will also need to recognize that an approach that works in one market may be a fool’s errand in another.

Competitive advantage will belong to organizations that can repeatedly measure performance, understand what drives it, test improvements, and incorporate what they learn into their operating practices. That is how scale becomes a capability rather than merely a measurement of size.

The difficult market conditions facing builders through 2027, and potentially into 2028, will make these distinctions more apparent. Management teams will face pressure to reduce overhead, preserve liquidity, reassess land commitments, control construction costs, and improve returns on capital. Some will need to reorganize divisions, consolidate functions, or change leadership.

The companies that emerge stronger will not necessarily be the ones that make the deepest cuts. They will be the ones that understand which costs can be eliminated without harming the business and which investments are necessary to improve its future performance. That requires financial discipline, but it also requires patience, sound leadership judgment, and a willingness to challenge established practices.

It may require replacing an operating system that has worked adequately for years. It may also mean changing the responsibilities of respected executives or asking local teams to adopt practices developed elsewhere in the enterprise.

It may also require resisting the temptation to standardize activities that rely on local relationships and judgment. The objective should be neither to preserve acquired companies exactly as they were nor to eliminate their differences in pursuit of corporate uniformity.

It should be to develop organizations that can achieve what their constituent businesses could not accomplish independently.

The returns earned by companies that participated in homebuilding’s consolidation era will not reflect the ultimate opportunity. American homebuilding remains a uniquely complex process of converting land, capital, materials, labor, knowledge, and time into a finished product that households can purchase. Every unnecessary delay, redundant process, avoidable error, excessive handoff, and poorly coordinated decision adds cost somewhere along that process.

Some of those costs are so sticky they seem almost unavoidable. Others reflect operating practices that have persisted through the decades because the industry has struggled to coordinate the many participants involved in building a home.

Larger enterprises with better information, stronger leadership, deeper technical capabilities, and greater capacity to invest in improvement can change that.

The goal should be a homebuilding value stream that produces more value with less wasted time, effort, and expense, i.e., less “stream.”

Better execution will not, by itself, overcome high land prices, expensive financing, restrictive regulation, infrastructure constraints, or the gap between household incomes and housing costs. Those barriers remain substantial. But homebuilders have meaningful control over how they organize their businesses and how efficiently they turn resources into finished homes.

The industry’s era of consolidation has brought together an enormous collection of land assets, operating organizations, local relationships, and management talent under larger ownership platforms. What happens next will determine whether those combinations yield more than additional market share and purchasing leverage.

The most important measure of homebuilding’s great acquisition era may ultimately have little to do with how many companies changed hands or how much their buyers paid.

It may be how much better those enterprises become at converting land, capital, talent, and knowledge into homes that more American households can afford.

#5384. GTA 6 Flu Is Here: The Impact on Crypto Markets

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

GTA 6 has finally arrived, and millions of gamers are putting everything else on hold, including crypto portfolios.

After 13 years of waiting, Rockstar’s blockbuster release is already disrupting workplaces, dominating social media, and pulling gamers away from their usual routines. Even our newsroom is feeling the impact.

Tonight, the HEAT trade Miami for Vice City when they host the Milwaukee Bucks on a never-before-seen court, wearing an all-new uniform.Tune in to the NBA on ESPN at 7PM ET for A Night in Vice City.Find out how to watch in your area at https://t.co/sLWQH9hxi7 pic.twitter.com/zeihbzB7th

Could GTA 6 be stealing retail’s attention just as digital asset markets struggle to bring individual investors back?

The scale of the launch is hard to ignore. Reports put GTA 6 pre-orders at well over 10 million copies before its worldwide release. The game also carries expectations of $1.85 billion in revenue during its first three days.

Workers are making room for it, too. BambooHR data showed time-off requests for launch day running 9% to 17% above a typical third Thursday of November. A separate Zety survey found 22% of Gen Z workers planned around the release.

That is a sizeable chunk of the demographic that crypto platforms have spent years trying to attract. Gaming and crypto compete for the same online attention, particularly among younger audiences who spend hours on streaming platforms, social media and digital communities.

For us, checking Bitcoin prices, chasing the latest meme coin and following market-moving posts can easily become part of the daily routine. But GTA 6 offers something considerably more entertaining than watching another sideways trading session.

The launch is also driving enormous engagement across YouTube and Reddit. Sensor Tower estimates point to more than 50 million additional visits to food delivery and restaurant apps in the US over 30 days.

Crypto’s social media ecosystem could find itself competing for a much smaller share of that attention.

There is another reason the timing is interesting. Retail crypto trading has been weakening even as the broader market has attracted fresh capital.

eToro clients placed 62% fewer crypto trades in October than a year earlier. Robinhood’s crypto trading volume also fell 48% year over year in October, while Coinbase consumer spot volume dropped 59%.

The figures show that rising market valuations have not translated into the same level of retail trading activity seen during previous cycles.

This leaves crypto exposed to competition for speculative attention. Institutional investors can continue trading through market cycles, but retail often depends on excitement, momentum, and whatever narrative is dominating the internet.

But GTA 6 has all three. The game could temporarily pull casual traders away from exchanges, particularly those who spend their evenings chasing small-cap tokens and following crypto KOLs. Meme coins could be especially vulnerable if their usual audience spends the next several days exploring Vice City instead.

There is also an ironic possibility that GTA 6 could create fresh opportunities for crypto speculation. Gaming-themed tokens and GTA-related meme coins could attract traders looking to profit from the launch itself.

Bitcoin does not need gamers watching charts every minute to keep trading. But an industry built around speculation, online communities, and retail enthusiasm cannot afford to ignore where that attention goes.

#5383. Why aren’t mortgage rates lower after massive stock sell-off?

Market moves that typically lower yields, including weaker oil and AI equities, have not pushed mortgage rates down. The piece points to persistent hawkish Fed rhetoric as the main factor holding the 10-year yield near 4.94%.  AI Summary

AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%. So what gives?

The Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through. Now AI stocks are being slammed, with moratoriums on data centers coming in the near future as the anti-AI backlash grows. In this environment, you could expect the 10-year yield and rates to fall, but that’s not what’s happening.

I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts. Let’s go over each part of this storyline.

Oil prices were very volatile earlier this year and bond yields started moving in synch with them — especially after the first MOU deal broke off. Now that oil prices have fallen, you might expect at least a few Federal Reserve members to say that this could be a positive, but they haven’t.

In fact, when oil was trading between $68-$82, no Fed members said anything positive, and Cleveland Fed President (and Fed hawk) Beth Hammack talked about how lower oil prices were were actually bad for inflation because people could then spend more money.

In any case, so far, lower oil prices haven’t helped the 10-year yield get below 4.70%. If oil can trade between $67-$82, that would help a lot, but the last time that happened was when we announced a deal with Iran in June.

I have used the CoreWeave stock price as an example of the problems with the AI companies. Since CoreWeave had some financing issues, the markets have soured on AI, and as you can see in the chart below, the company’s stock price has been crushed. This has helped keep the 10-year yield below 5.35% for sure and has assisted in lower yields this week. But we are still elevated versus what we saw after the MOU deal was announced.

The Fed has made AI a huge inflation talking point, and they need to see much more pain in the AI sector before changing their tune.

If we were getting all this news about AI and oil prices four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield and mortgage rates would be lower today. But all this stock drama and falling oil prices came in a 14-day period where the Fed hawks came out every day talking about more Fed rate hikes, even a 50-basis-point hike. I mean, look at how the U.S. dollar hasn’t been fazed by the market drama.

For the past two months, I have focused on two key levels for the 10-year yield: 5.35% and 5.15%. Both those levels held and yields have fallen from these points. So what lower oil prices and falling stocks have done is made sure bond yields don’t go much higher and for now, let’s take that as a victory. However, I do understand why people might be scratching their heads on why rates aren’t lower with lower oil prices and falling AI stocks.

The Fed hawks are the main reason bond yields aren’t lower; they want to make sure that the bond market doesn’t get relaxed, even with lower oil prices and falling stocks, and they have done their job well. They really want to take back all the insurance interest rate cuts from last year and because of this, the 10-year yield is still at 4.95%. If the Fed members weren’t so hawkish over the last two weeks, bond yields would be lower and we would have already had sub-7% mortgage rates.

#5381. Will the AI stock sell-off give us sub-7% mortgage rates before the holidays?

Mortgage rates can move below 7% if the 10-year yield drops toward 4.85% and mortgage spreads improve toward 2%. Purchase applications fell 3% week over week and 18% year over year as volatility remains elevated.  AI Summary

Sub-7% mortgage rates are back on the holiday menu! Just when it looked like we had no chance for a happy holiday, AI stocks are still taking a beating and pushing money into bonds. Oil prices almost went below $80 last week too. We have three holidays left before 2027 kicks into gear, so the question now is: Can we get the 10-year yield and mortgage spreads low enough to get lower mortgage rates?

In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:

If all this market drama happened four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield would be under 4.85% today, but this is happening amid a rapid-fire, two-week effort by the Federal Reserve to give forward-guidance about more rate hikes coming in the system. The key level of 5.15% for the 10-year yield held last week, and with the AI sell-off and oil prices down to $83 again, we have a shot to get sub-7% mortgage rates again, but that will require the 10-year yield to get to 4.85% and head lower — and for mortgage spreads to improve back down toward 2%.Mortgage rates have had a difficult time lately with the inflation data and the Fed’s hawkish tone. In addition, we still don’t have a resolution to the Iran conflict, and when President Trump talks about bigger tariffs with our partners, it makes it harder for yields to go down. We also have to be mindful that inflation is rising while the unemployment rate is falling; if those two things change, it will be better for rates. For now, let’s focus on getting rates lower before the holidays. What can get us there?1. Stocks selling off almost got us to 4.85% again; we got as low as 4.92% Friday. The problem is the speed of the decline doesn’t help mortgage spreads. However, if we see more market selling, that can be one positive variable.2. Any positive news on the Iran conflict or limiting the trade war.3. The hope that the Democrats will resolve the conflict and trade war after Jan. 3 might get bond traders and oil traders thinking differently.We don’t have much time before the end-of-year holidays, but the above will help. However, the reverse is also true: stocks rallying, the conflict getting worse or more negative trade war headlines can lead yields and rates higher.

Mortgage spreads have recently gotten worse, which is a big variable in why rates got as high as 7.60% recently, but they’re still close to multiyear lows. We need less volatility in the bond markets, and with time, the spreads can improve again. Since September, the markets have been a bit too wild, rising and falling, and the spreads’ job is to reduce mortgage rate volatility. A big key for mortgage rates to get below 7% is getting the spreads back to 2% and under.

Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.18% from 2.15% a week earlier.

Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle.

Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data.

We saw slight week-to-week growth last week and housing data has really stabilized in the recent weeks; however, I would just view this as an adjustment to the rate shock we saw when rates moved from 6.75% to 7.60%, and demand got noticeably hit. The year-over-year comps are going to be difficult for some time, as mortgage rates were much lower last year than today.Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years:

Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. Rates rose aggressively during inflation week, so this data line did get hit, down 3% week-to-week and down 18% year-over-year. Again, the year-over-year comps here are rough, as mortgage rates were a lot lower last year. Earlier in the year, all we had was positive year-over-year, but rates reached the range where housing data slows down, and the comps have been very difficult.

Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026:

Housing inventory had a slight decline last week and is in its seasonal decline for 2026, as the peak in inventory already happened. Inventory growth did pick up when mortgage rates headed toward 7.60%; before that, inventory growth was slow this year, and we even had some weeks when inventory was negative year-over-year. Until mid-June it was hard for the comps to show growth this year and now they’re much easier to show growth as housing demand was heading toward a nine-month high last year this time.

New listings have been in their seasonal decline since June, and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since early 2022. One concern always with higher rates is that sellers will decide not to put their homes on the market; that has not happened this year, which is a positive sign for housing.In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years.Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years:

Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point, demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%, and last week the year-over-year price-cut gap was 2% higher than last year when demand was picking up with lower rates.In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year, and my -0.62% forecast is going to have a hard time being right this year. I simply don’t have enough time to be correct, as most of the year prices have been rising roughly 1%-2 % with the Case-Shiller Index. It’s only recently that we can see some negative year-over-year data, and we only have a few weeks left in the year.The price-cut percentage for last week:

It’s Thanksgiving week, so this means we can see some crazy volatility with stocks and bonds — and some hours with not a lot of volume. Next week’s tracker will obviously be hit by the holidays. However, this week we do have some economic data that can move the markets. PCE inflation, new home sales, PMI and other reports will add to the mix of volatility. And who knows what “upgrades” might shut down another institution or part of our infrastructure from operating normally this week!

#5380. CrowdStrike reportedly in talks to acquire cybersecurity provider Zscaler

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.

Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%.

Software buyouts tend to value the acquired company at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.

CrowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.

Zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a company’s employees access its business applications.

Enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.

Zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.

The company’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical issues that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.

Zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.

The potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The company’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end users’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity issues.

#5379. DataBeyond Showcases AI Sorting Solutions for Circular Supply Chains at COP31

ANTALYA, TÃ¼rkiye, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hangzhou DataBeyond Technology Co., Ltd. (DataBeyond), a provider of intelligent waste-sorting equipment and solutions, presented applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics in resource recovery at a China Pavilion side event during COP31 on Nov. 19. The company also joined an international initiative to promote green and low-carbon supply chains.

At the "Jointly Building a Green and Low-Carbon Supply Chain" event, DataBeyond Chairwoman Zhuoya Mo outlined the company's approach to municipal solid waste (MSW) management. The approach prioritizes sorting recoverable materials, directing them to suitable recycling processes and sending residual waste for appropriate treatment.

The United Nations Environment Programme's Global Waste Management Outlook 2024 projects that annual global MSW generation will reach 3.8 billion metric tons by 2050. Mixed collection and complex waste composition make effective sorting an important step in recovering materials for further use.

DataBeyond combines AI hyperspectral optical sorting with robotic picking to recover recyclable materials from mixed waste. Optical sorters process high-volume material streams, while robots identify and pick individual recyclable items from complex mixtures. The combination helps operators expand material recovery and reduce reliance on manual sorting in demanding environments.

In MSW applications, the company's systems recover target plastics, including polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) films, while separating materials that are incompatible with the intended recycling process. Suitable recovered fractions can then be washed and processed into feedstock for manufacturing, helping reduce the amount of waste sent for final disposal.

For plastics recycling, DataBeyond offers AI hyperspectral optical sorters that distinguish materials by composition, including plastics with similar appearances. Applications cover mixed rigid plastics, PET bottles and PET flakes. By separating incompatible polymers and improving material consistency, the systems help recyclers prepare feedstock for downstream manufacturing.

In textile recycling, the FASTSORT-TEXTILE-AI-SPEC system from DataBeyond sorts used garments by fiber composition, including cotton and polyester content. Further sorting of shredded textiles can remove fragments containing buttons, zippers and other unwanted components. How Can You Short Anthropic Stock?Now that ANT is trading, some investors may want to express a bearish view. Short Selling Anthropic StockShort selling means borrowing ANT shares through a brokerage, selling them and buying them back later. Losses have no upper limit because there is no limit to how far a share price can rise, and a rising price can trigger margin calls.

#5375. Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier

We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries. The business question for buyers is how much control an organization needs over the systems that produce its intelligence, and what happens when that control is ceded to others.

U.S. companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on. Buyers need to understand the resulting jurisdictional, operating and commercial risks, and put in place compensating controls to mitigate them. This reality applies for U.S. firms operating abroad and even those in the US, especially for regulated firms.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis #334: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement.

In this episode we examine the issues around where data lives, who holds the keys, which model touches the data, who operates the system and who is exposed to the bill. Our premise is that sovereignty requires deliberate risk decisions, compensating controls and proof that those controls work. The appropriate architecture involves tradeoffs and will depend on the workload and the consequences of losing control.

Today we draw on three sources of input as shown below:

First, Amit Govrin’s buyer’s guide, which evaluates the documented controls across hyperscaler offerings and buyer territories. Second, a study we commissioned with our partners at Qualitate that brings the experiences of eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations. Third, John Furrier’s conversation with Amit at SC26, which explains the reasoning behind our framework.

The buyer’s guide independently measures vendors’ documented claims. The in-depth interviews show what buyers care about and what they’ve tested. theCUBE interview helps connect those findings to architecture and business risk. The survey sample is small but deep, so we use it to understand decisions and expose gaps.

Let’s start by hearing from Amit with why he developed a practical and uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data and local risk:

The first set of takeaways from our survey shows a gap between buyer priorities and operational reality. Legal exposures featured prominently in purchasing decisions within the sample. Yet seven of eleven respondents report no testing of disconnected systems, key-revocation or exit scenarios. So the hard evidence for practical operational control is somewhat shaky given the high levels of concern about losing that very control.

As shown below, buyers also tend to add controls to the platforms they already use. Only four of eleven have deployed or piloted a distinct sovereign or dedicated offering. Cost and the burden of adding another environment was the primary reason that explained such behavior.

As seen in the quote above, a European information technology and telecom buyer says deep support escalations “can still in some cases involve personnel or systems outside the EU, particularly for deep technical issues.” What’s the message there? Our take is that the support protocol must become a fundamental part of the architecture review; and that has to account for emergency and privileged access. The key point as Amit often stresses is sovereignty is not a purity test. Organizations can certainly live with such an exposure during an emergency. Our message is simply be aware of the condition, evaluate the risk and if necessary put in compensating controls or live with the exposure.

Costs heavily influence the scope of sovereignty investments. Buyers justify stronger controls for sensitive workloads while accepting different levels of exposure for lower-risk activity. Migration effort, retraining and the cost of exiting all affect that decision.  At the very least, this means customers should assess their sovereign exposure, much in the same way they would do so for cybersecurity.

AI inference introduces another gotcha. Nine of 11 respondents require inference inside the sovereign or regional boundary. Buyers report that model availability can lag inside those environments. As such, the architectural choice has to make a potential tradeoff between local jurisdiction risk and model capability for a specific workload. The question buyers are asking: Is it worth stepping outside the lines to get a business result? The answer depends on the degree of risk and the magnitude of the business value. Sometimes it’s worth just paying the parking fine.

We’re not going to go deep into the buyer’s guide – we did that last week and we’d encourage you to read the full report.

What we will share is one high-level comparison from the buyer’s guide as shown below.

Google LLC leads all measured cloud vendors with a score of 3.45 across all regions and tests. Google is followed by Oracle Corp. at 3.25. IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp.’s Azure score 3.0. AWS scores 2.7 – its score suffers from not having the ability to have a customer-run air-gapped stack without vendor management. Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. came in at 1.2.

Now to be clear, this is a point-in-time index from the Nov. 14 revision. It averages each supplier’s best live offering across five buyer regions. The framework has five pillars (territorial, legal, operational, technical and financial), 17 yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions, plus a separate legal evaluation.

As well, a low score at the highest level doesn’t mean a vendor won’t be chosen. We found many situations, for example, where Amazon Web Services Inc. was the choice despite its lower score because of its excellent quality and incumbent position. We found similar dynamics with Azure as a ubiquitous cloud and often a convenient option. Similar dynamics are in play within IBM and Oracle customer bases.

That said, we’re assessing the architecture and the vendor claims to help buyers make better decisions. Customer-run deployments generally improve the scores because the methodology rewards controls the buyer can exercise independently. Missing documentation also affects the grades. We would use the previous chart to start an evaluation, then examine the actual offering available in the buyer’s jurisdiction against your specific workload requirements and local laws.

These findings bring us back to five key questions:

Listen below to John and Amit connect operational controls and money flows to sovereignty. Those dependencies extend well beyond the physical location of the data center.

Seven of eleven buyers say a locally incorporated subsidiary does not completely clarify the local jurisdiction question. This is a buyer assessment, and it suggests the need for much deeper legal analysis beyond technical evaluations.

Under the U.S. CLOUD Act, a vendor subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be required to produce data in its possession or control, regardless of storage location. Corporate relationships and actual control do matter here.

Customer-held keys may limit outside access, but key ownership does not necessarily ensure legal immunity. Buyers also need to know what stops working if and when access is revoked.

The fuzzy gap is captured by a South American bank’s executive director for AI, talking about the absence of testing: “That’s probably the weakest point in our whole sovereign story.” Our takeaway is that legal review and operational testing serve different purposes and both are critical.

Coming back to the AI inference issue. As we showed earlier, nine of 11 buyers require inference to take place inside their sovereign or regional boundary. One Latin American financial-services buyer said: “If it calls out to a U.S. endpoint, it doesn’t count no matter what the contract says.”

This means you have to trace the end-to-end request cycle, from prompt, retrieval, model usage, outputs and even logs. An application that gets green lit can still depend on another service which lives in the execution sequence. The test is what happens to the data during its actual use.

For sensitive workflows, buyers should compare a self-hosted open-weight model architecture with an approved frontier service and evaluate the cost and quality of the outcome. Open weights create optionality but the frontier often produces superior results which may warrant easing up on sovereignty requirements.

Sovereignty needs ongoing attention because the architecture changes continuously. A model endpoint can move, a new model ships, a service contract changes or a new capability goes into production. Every change can affect exposure and risk.

In this clip, Amit describes an AI-driven five-pillar framework for continuous assessment and management of data sovereignty and third-party risk. The approach brings vendor capabilities and claims, and the customer’s architecture, into an ongoing assessment. Let’s hear how he puts it:

We see tremendous value in this framework. Our test for any assessment comes down to the evidence it produces. In other words, what’s the exposure, who has control, is there an accountable owner and ultimately, what’s the risk you’re absorbing? Our advice is that major changes to models, services or contracts should trigger a reassessment. Documented assurance from the vendor combined with technical tests should both be included in that process.

Our recommendation is to make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level. Start with a core business process, identify the exposures and agree on the controls it requires based on the risk you’re willing to absorb. Importantly, for critical workloads, we suggest obtaining proof that those controls work in a safe sandbox environment and then push into production.

This means you have to pay attention to privileged access. And you must test what happens when a key gets revoked and you have to recover. As we’ve talked about in previous episodes, verifying what the model did and the route of the execution path is something most organizations can’t observe today. Testing and telemetry are major gaps with most customers. Can you observe the route and exercise an exit or completely disconnected scenario if a workload requires it? Your financial assessment should include ongoing operation, migration, retraining, the cost of leaving and business disruption. And importantly, a business owner has to accept the risk, not an IT pro.

For vendors, we believe the opportunity is substantial to document controls, establish predictable operating economics and provide credible evidence that can support your proposed solution. In many cases we’ve seen public documentation and evidence lack marketing claims.

Sovereignty is becoming part of enterprise architecture because intelligence now depends on these relationships. Buyers need the ability to make an informed choice and demonstrate that the resulting system behaves as intended.

Check out the Hyperscaler Sovereign Buyers Guide – it’s the first of its kind and very comprehensive.

And do let us know if you you have any questions – we’re here to help.

Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. Join theCUBE’s Alumni Trust Network, where technology leaders connect, share intelligence and create opportunities.

Founded by tech visionaries John Furrier and Dave Vellante, SiliconANGLE Media has built a dynamic ecosystem of industry-leading digital media brands that reach 15+ million elite tech professionals. Our new proprietary theCUBE AI Video Cloud is breaking ground in audience interaction, leveraging theCUBEai.com neural network to help technology companies make data-driven decisions and stay at the forefront of industry conversations.

#5374. AIPro Releases Free Version of 'VistaPro' AI Fire Early-Detection Software, Working with Existing CCTV

Download requires no sign-up; basic features available with no time limit; includes 1 AI detection channel and 2 general monitoring channels

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AIPro, an AI video analytics company, has released a free version of VistaPro, its fire and smoke detection monitoring software. The release allows facility operators to use basic functions with their existing CCTV cameras and PCs, confirm whether the software suits their actual site, and then add features as needed.

The free version can be downloaded from the AIPro official website (www.aipro.ai/download) without registration or login. The basic functions provided free of charge have no usage time limit. Users connect existing CCTV cameras that support RTSP video streaming to an Intel-based Windows PC that meets the recommended specifications, and the software runs without a separate high-performance graphics card.

The free version supports a total of three channels: one AI fire detection channel and two general monitoring channels. The fire detection channel analyzes flames and smoke, and video from multiple cameras can be viewed on a single screen. Detection history, statistics, and automatic reporting are also provided.

Real-time video analysis is performed on the user's PC. Both the free version (Free) and the paid Pro plan require an internet connection for updates and version management. Before installation, users can check the recommended PC specifications and CCTV integration requirements on the website.

The free distribution is designed so that users can verify CCTV compatibility and fire and smoke detection in their actual operating environment, and determine the features and operating scale their facilities need.

AIPro recommends first trying the software in a single area where fire risk needs to be monitored. Because camera angles, lighting, and work conditions differ from site to site, the company explained that it is important to review detection results at different times of day and decide on the operating approach accordingly. AI analysis results are used by managers to judge on-site conditions and the need for a response.

Real-time alerts, email notifications, and fire and map-based monitoring are provided in the paid Pro plan. AI detection channels can be added as needed, and a Business plan is available for companies and organizations that operate more cameras or need closed-network or site-specific configurations. Users start with the basic functions and then choose whether to expand according to their operating scale and purpose.

AIPro is an AI video analytics company founded in 2020 by Professor Cheon-Su Park of Sungkyunkwan University. It has built experience applying video analytics technology in the field for public institutions, including supplying fire and wildfire detection software to the Korea Asset Management Corporation.

AIPro believes that even small stores, warehouses, and workshops can evaluate the feasibility of AI safety management using their existing equipment. Going forward, the company plans to continue research to enhance fire and smoke detection performance and reduce false alarms, while improving ease of use from installation to reviewing detection results and managing records.

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup launched by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel plans — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.

That includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The company says Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, said last month that it plans to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

Companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

When Vayo launched last month, Fridgen said it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo says no site has blocked its bookings so far.

How the bookings work: Vayo’s new booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister company Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

For flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the company says.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the company says. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever company they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo users get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

The service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

His co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it launched last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the company says it plans to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

#5372. Seattle fleet tracking company Zonar names Atlanta-based CEO, who says HQ is staying put

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a new CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He said he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based company acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software company Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and says it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli said Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but said Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Zonar has added 1,000 new customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 plan, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli said.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the big players.”

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

“Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”

Founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

Three-year committed facility provides MetaOptics with flexible growth capital, drawn down at the Company's sole discretion

SINGAPORE, Nov. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MetaOptics Ltd (Catalist: 9MT) (OTCQX: MOTLY) ("MetaOptics" or the "Company", and together with its subsidiaries, the "Group"), a Singapore-headquartered semiconductor optics company pioneering glass-based metalens solutions enhanced by AI-driven image processing, announced that it had on 20 November 2026, entered into a share subscription facility agreement with GEM Opportunities Fund ISA Ltd. ("GEM"), the Bermuda-based investment vehicle managed by Global Emerging Markets (GEM), New York, for an aggregate commitment of up to S$32 million (the "Share Subscription Facility"). As part of the Group's plans to grow its existing business, the Group intends to establish a new 12-inch glass semiconductor fabrication line in the United States to produce metalenses for co-packaged optics ("CPO") and colour imaging applications. #5370. Stablecoin Market Loses Billions: Where Is Crypto’s Liquidity Going?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Crypto’s stablecoin market has shed $16 billion in a month, marking its sharpest contraction since the 2022 bear market. The retreat is hitting USDT and USDC hard, leaving fewer dollar-backed tokens circulating.

Total stablecoin market cap now stands at $283 billion, down more than 5% after losing $16.5 billion in a month. The decline puts the market under pressure just as crypto struggles to recover, with investors showing little appetite for buying the dip.

Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC account for most of the latest contraction. USDT is holding a market cap of $175.02 billion, down 4.3% over 30 days, while USDC fell to $68.58 billion, losing 5% during the same period. Together, the two stablecoins represent 86% of the entire market.

The contraction also extends beyond dollar-backed tokens. Sky Dollar’s USDS supply dropped 22.32% over 30 days, while Ethena’s USDe expanded 4.36%. The gap shows that some are still moving between stablecoin products.

CryptoQuant data points the same way. CryptoQuant data published on November 11 showed USDT market cap had fallen $6.6 billion over 60 days through November 7. It was more than twice the $3.2 billion decline recorded after FTX collapsed in November 2022.

The current contraction brings back an ugly history. Stablecoin supply reached $161.5 billion in March 2022 before entering a prolonged decline. Terra’s UST collapse accelerated the withdrawal of capital, with nearly $30 billion disappearing from stablecoin supply in June alone.

That monthly decline was almost twice the latest $16.5 billion contraction. Back in 2022, the damage continued into the following year. By September 2023, aggregate stablecoin supply had fallen by 26% from its March 2022 peak, a contraction of $43 billion.

Bitcoin endured a similar period of weakness. After reaching nearly $69,000 in November 2021, BTC eventually plunged to around $15,500 in November 2022. Stablecoin supply continued shrinking even after the initial market shock initiated by Terra. Crypto’s liquidity problems then became a prolonged market condition.

Yet, in 2023, not every stablecoin experienced the same fate. USDT supply rose $13.3 billion from its November 2022 lows, while USDC lost $16.7 billion. During that period, investors were not simply abandoning every stablecoin. Some were moving toward Tether as the market reassessed issuers and available returns.

This time, arguably, the stablecoin contraction is happening against a different market backdrop. Crypto traders have fewer reasons to keep large amounts of capital parked in stablecoins when Bitcoin and major altcoins struggle to attract buyers. Some holders may be redeeming their tokens for traditional dollars, while others are moving into interest-bearing assets outside crypto.

A shrinking stablecoin market does not mean every dollar has left digital assets. But the simultaneous decline in USDT and USDC supply makes the latest contraction harder to dismiss as simple rotation between issuers.

A crypto recovery needs buyers willing to commit fresh capital, and stablecoins have historically provided traders with an immediate way to enter the market.

#5369. Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software company, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

His co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health plans that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”

But after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

“Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it says.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”

Kelman, by his own account, is new to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman said the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:

Chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software company he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”

The Sojourn site says the company is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”

That fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn plans to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”

A new health plan typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the company hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a new mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He said at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

#5367. Early data points to Vulcan’s first stage in launch failure that cost Amazon 40 Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

That stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA said it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA said. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.”

Impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Amazon has said it plans to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.
