#5366. Zepp Health Corporation Reports Third Quarter of 2026 Unaudited Financial Results

MILPITAS, Calif., Nov. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zepp Health Corporation (NYSE: ZEPP) ("Zepp", the "Company" or "we") today announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter of 2026.

Third Quarter of 2026 Financial and Operating Highlights:

[1] Adjusted net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation represents net income/(loss) excluding (i) share-based compensation expenses, (ii) amortization of intangible assets resulting from acquisitions and business cooperation agreements, (iii) gain/(loss) from fair value change of long-term investments, (iv) impairment loss from long-term investments, (v) income/(loss) from equity method investments, (vi) investment income/(loss) and (vii) tax effects of the above non-GAAP adjustments. See "Reconciliation of GAAP and Non-GAAP Results" at the end of this press release.

"The third quarter was a period of adjustment for us," said Wayne Huang, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Zepp Health. "Tight supply for some of our core products weighed on revenue, while unfavorable exchange rates and higher prices for memory and other chips put pressure on gross margin. The adjustments we made across our products, training software, supply, and retail are already beginning to pay off in the fourth quarter, and we are heading into the holiday season and the year ahead with momentum.

In the third quarter, global activations across the Balance family rose approximately 40% from the second quarter, driven by our new, higher-priced models. Combined global activations for Active 3 Premium and Active Max, our two US$169 models, grew approximately 35% over the same period. We also expanded our premium outdoor lineup with T-Rex Dual Solar, a watch priced at about US$650 that pairs a bright AMOLED display with dual-sided solar charging and offline navigation for multi-day trips. Through Zepp OS 6 and HYROX updates, we brought new training tools to more watches that customers already own, giving them more value from their devices.

Product availability has started to improve in some markets in the fourth quarter, including for T-Rex 3. We have also made it easier for customers to compare watches in stores. At REI, we provided materials to help shoppers compare models. Large screens are now in place at our Amazfit counters in select Best Buy stores. They make the counters easier to spot and show shoppers how our devices fit into everyday activity, training, and recovery. As more products reach store shelves, we believe we will be better positioned to meet holiday demand."

Leon Deng, Chief Financial Officer of Zepp Health, commented, "Third-quarter revenue reached US$68.3 million, up 7.5% sequentially and within our guidance range. While revenue declined 9.9% year-over-year, we continued to see encouraging momentum in our Active series. Supply constraints on certain higher-margin products, including Balance 3 and Helio Strap, limited our ability to fully capture market demand during the quarter.

Gross margin was 35.0%, compared with 37.4% in the previous quarter and 38.2% in the same period last year, reflecting unfavorable foreign exchange movements, continued increases in memory component costs, and supply constraints on our higher-margin products. Importantly, excluding the tariff-related benefit recorded in the second quarter, our underlying gross margin remained strong sequentially. Continued improvement in our product mix helped offset a meaningful portion of these external cost pressures, demonstrating the progress we have made in strengthening our premium product portfolio and underlying unit economics.

We continued to balance financial discipline with targeted investments to support future growth. On a sequential basis, adjusted operating expenses decreased to US$34.2 million, and adjusted operating loss narrowed to US$10.3 million. The year-over-year increase in operating expenses was primarily driven by strategic investments in new product launches, brand building, athlete partnerships, and distribution expansion. At the same time, general and administrative expenses declined, reflecting our ongoing efforts to improve operational efficiency and manage our structural cost base.

We ended the quarter with US$99.0 million in cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash, while inventory declined to US$68.6 million from US$87.7 million a year earlier. We also continued to strengthen our balance sheet by extending our debt maturity profile, converting an additional US$26.6 million of short-term borrowings into longer-term obligations during the quarter. We remain committed to returning value to shareholders through our ongoing share repurchase program. As of September 30, 2026, we had cumulatively repurchased US$17.8 million under our US$20 million authorization, and our board of directors recently approved a one-year extension of the existing program.

Looking ahead, we expect fourth-quarter revenue to be between US$90.0 million and US$95.0 million, representing year-over-year growth of approximately 6% to 12%. As product availability improves and our expanded distribution channels begin contributing more meaningfully, we remain focused on translating our investments into stronger revenue growth and greater operating leverage. Despite near-term external cost pressures, we believe our improving product mix, disciplined cost management, and continued investment in the Amazfit brand are building a stronger foundation for sustainable long-term growth and profitability."

Revenue reached US$68.3 million, representing a year-over-year decrease of 9.9% and a quarter-over-quarter increase of 7.5%. The year-over-year decline was due to the broader macroeconomic environment and a strong comparison base, as well as supply constraints on top-selling offerings, particularly Helio Strap and Balance 3. However, revenue from the Active series increased significantly year-over-year.

Gross margin was 35.0%, compared with 38.2% and 37.4% in the same period of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, respectively. Gross margin faced several headwinds during the quarter, primarily elevated memory and other component costs, as well as foreign currency impacts. While product mix improved year-over-year, supported by new product introductions including the Active series, this favorable mix benefit was more than offset by higher memory costs within our entry-level price segments. Gross margin for the second quarter of 2026 benefited from tariff refunds that the Company recorded related to duties previously remitted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act ("IEEPA"). Excluding the impact of these refunds, gross margin increased sequentially.

Research and development expenses in the third quarter of 2026 were US$11.4 million, compared with US$10.8 million and US$11.5 million in the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, respectively. Excluding US$0.6 million of foreign currency headwinds, research and development expenses were flat compared with the same period of 2025. We continued to invest in a series of cutting-edge products as well as new technologies, including AI, to maintain our competitive edge against our peers. At the same time, we focused on refined research and development approaches, consistently evaluating resource efficiency to optimize return on investment and productivity.

Selling and marketing expenses in the third quarter of 2026 were US$18.0 million, compared with US$12.0 million and US$18.3 million in the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, respectively. The US$6.0 million year-over-year increase was primarily attributable to US$1.9 million investment across online and offline channels for content refreshes, in-store displays and holiday season readiness, and US$1.5 million of launch campaigns for new products including the Balance 3, Balance Ultra and T-Rex Dual Solar. The remainder of the increase reflected US$1.4 million for marathons, Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) and media sponsorships, and US$1.2 million related to the HYROX and new athletes partnerships.

General and administrative expenses were US$5.6 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared with US$7.0 million and US$6.2 million in the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, respectively. We continued to streamline overhead, maintaining disciplined cost control while improving operating efficiency.

GAAP and adjusted operating expenses[2] for the third quarter of 2026 were US$35.0 million and US$34.2 million, respectively, compared with US$29.8 million and US$28.6 million in the third quarter of 2025, and US$36.0 million and US$34.8 million in the second quarter of 2026. Out of the year-over-year increase of US$5.2 million in operating expenses, US$0.8 million was due to foreign currency impacts. The remaining US$4.4 million was primarily due to higher selling and marketing expenses as mentioned above. On a quarter-over-quarter basis, operating expenses decreased slightly.

GAAP and adjusted operating results[3] were loss of US$11.1 million and loss of US$10.3 million, respectively, compared with loss of US$0.9 million and income of US$0.4 million in the same quarter of 2025. The net operating loss was due to lower gross margin mainly resulting from higher memory and other component costs and foreign currency headwinds, as well as increased investment in marketing and branding activities, but the operating loss narrowed compared with the second quarter of 2026.

GAAP and adjusted net loss attributable to Zepp for the third quarter of 2026 were US$12.6 million and US$11.6 million, respectively, compared with GAAP and adjusted net loss of US$1.6 million and US$0.7 million for the same quarter in 2025. The US$10.9 million year-over-year increase in adjusted net loss was primarily driven by a US$6.0 million increase in selling and marketing expenses, as discussed above, followed by a US$3.2 million unfavorable foreign exchange impact. In addition, higher memory and other component costs resulted in a net US$2.7 million gross profit headwind, partially mitigated by a more favorable product mix. These unfavorable impacts were partially offset by US$1.1 million in savings from general and administrative expenses.

[2] Adjusted operating expenses represent operating expenses excluding (i) share-based compensation expenses and (ii) amortization of intangible assets resulting from acquisitions and business cooperation agreements. Please refer to the section titled "Reconciliation of GAAP and Non-GAAP Results" at the end of this press release.

[3] Adjusted operating income/(loss) represents operating income/(loss) excluding: (i) share-based compensation expenses and (ii) amortization of intangible assets resulting from acquisitions and business cooperation agreements. See "Reconciliation of GAAP and Non-GAAP Results" at the end of this press release.

As of September 30, 2026, cash and cash equivalents and restricted cash were US$99.0 million, compared with US$102.6 million and US$106.3 million as of September 30, 2025 and June 30, 2026, respectively.

The Company recorded inventory of US$68.6 million as of September 30, 2026, compared with US$62.4 million as of June 30, 2026 and US$87.7 million as of September 30, 2025. We will continue to manage the inventory level tightly and working capital closely.

Long-term and short-term debt levels remained flat as of September 30, 2026 compared with June 30, 2026. We remain committed to prudently managing our debt profile. Our primary objective is to maintain overall debt levels broadly stable while actively extending the maturity profile by replacing short-term borrowings with long-term debt. During the third quarter and for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we successfully converted US$26.6 million and US$56.5 million, respectively, of short-term debt into long-term obligations, and we expect to continue this strategy in the coming quarters, supported by sufficient financial headroom and liquidity capacity. Since the beginning of 2023, the Company has cumulatively retired US$38.1 million of debt, and will continue to optimize its capital structure.

The Company announced in its third quarter 2021 earnings release that the board had authorized a share repurchase program of up to US$20 million through November 2022. On November 21, 2022, the board authorized a 12-month extension of the Company's share repurchase program. On November 20, 2023, the board further authorized the Company to extend its share repurchase program for another 12 months. On November 18, 2024, the board further authorized the Company to extend its share repurchase program for another 24 months. On November 22, 2026, the board further authorized the Company to extend its share repurchase program for another 12 months. Pursuant to the extended share repurchase program, the Company may repurchase its shares in the form of ADSs and/or ordinary shares through November 2027 with an aggregate value equal to the remaining balance under the share repurchase program. As of September 30, 2026, the Company had used US$17.8 million to repurchase approximately 2.4 million ADSs. The Company expects to fund the repurchases under the extended share repurchase program out of its existing cash balance.

For the fourth quarter of 2026, the Company's management currently expects net revenues to be between US$90.0 million and US$95.0 million, which would represent an increase by approximately 6% to 12% from US$85.2 million in the fourth quarter of 2025.

This outlook is based on current market conditions and reflects the Company's current and preliminary estimates of market, operating conditions and customer demand, which are all subject to change.

Additionally, a live and archived webcast of the conference call will be available at http://ir.zepp.com.

A telephone replay will be available one hour after the call until November 29, 2026 by dialing:

Zepp Health (NYSE: ZEPP) is the technology company behind Amazfit, a global sports technology brand. Its wider portfolio includes Zepp Clarity hearing technology and Zepp Aura sleep and recovery services.

The company's vertically integrated technology platform brings together Zepp OS, wearable chipsets and biometric sensors designed in-house, and algorithms for biometric measurement and personalized guidance to enhance product performance and user experiences across devices, software and services.

Zepp Health operates as a global multi-hub organization, bringing together R&D, product, design, brand and business expertise across the Americas, Europe and Asia. These teams co-create and share responsibility for innovation, product performance and global growth.

Founded in 2013, Zepp Health has shipped more than 200 million units of smart wearable devices, with products available in more than 90 countries. Its principal office is in Gorinchem, the Netherlands. For more information, visit: www.zepp.com

We believe that adjusted EBIT and adjusted net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation help identify underlying trends in our business that could otherwise be distorted by the effect of certain expenses that we include in net income/(loss) and net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation. We believe adjusted EBIT and adjusted net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation provide useful information about our operating results, enhance the overall understanding of our past performance and future prospects and allow for greater visibility with respect to key metrics used by our management in its financial and operational decision-making.

Adjusted EBIT and adjusted net income/(loss) attributable to Zepp Health Corporation, should not be considered in isolation or construed as an alternative to net income/(loss), basic and diluted net income/(loss) per share and per ADS attributable to Zepp Health Corporation or any other measure of performance or as an indicator of our operating performance. Investors are encouraged to review the historical non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures. #5365. Inference now drives two-thirds of AI workloads, changing where chips get deployed

AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, quickly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads. Power, cooling and memory supply now shape where tokens get generated as much as raw chip performance does.

Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift. Positron AI Inc., which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, builds inference appliances around commodity memory instead of scarce high-bandwidth memory. Inference has overtaken training as the force behind infrastructure buying decisions, according to Cameron McCaskill (pictured), head of sales and business development at Positron.

“We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training. And back in 2023, it was like 85% training, 15% inference,” McCaskill said. “So now you can see why inference is driving the economic decisions of how they’re going to build out their infrastructure.”

McCaskill spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed inference overtaking training, Positron’s commodity-memory chip design and why low-power modular data centers suit inference. (* Disclosure below.)

Positron’s first-generation Atlas server ran on a programmable chip, and the company plans to tape out its own silicon early next year for its Titan server. Oracle Corp. is bringing about 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud this quarter, McCaskill noted. A neocloud provider has also signed on for Atlas and committed to Titan. Positron’s central design choice was skipping high-bandwidth memory.

“Everyone else pretty much in the industry is using what’s called HBM or high bandwidth memory. It’s very limited in supply, very expensive,” McCaskill said. “We went with commodity memory.”

That choice also keeps power low enough for air-cooled rooms. A single Positron server draws about 4,500 watts, and a full rack of Titan servers fits within 40 kilowatts, McCaskill explained. That footprint suits sites where operators can find a few megawatts of cheap power without heavy regulatory hurdles. For inference providers monetizing new capacity, deployment speed is a big part of the appeal, according to McCaskill.

“One of the groups of companies that we’re seeing a rise in right now and coming to us for product is these modular data centers, where they have a half megawatt or, 1 megawatt or 2.5 megawatt modular data center, and those can be deployed very quickly,” McCaskill said. “And the goal of a lot of these inference players is I want to get from land and power to monetizable tokens within 90 to 120 days. And those modular data centers, coupled with our technology, can be a great solution.”

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:38 pm

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.

Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella said the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”

“We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he said. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”

The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

It was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.

From there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here.

#5363. LG ELECTRONICS' ULTRAVIEW WINDSHIELD DISPLAY WINS 2026 AUTOMOTIVE NEWS PACE PILOT AWARD

Award Recognizes LG's Context-Aware Approach to In-Vehicle Information as Company Advances Validation with Global Automakers

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LG Electronics (LG) has won the 2026 Automotive News PACE Pilot Award for its UltraView Windshield Display, an in-vehicle display solution that shows driving information and infotainment content across a large area of the windshield.

Presented by Automotive News, the PACE Pilot Award recognizes early-stage automotive innovations that are not yet commercialized but have demonstrated their potential through pilot programs. LG's win highlights its approach to organizing information within the driver's field of view.

Rethinking In-Vehicle Information Delivery

As vehicles add more digital functions and connected services, the amount of information presented to drivers keeps growing. With driving data, navigation, entertainment and vehicle controls often spread across multiple displays, drivers may need to shift their gaze between the road and different screens more frequently.

Rather than adding more screens or expanding display size, LG developed UltraView Windshield Display to rethink how, when and where information reaches the driver. The solution organizes information by importance and driving context, supporting a more intuitive driving experience. This reflects LG's broader vision for next generation automotive displays, which shifts the focus from individual display devices to a more integrated and context-aware information experience.

Bringing Context-Aware Information to the Windshield

UltraView Windshield Display combines a compact, focus-free AR-HUD with LG's proprietary Hover HUD in a single optical system, presenting different types of visual data at distinct virtual distances. The AR-HUD projects driving-critical information, including vehicle speed, advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) alerts, and navigation cues, at a far virtual distance aligned with the road. Its focus-free design reduces the difference in focal distance between the road and the projected image, so drivers can check information more naturally while keeping their eyes on the road. Meanwhile, the Hover HUD displays navigation, vehicle status, climate controls and multimedia content on a large virtual screen that appears closer to the driver.

Together, these two technologies allow UltraView Windshield Display to adjust screen size and information density to driving conditions, helping drivers access relevant information while minimizing unnecessary shifts in visual attention. Its compact design also gives automakers greater flexibility in cockpit design and display configuration.

Advancing Toward Real-World Vehicle Applications

LG has been conducting vehicle-level proof-of-concept evaluations of UltraView Windshield Display with multiple global automakers, including premium brands in Europe and Asia. These collaborations include vehicle-level validation and sourcing discussions, and vehicle demonstrations and technology showcases have drawn further inquiries from automakers. Building on this progress, LG plans to further validate the technology for real-world vehicle applications and explore opportunities for future production programs.

"Winning the Automotive News PACE Pilot Award recognizes our approach to rethinking how information is delivered inside the vehicle," said Eun Seok-hyun, president of the LG Vehicle Solution Company. "We will build on this recognition by working closely with automakers to bring new display experiences from innovation to real-world mobility."

#5362. Seattle tech vet and Sounders FC minority owner Chee Chew joins front office to lead AI push

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”

Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years. It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

He recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew said, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew said he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

“It has to be approachable for folks,” he said. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he said.

#5360. Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am

Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD said a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”

#5358. Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, says Stuttgart AI factory chief

A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

In Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

“It’s very important to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller said. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”

Koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.)

Industrial users no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the new hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

“The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller said. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”

That pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

“We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller said. “We have to look for the data.”

Efficiency is part of the equation, too. The new system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. The bigger lesson is human: A concierge model pairs each customer with a consistent contact, according to Koller.

“We learn more how the users are working and thinking, to be honest,” Koller said. “… We can build up a system which is highly fancy, whatever there, nobody will use it because we never thought about what the user needs.”

#5357. Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” said Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” users of each company’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

New MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature shows business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5356. ModelBest opening up access to AI technology on an international scale

LISBON, Portugal, Nov. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- This is a report from China Daily:

The global race for artificial intelligence is often perceived as a competition over who controls the largest data centers. However, ModelBest offers a different perspective: how inclusive intelligence becomes depends on its accessibility and how widely it can be deployed.

This Chinese on-device AI unicorn has made efficiency the cornerstone of its overseas expansion strategy. By November, its self-developed MiniCPM series of models had recorded more than 70 million downloads worldwide.

"MiniCPM is not just one model. It is an entire family," Li Dahai, CEO of ModelBest, said at the Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal, which took place from Nov 9 to 12.

Each model serves a different form of intelligence, but they share one goal: higher intelligence density, faster speed, and lower cost on devices, he added.

That efficiency-first approach has been put to work abroad. In April, ModelBest revealed the Lao national model, LaoAI, which marked a landmark case of a Chinese AI company helping another nation build its own national AI foundation.

Built on the company's MiniCPM architecture and high-efficiency training methods, the system is integrated into G-Chat v2, the national government communications platform, and is used across government agencies and key industries.

Sovereign AI has largely been dominated by chipmakers, for whom sovereignty implies acquiring advanced computing power and constructing national data centers. LaoAI offers another path: instead of relying on a national supercomputing cluster, the team made multiple field research trips to Laos in the months leading up to the launch, building the system on high-efficiency model architecture rather than massive computing power.

The team also incorporated Lao culture and values into training through field research. The Lao translation capability of their model outperforms mainstream systems on international benchmarks.

Crucially, the underlying model and application programming interfaces are open to local developers. The complete model weights have been delivered to the Lao side, giving them control over everything from the model to the data.

"Efficiency is the key to making large model technology available to everyone," Li said. "In the Lao national model project, an 8-billion-parameter system achieved world-leading Lao-language capability. This demonstrates that developing countries need not wait for top-tier computing power to benefit from AI," he added.

The significance is more developmental than commercial: countries of the Global South no longer need access to high-end computing capacity to step into the AI era.

The same principle applies to businesses. Making AI affordable for small and medium-sized enterprises is often touted but rarely realized. ModelBest's on-device approach changes that. When inference happens on the device, small businesses need neither cloud capacity nor data uploads to access usable AI.

The technical foundation is what the company calls the "Densing Law". The capability density of large models doubles roughly every 3.5 months, reducing the number of parameters needed for a given level of intelligence.

For such businesses, on-device AI is not merely cheaper: it is their first realistic chance to possess AI capability, with data on-premises, no per-inference fees, and no dependence on network coverage.

From sovereign models to on-device intelligence, ModelBest's international narrative aims to share the benefits of China's AI advancements with more countries, ensuring that each nation can develop its own AI capabilities in its own languages.

This direction echoes national policy: China's 2026 Government Work Report endorsed open-source AI ecosystems, and this year's World Artificial Intelligence Conference and the World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit both advanced initiatives for a fair, open and sustainable global AI ecosystem.

For ModelBest, the overseas initiatives represent a microcosm of this broader vision. By prioritizing efficiency and openness, AI can be extended to countries and businesses that have been waiting on the sidelines.

Beyond expanding access, ModelBest is also rethinking how AI itself is built. The next step is to use AI to build AI itself.

"This is not only a technological change; it is a fundamental shift in how intelligence is produced," Li said.

#5355. Seattle startup Aarden raises $8M to help landowners navigate the AI and energy building boom

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 1:36 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 5:15 pm

Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other projects.

Founded last year, the company says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team said it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more important than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason said in a statement.

The company combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.

Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

The new funding brings Aarden’s total investments to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The company has 13 employees and plans to nearly double in size over the next 12 months.

Margason said he launched the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations.

One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses.

“Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” said Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres, which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id, which offers property insights and mapping tools.

Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, said the company is already having an impact.

“We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson said on LinkedIn.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5354. Rene Haas to Take Over Nvidia? What Will Happen to Crypto?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Nvidia could be about to hand its biggest job to the man who helped turn Arm into one of the world’s most valuable chip companies. Rene Haas is now being considered as a potential successor to Jensen Huang at Nvidia, a familiar face at the center of the AI industry’s biggest leadership change.

Bloomberg reported that Nvidia’s recruitment firm had approached Haas as part of its search for a new chief executive. Haas previously spent seven years at Nvidia before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in 2022 and has since overseen its expansion into the booming AI infrastructure market.

Rene Haas has been approached regarding the CEO role at Nvidia by recruiting firm Heidrick & Struggles, which was hired by the board to replace Jensen Huang https://t.co/yiJ6NkvEtS

An appointment would put someone with experience at both companies in charge of Nvidia’s next chapter. But what does it mean for crypto? Could Haas push the AI boom even further, and what would that mean for Bitcoin and the rest of the market?

Haas is not an outsider to Nvidia. He previously ran the company’s computing products business between 2006 and 2013, giving him direct experience with the company before its transformation into an AI powerhouse.

His subsequent run at Arm offers a glimpse of what he might bring to the role. Arm reported $4.92 billion in revenue for its fiscal 2026, up from $4.01 billion the previous year. Its profit before tax climbed from $756 million to $960 million. The company has also moved beyond its traditional chip-design licensing business, introducing its own AGI CPU for AI data centers in March 2026.

Arm’s technology already reaches more than 99% of smartphones sold worldwide. Its designs also power computing infrastructure used by major cloud providers and Nvidia itself.

Haas helped position the company for a much larger role in the AI economy. Now, his next challenge could be taking Nvidia beyond selling the chips powering that expansion.

Nvidia’s existing business gives him an enormous starting point. The company generated $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue in its latest results, with data center sales accounting for $107.6 billion. Revenue increased 103% from a year earlier.

Its next-generation Vera Rubin platform has also entered production and begun shipping. A new CEO would inherit an extraordinary growth engine, but also the responsibility of deciding how aggressively Nvidia should expand its influence across the AI industry.

If Haas brings his Arm strategy to Nvidia, we could see a push into integrated computing platforms, data center infrastructure and new AI applications. That could create another wave of investment across the technology sector.

Crypto could benefit if Haas turns Nvidia’s next chapter into another catalyst for AI infrastructure spending. The connection extends beyond tokens carrying artificial intelligence branding. Bitcoin and Ethereum have increasingly moved in tandem with technology stocks during periods when investors shift between risk assets.

A stronger Nvidia could help restore confidence in the AI investment cycle, especially if investors believe its leadership transition will not interrupt infrastructure spending.

Decentralized computing projects such as Render, Bittensor, Artificial Superintelligence Alliance, and Akash could also benefit. These networks are trying to capture demand for GPU resources, distributed computing, and AI development.

More spending on AI infrastructure would create opportunities for decentralized alternatives. Developers need computing power, and centralized providers cannot always meet every requirement at the right price.

The bigger opportunity could come from investor appetite rather than immediate demand for crypto tokens. If Nvidia shares regain momentum under Rene Haas, technology investors could become more comfortable taking risks elsewhere. That would give crypto a potential source of buying interest.

Haas has already demonstrated what he can do with Arm. Taking over Nvidia would give him a considerably larger platform, with consequences extending well beyond semiconductor stocks.

#5351. ‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.”

The change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

For Muse users, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas said any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

What’s new is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the company had nothing to share.

Amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

#5350. Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia’s board on its CEO search

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 5:05 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:50 am

Jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the company for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos said. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”

Nvidia’s board says it has no plans to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Jones said the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place quickly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He said he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”

The Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

He said he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”

Huang himself said in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the company.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also said Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she said customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”

In case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”

ALBANY, N.Y., Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As New Yorkers prepare to hit the road during the busiest travel week of the year, the New York State Association of Town Superintendents of Highways (NYSAOTSOH), the state's largest transportation organization, released an expert analysis (https://tinyurl.com/paving-needs) showing that the state's locally-owned roads need an investment of $3.4 billion annually to achieve a state of good repair.

The network of roads and bridges in New York State's counties, cities, towns, and villages is massive: the 97,000 centerline miles of highways represent nearly 85% of the state's total public highway mileage. These thoroughfares are critical to the state in myriad ways: they function as essential corridors for freight movement, agriculture, tourism, and emergency response.

"Unfortunately, funding levels for local road maintenance has been significantly eroded by inflation, allowing for pavement conditions to worsen and they are now accelerating at an alarming rate," said New York State Association of Town Superintendents of Highways President Theresa Burke. "Both state and local government highway funding has fallen far short of meeting the needs, resulting in higher vehicle operating costs for motorists, reduced safety and reliability, and greater future repair costs."

According to "An Assessment of Paving Needs for Local Jurisdiction Highways in New York State," published in October 2026 (https://tinyurl.com/Trip-Net) the total annual contract cost required to achieve and maintain a state of good repair for local highways is estimated at $3.4 billion per year. Today, the New York State Comptroller's office estimates local governments are spending about $1 billion a year on pavement resurfacing projects, meaning current funding levels are $2.4 billion below the actual need.

Region 1 (Albany, Essex, Greene, Rensselaer, Saratoga, Schenectady, Warren, Washington)Region 3 (Cayuga, Cortland, Onondaga, Oswego, Seneca, Tompkins)Region 4 (Genesee, Livingston, Monroe, Ontario, Orleans, Wayne, Wyoming)Region 5 (Cattaraugus, Chautauqua, Erie, Niagara)

Region 2 (Fulton, Hamilton, Herkimer, Madison, Montgomery, Oneida)Region 6 (Allegany, Chemung, Schuyler, Steuben, Yates)Region 7 (Clinton, Franklin, Jefferson, Lewis, St. Lawrence)Region 9 (Broome, Chenango, Delaware, Otsego, Schoharie, Sullivan, Tioga)

Region 8 (Columbia, Dutchess, Orange, Putnam, Rockland, Ulster, Westchester)Region 10 (Nassau, Suffolk)

In addition to the significant pavement needs facing local highway systems, the Office of the New York State Comptroller (OSC) released an analysis estimating the investment needed to maintain New York's locally owned bridges in "acceptable condition." (https://tinyurl.com/ny-bridges)

Using Federal Highway Administration's National Bridge Inventory data, OSC defined acceptable condition as maintaining a bridge's primary structural components in either Good (ratings of 7â8) or Fair (ratings of 5â6) condition, and preventing them from deteriorating into Poor condition (ratings of 4 or below), where structural deterioration becomes more significant.

OSC estimated that, as of 2023, approximately $9.6 billion would be needed to bring locally owned bridges outside New York City into acceptable condition. The Comptroller also cautioned that these costs are likely to increase as bridges age and increasingly severe weather accelerates their deterioration.

If these bridge investments are spread over a 10-year period, the combined annual pavement and bridge investment needs outside New York City exceed $4.6 billion.This underscores the substantial and growing investment challenge facing local governments and the importance of addressing these needs in the development of the next NYSDOT capital program.

In 2011, state lawmakers instituted the local property tax cap on municipalities outside of New York City. Property tax revenues are the largest source of revenue for most of the state's 1,600 municipalities. They fund the core operations of municipalities including salaries, highway maintenance and snow and ice control operations. A 2022 report by New York State Comptroller Tom DiNapoli, "Locally Owned Roads by the Numbers," noted that over the past decade local road spending by municipalities actually declined by seven percent.

"All levels of government need to make a substantial and sustained commitment to close this massive gap," Burke said. "If driver fees, excluding tolls, collected by the state were distributed based on motorists' actual use of the local highway system, local governments would receive an injection of $2 billion annually."

New York State has more than 12.3 million licensed drivers who travel nearly equal amounts on state-maintained and locally maintained roads. In 2023, New York State collected approximately $5.7 billion from its motorists through various taxes and fees, including DMV fees, state sales taxes on gasoline and motor vehicle purchases. Yet only $1.9 billion of these motorist fees were dedicated to highway infrastructure. If the state simply split these revenues with local governments the annual $3.4 billion local highway need would be met when combined with local investment.

Burke, who also serves as Town of Red Hook Highway Superintendent in Dutchess County, added, "That infusion of desperately-needed funding would help to narrow the gap between needs and available resources, help stabilize pavement conditions, reduce long-term rehabilitation costs, and most importantly, ensure a safe and reliable highway system for the citizens of New York State."

The 2025 report, "New York Transportation by the Numbers," (TRIP) (https://tinyurl.com/Trip-Net), found "New York roads provide a rough ride. 25% of major state and locally-owned roads and highways in New York are in poor condition. Driving on rough roads costs the average New York driver $733 annually in additional vehicle operating costs." That figure includes maintenance costs that are the result of hitting potholes and driving on poor road surfaces. This figure does not include the higher cost of fuel, which the AAA reports to be $4.13 a gallon.

"Local highways are indispensable to New York's economic vitality and public safety," Burke said. "But growing fiscal pressure facing local highway departments across the state need immediate, direct relief for local governments that are responsible for 87% of New York's highways. Governor Hochul and state legislative leaders need to take action in the coming budget cycle to help communities absorb rising costs while preserving the condition and safety of essential infrastructure."

The New York State Association of Town Highway Superintendents acts as a medium of instruction in highway construction and maintenance, ensures better and safer highways, and promotes and supports legislation that will benefit the best interest of the people in the towns of New York State.

#5347. ‘You said spicy, right?’ Panel takes on Washington’s economic blind spots — and what needs to change

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You said spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

“Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and said, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

“The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she said. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

The region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn said, should be judged by the communities themselves.

“And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he said. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”

#5345. Bezos and Bond: Amazon founder played a big role in casting new 007

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

#5344. Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, plans Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.
