#5343. ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

#5342. Vertex’s executive chairman: Here’s how we got our drug-trial success rate over 70% when the industry’s is 10% to 20%

Corporate America is locked in an innovation arms race – a race that is turning out very few winners. Companies are spending billions on R&D, acquisitions and new technologies, operating on the seemingly intuitive premise that making more bets is the best way to approach the uncertainty of the future.

But more bets don’t necessarily produce more successes.

There’s no more extreme example of this problem than pharmaceuticals and biotech. It takes an average of 10 to 15 years for a drug to go from the lab to regulatory approval. And more than 90% of drugs that enter clinical development fail. Just look at the headlines: one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies recently suffered three drug trial failures in a single week despite an enormous R&D budget, many talented scientists and a deep pipeline.

But this problem is far from unique to healthcare. In consumer tech, many startups flame out after a single hit; in automotive, EV pioneers are routinely outpaced by fast followers; digital investments in retail often fail to translate into customer growth.

The instinctive response when innovation fails is to do more of it: fund more projects, pursue more ideas, make more acquisitions and place more bets. If innovation is inherently unpredictable, the thinking goes, the best way to improve your chances of success is to increase the number of shots you take.

This kind of thinking is completely backward. It’s not about the shots. It’s about the target.

Imagine entering a darts tournament and throwing five consecutive bull’s-eyes, only to discover that you have been throwing at the wrong board. Your accuracy doesn’t matter. You’ve lost.

More activity creates the appearance of innovation without improving its effectiveness. I learned this the hard way.

When I joined Vertex Pharmaceuticals in 2009, the company had spent two decades investing heavily in R&D across 20 different programs. Yet, it produced only a single breakthrough product, which was rendered obsolete just two and a half years later with the approval of a better and more tolerable treatment discovered by another company.

When we examined why drug development failed so frequently, the problem wasn’t that scientists had failed to create a drug that hit its intended biological target. The problem was that they had chosen the wrong target in the first place.

The solution was to take away choices, constraining ourselves to a “sandbox” of diseases with genetically- or pharmacologically-validated targets where we believed we had a much higher probability of success.

Most importantly, both R&D and business development had to stay inside the same sandbox. A fascinating scientific discovery or enticing acquisition wasn’t enough. If it didn’t fit our strategy or if we didn’t have a validated target to address, we walked away.

That last part may be the most difficult lesson for any leader. Companies often celebrate the ability to say yes to innovation. Sustainable innovators also become very good at saying no. Focus and strategy don’t limit innovation, they accelerate it.

A thriving innovation program requires many parts of an organization working in harmony. Yet companies unintentionally divide innovation into functional silos, with each group incentivized differently and no one focused on the big picture.

Researchers discover something and hand it to developers. Developers hand it to manufacturing. Eventually, commercial teams are asked to sell it. Business development may operate on a separate track entirely, hunting for external opportunities.

But a brilliant invention that cannot be efficiently developed, manufactured or commercialized isn’t a successful innovation.

To break down internal silos, leaders from research, development, regulatory, manufacturing, commercial and other key business units should be included in decisions about new product development from the earliest stages of the innovation process. And internal and external innovation must be tightly integrated into the same strategy. Business development can’t be given permission to roam the universe looking for any interesting assets; partnerships and acquisitions must reinforce the same strategy, diseases, and targets where a company believes it has a high probability of success.

Innovation shouldn’t be measured by how many ideas an organization generates. It should be judged by how effectively the entire organization converts its best ideas into products that meet people’s needs and create meaningful value.

Once innovation succeeds, companies tend to become complacent and stop innovating to create better and better medicines for the same disease. Our experience seeing one of our breakthrough drugs quickly made obsolete by an innovative competitor created a sense of urgency, and even some paranoia, which drove our organization to continuously try to “out-innovate ourselves.”

Being first doesn’t guarantee long term success. Competitors will learn from your breakthroughs and improve on the foundations you laid. We decided that if someone was going to build a better second-generation product, it should be us.

The results were dramatic. Vertex went on to develop multiple transformative medicines, including 5 medicines that alter the course of cystic fibrosis for 95% of patients and, with CRISPR Therapeutics, the first FDA-approved human gene-editing therapy for patients with severe Sickle Cell Disease and transfusion-dependent B-thalassemia. More recently we created a completely new class of non-opioid medicines for moderate to severe acute pain.

Even more important to me is what happened to the odds. Our R&D success rate, measured by positive Phase II proof of concept, exceeded 70% across six diseases — far above the 10% to 20% industry average. We didn’t eliminate risk. Innovation can’t exist without risk. But we became much more deliberate about which risks were worth taking and therefore more successful.

Before approving the next project, acquisition or moonshot, leadership teams should ask themselves an important set of questions: Do we understand why innovation has failed here before? Are we pursuing opportunities where we possess a genuine advantage? What evidence tells us that the underlying problem is solvable? Does this opportunity reinforce our existing capabilities – or merely distract from them? And, perhaps hardest of all, what are we willing to stop doing so that our best ideas have the resources to succeed?

The innovation economy has conditioned leaders to admire the size of the pipeline, the number of experiments and the volume of bets. Those are measures of activity, not success.

The companies that sustainably innovate will not be the ones willing to make the most bets. They’ll be the ones that understand their odds better than anyone else and have the discipline to walk away when those odds aren’t good enough.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune. This headline has been updated to resolve a discrepancy with the text.

Jeffrey Leiden, M.D., Ph.D., is executive chairman of Vertex Pharmaceuticals. He is a physician and scientist who has dedicated his career to improving the lives of people with serious diseases. He previously served as Vertex’s president, chief executive officer and chairman from 2012 through March 2020, and has been a member of Vertex’s board since July 2009. Under his leadership, Vertex delivered the first and only medicines to treat the underlying cause of cystic fibrosis for patients with certain forms of the disease, including Kalydeco, Orkambi and Trikafta.

Dr. Leiden serves as lead independent director of Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company, chairman of Odyssey Therapeutics and chairman of Casana. He is also a member of the MIT CEO Advisory Board, serves on the Massachusetts Governor’s Digital Healthcare Council, Governor’s Task Force on Artificial Intelligence and Governor’s STEM Advisory Council. Dr. Leiden received his M.D., Ph.D. and B.A. degrees from the University of Chicago.

The XRP Ledger Foundation assessed the network against all ten principles in the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. CertiK independently verified the network’s evidence under the Architecture and Resiliency principles.

Garlinghouse said investors have been moving money out of crypto, including XRP, to fund major listings. He expects the market to recover after Anthropic’s debut, just as it did following SpaceX’s IPO.

This makes the assessment relevant to banks exploring tokenized markets. Institutions need to understand how networks handle operational risk, governance, and settlement before building financial products on them.

XRPL’s case is notable because it is public and permissionless. Traditional financial networks often operate behind controlled access. Public blockchains must show how risks are handled across distributed governance, protocol upgrades, and open participation.

The Foundation assessed XRPL against all ten principles. It also supplied supporting evidence for each control. CertiK then examined the Architecture and Resiliency sections, using code, configurations, logs, and test results.

The XRPL Foundation called it the first such verification for a public, permissionless Layer 1. The milestone gives institutions a structured reference when evaluating networks for tokenized deposits, stablecoins, funds, and other assets.

In the interview, Garlinghouse addressed the gap between Ripple’s expansion and XRP price performance. He said the SpaceX IPO triggered a similar pullback as investors shifted liquidity out of crypto. He specifically named Bitcoin and XRP among the assets affected.

He also expects digital assets to stop moving in lockstep. In his view, real utility and demand will increasingly separate stronger projects from speculative tokens. That puts the XRP price debate back on XRPL’s ability to attract activity.

#5339. A ‘mismatch in timing’: Data center power demand is growing 19% a year. The grid is growing 2%

The tech industry is famous for moving fast. The power grid is famous for not. That collision now sits at the center of the AI buildout, a project estimated to cost trillions: Citigroup projects Big Tech will spend more than $2.8 trillion on AI infrastructure through 2029, and a Brookings study puts U.S. investment at $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032.

The grid isn’t built for that pace. Since 2000, power to data centers has risen an average of 19% a year while U.S. grid capacity has expanded just 2% annually, according to an analysis by insurance broker Howden. Data center power use is growing 10 times faster than the system meant to supply it.

That gap has become one of the biggest bottlenecks facing the AI industry. And after this month’s midterms, in which voters rejected data center projects almost everywhere they appeared on the ballot, power is now a political problem, too.

Data centers took about 5% of U.S. grid capacity in 2025. Howden estimates that to hold that share through 2030 at current growth rates, they would have to source up to 58% of their power off the grid, roughly 110 gigawatts, a level the firm itself considers unlikely.

Consumption tells the same story. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could use as much as 12% of U.S. electricity by 2028, about six times their 1.9% share in 2018, before the AI boom.

Rob Gramlich, president of consulting firm Grid Strategies, told Fortune in September that there’s a real “mismatch in timing” between how quickly data centers want power and how quickly the grid can expand. Grid capacity is slow to build because thousands of interconnected parts must work together, he said, which requires “deliberate study and planning” that can take years.

The industry is also rusty. After roughly 25 years of little growth in power demand, Gramlich said, utilities “got out of practice on building new infrastructure.”

Kathryn Burke, who leads U.S. specialty energy and power growth at insurance firm Marsh, told Fortune she expects around 50% to 60% of data center projects to be delayed beyond the one-to-two-year timelines developers are counting on.

Public backlash over grid strain and rising residential electricity prices has added a second hurdle. On Nov. 3, voters rejected data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, the same night Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress.

Opposition runs deepest among the young. A University of Pennsylvania Annenberg Public Policy Center survey conducted this summer found that 70% of adults under 30 oppose new data centers in their area, compared with 61% of all adults.

Voters’ fears aren’t unfounded. Northern Virginia hosts the world’s largest concentration of data centers, and Virginia sells 59% of its electricity to commercial customers, including data center clients. As of 2025, commercial energy demand exceeds residential demand in 23 states and Washington, D.C.

A study in Nature Energy by Cornell University researchers Cheng Feng and Fengqi You found that data centers raised wholesale power prices unevenly. In California’s southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to lift wholesale prices by nearly 20% in 2025; around Dallas–Fort Worth, the increase approached 17%.

Across the four grids studied, the researchers found that data centers paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs tied to their growth in 2025: $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill.

Wholesale prices make up only about 30% to 50% of a household bill, but experts say residential customers will end up covering part of the AI buildout. The Cornell researchers found the costs land hardest on lower-income and rural households, a pattern they call a “paradoxical mismatch.”

“The idea of now having to grow up and compete in terms of water prices and energy prices with a tech company is not something I can say I’m excited about,” Elijah Lee, an 18-year-old organizer with the Gen Z advocacy group Voters of Tomorrow, told Fortune before the midterms.

Tech companies are adapting by moving into energy themselves, under a model the industry calls “bring your own power.”

Some states now require it. In August, Delaware became the first state to legislatively enact a “bring your own generation” policy, requiring large energy users such as data centers to produce or secure 100% of the power they use, including a share of clean energy, within 10 years of starting operations.

President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge asks signers to “build, bring, or buy” the new-generation resources and electricity they need. Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI signed in March, and more than 200 utilities, cooperatives, developers and Republican governors have since joined. The pledge is not binding.

On-site generation is still small but growing fast. BloombergNEF counted just 2 gigawatts of on-site gas generation operating at data centers worldwide as of March. It has since tracked 181 gigawatts of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, more than 90% of it in the U.S.

SpaceX, for one, has proposed a roughly $24 billion supercomputing facility and gas-fired power plant at Starbase, Texas. The shift carries a climate cost: planned gas plants for data centers could raise U.S. power-sector emissions by 20%, according to a Bloomberg News analysis published by Fortune.

It isn’t a cure-all. Data center development experts say the model isn’t a long-term solution because major swings in power demand at AI data centers can cause outages and damage on-site generation equipment.

The next tests come quickly. Democrats take control of congressional committees in January. Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data center development, and Ohio, which already has 125 local data center moratoriums, is set to add more.

While those buildouts are planned, none are promised.

#5338. Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The last quarter of the year is the best time to find out what’s actually earning its keep in your business.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your plans for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Revenue is important. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in new customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

Before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying new things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

So figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a big deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

I love setting goals. I’m a big believer in having a vision and building a plan to get there. I’ve also learned that a new calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

For the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

You don’t have to overhaul the whole company all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

#5337. Should you stock up to prepare for outages? The U.S. intelligence chief points to COVID as proof ‘America is the most amazing and resilient place’

The country is on edge about the recent string of network outages, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tried to offer some reassurance but drew on an unsettling example.

Worried about an imminent catastrophe, many Americans are panic buying supplies at Costco and Walmart. In an interview on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Clayton was asked if it’s time to stock up to prepare for new, possibly extended, outages.

“America is the most amazing and resilient place, and we have been living with interruptions,” he replied. “Let’s give ourselves some credit. Let’s go back to COVID, other things. Americans fought their way through these terrible things in an incredible, resilient way.”

During pandemic-era lockdowns, Americans frantically hoarded so many supplies that grocery stores had to ration necessities like toilet paper.

CNN’s Dana Bash immediately stopped him right there and asked if we could be in another COVID-like situation.

“Not at all, let me be clear. But what I’m saying is the American people are resilient,” Clayton reiterated, pointing out that officials and companies are being straightforward with what’s happening.

“I have such incredible faith in the American people. As we have this technological step change, we will handle it as a country,” he added.

But when pressed on what Americans should actually do to ensure their resilience, Clayton suggested that it’s enough to just be aware.

“How do you prepare? By knowing that systems are going to be upgraded,” he said. “They may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and the government are dealing with this on the front foot.”

The U.S. intelligence chief may not soothe many nerves by reminding people about COVID, as the number of outages at a wide range of places has stunned the country.

Last Thursday, Microsoft’s email and other office tools went down. Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all planes for more than four hours. It later blamed a copper wire that was being upgraded to a fiber-optic cable.

Day later, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, and Apple saw temporary service disruptions. The National Security Agency’s internal classified communications network also suffered an outage, further fraying nerves.

U.S. officials, including Clayton, have said there’s no evidence of coordinated, state-sponsored attacks, suggesting network upgrades meant to patch vulnerabilities recently uncovered by AI were deployed hastily before all the bugs were worked out.

But reports also revealed that there have been cyberattacks elsewhere in recent days, including at the FBI and Agriculture Department. And last month saw so many cyberattacks that it was dubbed “Black October.”

Meanwhile, two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.

One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.

“There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post. “This is scary, and there is no leadership.”

Even before everything appeared to break down, Americans were already nervous after the Pentagon launched an initiative called FORTRESS, which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains.

Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption.

But in an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages.

“This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he explained. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”

Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune, where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

#5336. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 11:47 am

Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

#5334. She was a go-to Manhattan babysitter as a teen. Now she’s running a $100 million-a-year AI startup whose clients include the billionaire Koch family

From a nationwide FAA ground stop to Microsoft and Chase outages that disrupted millions of customers, a string of recent technology failures has highlighted the need to modernize aging infrastructure while raising new fears about the risks of an increasingly AI-dependent world.

But for Jaclyn Rice Nelson, cofounder and CEO of Tribe AI, that tension is exactly why businesses should embrace the technology—not run from it.

“I don’t think that anxiety around AI is unwarranted. I think it’s very real,” Nelson told Fortune.

“[AI] is ours to shape,” Nelson said. “And the only way you can shape it is if you understand it, and the only way you understand it is if you use it—and use it a lot.”

Nelson, 41, has built her business around helping companies do just that. Founded in 2019, Tribe AI has grown to a $100 million annual run rate by helping organizations—from Fortune 500s like Hyatt and MetLife to multibillion-dollar private conglomerates like Koch Inc.—put AI to work.

Tribe said on Nov. 18 that its annualized revenue had crossed $100 million, up 3.8 times from a year earlier, as more clients moved AI projects out of the pilot stage. “The hard part is getting AI into production inside a complex business,” Nelson said in the announcement.

Nelson’s instinct to build something of her own predates the AI boom by decades.

She grew up in New York City with a single mother raising two children. After transitioning from teaching to business, her mother managed to send both kids to private school in Manhattan—a sacrifice that left a lasting impression on Nelson.

“It was someone in my life who had done really hard things, who I had seen do hard things, and who also refused to let things slip for me,” Nelson said.

That set Nelson in motion to seek her own financial independence. As a teenager, she started babysitting and grew the side hustle into what she once described as a “babysitting empire.”

“I became this trusted, fairly scarce asset,” she said, adding that she became the go-to babysitter for entire New York apartment buildings, with parents competing to book her on Saturday nights.

But beyond the money, it also taught her an early lesson in business: “Be the trusted person, be dependable.”

After graduating in 2008 with a degree in political science from the University of Michigan, Nelson then took a more traditional route to financial independence: Wall Street. She spent two years as an analyst at Citigroup, before moving to Silicon Valley to work for Google—and brought the same work ethic that had served her in banking.

“I moved to a new city where I didn’t really know anyone,” she said. “And so I just worked banking hours at Google. I was always like the person still in the office, waving my hand to get the light sensors to go back on.”

Her work ethic, and willingness to take on responsibilities outside her core role, led her to make a career jump to Google’s growth equity fund, CapitalG (then known as Google Capital) in 2015 as its first business-focused employee among a team of dozens of engineers. Three years later, she left to pursue an opportunity of her own, cofounding Tribe AI in 2019.

Since 2019, the company has grown to roughly 250 employees, after its team grew fivefold this year, the company said—all while raising less than $10 million in venture funding and reaching profitability.

As Tribe continues to expand, Nelson said she’s looking for people who are deeply curious about AI, willing to take on difficult challenges, and humble enough to recognize how much they still have to learn.

“You have to be kind of humbled by how little you know every day and motivated by learning and getting better,” she said.

One of Tribe AI’s major customers is Koch Inc., one of the world’s largest privately held companies. The business conglomerate employs about 130,000 people and generates more than $125 billion in annual revenue.

“There’s a lot of businesses that run through the smartest guy in the room telling people what to do. We are the opposite of that,” Chase Koch, executive vice president of origination and partnerships at Koch and son of Charles, told Fortune.

Koch wanted to bring its decades-old management philosophy—centered on bottom-up principles developed by chairman and co-CEO Charles Koch—into the AI era. Working with Tribe, the project went from an idea to a launched product in just five months. The result is an AI-powered coaching tool designed to help employees put the principles into practice. Employees can describe a challenge at work and receive personalized guidance on how to approach it.

Chase Koch said he tried the tool himself after his boss told him he was taking on too many responsibilities. Talking through the problem with the AI helped him develop a plan to prioritize his work, delegate more effectively, and focus on his strengths.

For Nelson, the project and its speed points to a bigger opportunity for AI: making personalized coaching and development more accessible, without losing sight of the people it’s meant to help.

“The goal of this is not just to scale AI, it’s to make people better, to help them lean in on the things that they are going to be the most uniquely suited to do,” Nelson said. “I believe AI is giving people these superpowers, and this is a good example of that.”

For young professionals facing the same shift, Koch and Nelson had similar but straightforward advice: Figure out what makes you uniquely valuable, then learn how to use AI to make the most of it.

“If you understand the technology and how it works, what are the places you can use that power and strength to then change the trajectory of how it is used and the impact that it has on people and workforces and society?” Nelson said.

Koch echoed an emphasis on individual strengths: “Understand what your comparative advantage is. What is your gift combined with what you’re really passionate about learning and what gets you excited and gets you out of bed in the morning?”

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

#5333. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5332. Alibaba and Tencent put their faith in Chinese chips as U.S. curbs threatens to slow down their AI development

Tencent and Alibaba said this week that domestic chips can cushion their cloud businesses from new U.S. restrictions on access to advanced AI processors, yet acknowledged that they could still slow the development of new AI models.

Both tech giants reported earnings after the U.S. Department of Commerce released an interim rule expanding export controls on Monday, making them some of the first Chinese corporate responses to the restrictions.

Chipmakers and exporters now need a license to sell advanced chips to data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The rule also requires a license for large data centers to offer substantial computing power to Chinese customers. Together, the measures are likely to restrict the amount of computing power available to Chinese companies like Alibaba and Tencent as they develop AI models and offer them to users.

Tencent executives, in the company’s earnings call, drew a distinction between the computing power needed to train new models and running existing ones.

“We actually don’t see an impact because our cloud business today is primarily running inference,” James Mitchell, Tencent’s chief strategy officer, told analysts on Wednesday. (Inference is the running of AI models, as opposed to training them.)

Mitchell added that Tencent had reached a stage where the inference could run on what he called a “surprisingly limited number” of domestically produced chips.

Martin Lau, Tencent’s president, agreed that the domestic supply chain should be able to cover inference, particularly for Tencent’s smaller, more efficient models.

Still, Lau called the restrictions “unfortunate” and admitted that it would now take longer for Tencent to train the next version of its Hunyuan model. “It sets everyone back in China,” he said.

In the long run, Lau predicted that U.S. controls would “speed up” the development of China’s domestic chip industry. “We believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips.”

Tencent reported 207.3 billion yuan ($31 billion) in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, up 8% year-on-year. Fintech and business services revenue, which includes cloud computing, rose 9.4% to reach 63.6 billion yuan ($9.5 billion).

Net profit rose 0.3% to 65.1 billion yuan ($9.8 billion). Capital expenditure rose 527% to 81.4 billion yuan ($12.2 billion).

On Thursday, on its earnings call, Alibaba said its 2030 targets—including $100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20% EBITDA margin—remain on track despite the new restrictions.

“Our own progress in developing domestic computing power is in fact already ahead of our original expectations,” Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu told analysts on the call. The company has invested heavily in its in-house chip division, T-Head, which it plans to list in Hong Kong.

Alibaba reported 271.5 billion yuan ($40.5 billion) in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, up 10% year-on-year. AI and cloud revenue rose 53% to reach 61.0 billion yuan ($9.1 billion).

Net profit also rose by 213% year-on-year to 64.4 billion yuan ($9.6 billion). Capital expenditure rose by 60% to reach 50.5 billion yuan ($7.5 billion).

Alibaba’s confidence in its longer-term targets came with a warning about the near term.

“The new compute export control rules will affect next year’s products and services, and there is still uncertainty as regards the supply chain,” Wu said during the earnings call. He suggested that cloud revenue growth could slow to between 30% and 45%, then rebound to 50% or higher by 2028.

Wu said it was “too early at this stage” to know how U.S. restrictions might affect the development of its Qwen family of models, though he added that the company’s current T-Head chips “are already capable of fully supporting the training of large-scale, including ultra-large-scale, models.” Wu predicted that T-Head production would ramp up in 2027 or 2028. “Once we get there, we will actually be in a better position to control and pace the speed at which we iterate our foundation models,” he said.

Alibaba, however, is in the spotlight after the Nvidia scandal, which toppled CEO Jensen Huang last week. Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, before U.S. chip export controls took effect in 2022, the Information reported. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, is suspected of funneling advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls; Megaspeed denies the allegations.

On Thursday, a group of Alibaba shareholders sued the company, accusing it of concealing its ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. The shareholders said media reports of the ties contributed to a 14% drop in Alibaba’s share price over four days, and accused it of understating the risk that export-control violations could harm its business.

Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Commerce Department faces increased scrutiny over whether it has done enough to keep advanced chips out of China. On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released data showing the department had approved nearly 880,000 AI chips for Chinese companies—including 75,000 for Alibaba and 150,000 for Tencent—out of more than 3.4 million chips that Nvidia and AMD sought to export to Chinese companies.

Chinese AI developers beyond Tencent and Alibaba are preparing for the likely impact of tighter U.S. chip restrictions. The Information reported Thursday that Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based developer of the Kimi models, had scrapped a $150 million deal to access Nvidia’s Blackwell chips through an Indonesian data center.

The new controls also constrain the ability of Chinese companies to manufacture their own semiconductors using overseas foundries. New U.S. rules narrow the exemptions that chip manufacturers can use to ship advanced chips without a license. The Financial Times reports that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Samsung Electronics have suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers.

#5331. High-end genealogy travel is booming, offering luxe journeys to the roots of your family tree

The most exclusive itinerary is written in your DNA.

My great-great-grandfather came to the Tuscan ghost island of Pianosa as a prisoner. I arrived there on a luxury vacation.

The island lives up to its name, I thought as my ferry drifted toward the sole dock on this protected isola fantasma. “Pianosa” is derived from piano, Italian for “flat,” and indeed the island crouches low to the cyan Tyrrhenian Sea, its shores fringed by parasol pines and deserted prison watchtowers. From 1856 to 1998, Pianosa was a remote penal colony—and the place where my ancestor, Salvatore Giovanni Pellegrino Irace, died.

I’d learned this family lore thanks to a partnership between Ancestry, the Blackstone-owned leader in the at-home DNA-testing space, and Kensington, a bespoke travel outfitter, which invited me to test-drive its Personal Heritage Journey. After I submitted a DNA sample, Ancestry got to work filling in my Italian family tree, with researchers combing archives in Tuscany, Molise, and Campania. “So the interesting thing about Salvatore,” genealogist Kyle Betit said on our initial call, “is that he died in prison of tuberculosis in 1894—and we don’t know why he was there.”

Who doesn’t love a good family mystery? That’s part of what draws clients to Kensington’s genealogical-based trips. The journeys average $20,000 to $25,000 per person, with the company’s travel desk handling all the details in high style.

For me, that meant a chartered boat from mainland Tuscany to the island of Elba; chauffeured SUVs between regions; a private guide in Pompeii; and some spectacular accommodations, including Casa Angelina and Palazzo Avino on the Amalfi Coast. The major flex, though, was having a professional genealogist, Gabriele Musumeci, riding shotgun.

Once upon a time, possessing one’s comprehensive genealogy was a signal of wealth and pedigree. Then, in the 2000s, the rise of at-home DNA-testing kits from Ancestry and 23andMe made such knowledge commonplace. The ultrawealthy can now seek out deeper stories through first-person ancestry tourism, from China to Ghana. Kensington reports that demand has doubled and revenue has quadrupled in five years. Grand View Research put the global value of “heritage tourism”—of which ancestral travel is a segment—at $625 billion in 2025. It’s expected to reach almost a trillion by 2033.

“I think there’s a deep need in any of us to understand who we are,” Musumeci said as we descended the concrete steps to Pianosa’s white-sand beach, Cala Giovanna. “For most Americans, your story is cut.” He made a chopping motion. And then a sewing motion: “We stitch it back together.”

Most luxury travel planners now offer some variety of ancestry service. Alexandrea Padilha, director at the membership-based Fischer Unlimited, recently hired genealogists in Germany and the U.S. to trace a Louisiana tech entrepreneur’s ancestry. The results were bound into a book for the client’s father’s 80th birthday and also informed the itinerary for a trip to Germany—a way to show younger family members their roots. “I think that’s grounding for young adults today,” Padilha says, “living in a world that’s slowly slipping away.”

Existential dread is one hell of a motivator. “When it feels like the world may be shifting every second, people reach for something enduring,” says Dr. Katie Blake, a Texas-based social psychologist who specializes in travel. “The archives give you the facts, but it’s the place itself that gives you the identity pull that’s different than something you just see on paper.”

A sudden, biblical rainstorm broke open during our mile-long bike ride from Cala Giovanna to Pianosa’s imposing Agrippa Prison. We sheltered inside the Zante wing, where prisoners like Salvatore slept four to a concrete cell on metal beds, as thunder rattled the rusty gates.

My itinerary traced Salvatore’s life backward. A few days later, Musumeci and I rendezvoused in Molise, where Salvatore grew up. My great-great-great-grandfather, Vincenzo, moved his family to Montenero di Bisaccia, a mountain keep surrounded by vineyards and wheat fields sloping down to the Adriatic, in 1838, when Salvatore was a boy. At Montenero’s city hall, the clerks hauled out massive, crimson-bound books, and Musumeci leafed through until he found the birth and marriage records of Salvatore’s second son, Giuseppe—my great-grandfather.

Walking through Montenero’s hilltop puzzle of alleys brought those pieces of paper to life—and conjured a story of downward mobility. Along the town’s outer promenade, ringing the remains of medieval stone walls, a lookout faced the amber foothills where Vincenzo bought land and a farmhouse. I walked the narrow alley the family lived on after they lost the farm. Within four years, Vincenzo had spiraled from merchant and farm owner to street sweeper. He died in 1842, leaving his son on the poverty-to-prison pipeline.

I also saw the house in the old ghetto where my great-grandmother, Nicoletta, grew up. She and Giuseppe had a daughter out of wedlock, Mattia. (Nobody in my family had known Mattia existed until Musumeci discovered her.) The infant likely died during the couple’s 1900 journey to America, where, at Ellis Island, Irace became Erace. Giuseppe and Nicoletta settled in Philadelphia and had 16—yes, 16—more children, including my paternal grandfather, Michael Erace, who died in 2013.

It was like I was looking at Grandpop Mike’s long-lost brother when we met Bruno Irace, a 74-year-old Ironman triathlete and my fourth cousin, that afternoon. Smile, hair, complexion, bone structure; it was uncanny. We sipped espresso and compared photos, then visited a cemetery where “Irace” seemed to be engraved on every other gravestone. Two Iraces were listed on an obelisk in the village park honoring fallen soldiers. When it was time to leave Montenero, Bruno told us to come back soon. “You have family here,” he said.

The name Irace was also everywhere in the archives of San Luca, the family’s neighborhood church, in Praiano, on the Amalfi Coast, the final stop on my journey. This dramatic shoreline of improbable cliff-top villages and citrus groves set high above the sapphire sea is one of the most beautiful places in the world. I couldn’t help but wonder about the Iraces: Why did these fools leave? What misfortune befell my reasonably prosperous ancestors to make them abscond from this stunning seaside real estate?

Musumeci had coordinated with the pastor, who granted us free rein of his office, a charmingly cluttered room with sea views through diamond-paned windows. Hundreds of books, some dating to the 1600s, filled a tall cabinet, their yellowed pages brittle as autumn leaves. Handwritten in meticulous script were the births and baptisms, marriages and deaths of San Luca’s parishioners, which included generations of Iraces.

“Oh, wow … ” Musumeci stopped suddenly as his finger moved across a page. He pointed to Vincenzo’s marriage record. “Adam, the date … ” October 10, 1807.

It took a few seconds to dawn on me. I checked my phone: October 10, 2026. Exactly 219 years earlier, Vincenzo Irace and Mariangela Rispoli, ages 21 and 18, had stood at San Luca’s resplendent altar and exchanged vows. Until then, I’d encountered Vincenzo mostly through his losses: his farm, his livelihood, his family’s good name. Here was a record of a beginning. Whatever came later, my great-great-great-grandparents had first been two young people at the altar of a church above the sea.

I hadn’t found all the answers in Italy. We never learned why they left the Amalfi Coast, what sent their son to prison, or what compelled their grandson to cross an ocean. The private guides, chauffeured SUVs, and beautiful hotels couldn’t make the records yield answers they didn’t contain.

But the distance between my ancestors’ lives and my own no longer seemed quite so great. Standing in San Luca, I wasn’t the discerning traveler whose preferences shaped the itinerary. For all the choices I’d made on this trip, the ones that mattered most had been made two centuries earlier.

For once, the point wasn’t being made to feel important. The real privilege was the opportunity to feel very, very small.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune with the headline “The most exclusive itinerary is written in your DNA.”

#5330. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5329. The 5 Little Habits That Made a Bigger Difference in My Business Than I Expected

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Growth doesn’t always come from big strategies. Here are the small habits that had a bigger impact on my business than I ever expected.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the big moves: landing a major client, launching a new service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. That’s why I’m starting with the health habits that changed how I work, before moving on to the habits tied directly to running my business.

None of these were clever strategies or big investments. They were simple habits I built into my everyday routine. On their own, each one seemed minor. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most.

One of the simplest habits that made a surprisingly big difference in my business was walking every day. When I first started spending long hours behind my laptop, I could easily go through an entire day barely moving. Eventually, I realized that waiting for free time to exercise wasn’t working, so I decided to make walking part of my daily routine.

The more I thought about it, the more I noticed how many people around me had the same problem. Founders, freelancers, marketers: Most of us spend our days at a desk and tell ourselves we’ll be more active once work slows down. But that moment rarely comes, and the effects build up quietly. According to Okdermo, about 41.9% of American adults are affected by obesity. There are many reasons behind that number, but a lack of daily movement is one of them, and it’s something I could actually control. I didn’t want my work to slowly become the reason my health got worse. Walking was the easiest way I found to change that, and I didn’t have to rebuild my whole schedule to do it.

And it turns out that you don’t need an extreme daily step count to see meaningful health benefits. According to Solace, walking 7,000 steps a day was associated with a 47% lower risk of death from any cause compared with walking 2,000 steps. Personally, I aim for around 15,000 steps a day, not because I believe it’s some magic number, but because I’ve noticed that I feel better, sleep more soundly and think more clearly when I reach it. Everyone should find a daily step count that works for their own body and lifestyle rather than blindly following someone else’s target.

Over time, my walks have also become some of the most productive parts of my day. I listen to podcasts, think through ideas and sometimes even take calls and meetings while I walk. I record voice memos and jot down notes whenever something useful comes to mind. Walking and talking at the same time helps me let go of stress, but more importantly, it clears my head. Some of my best business decisions were made not at my desk, but halfway through a walk.

Business impact: Walking helps me clear my mind, solve problems faster and make better business decisions.

Walking was a great start, but I knew I needed more than daily steps to stay in good shape. The problem was that I used to skip workouts whenever work got busy. There was always another deadline or client who needed my attention. That’s why I decided to hire a personal trainer. I knew that having someone waiting for me would make it harder to find excuses.

And it worked. According to PersonalTrainers, 88.2% of people training with in-person supervision met their workout attendance target, compared with 52.2% of those training on their own. Having someone hold me accountable made all the difference.

Now I treat workouts like client meetings. I put them on my calendar and rarely cancel. I’ve learned that sometimes the best way to stay consistent is to make a commitment to someone other than yourself.

Business impact: Working with a trainer helps me stay disciplined, manage my schedule better and maintain the energy I need to run my business.

Taking care of my health gave me more energy and focus, but some of the habits that made the biggest difference were directly tied to how I run my business. One of them was giving more attention to existing clients instead of constantly chasing new ones. Early on, I was so focused on winning new projects that I sometimes overlooked the people who were already paying for my services. Eventually, I realized that building long-term relationships was far more valuable than constantly starting from scratch.

I began listening more carefully, communicating more openly and looking for ways to deliver more than clients expected. The results have been worth it: Today, clients stay with my business for an average of 3.5 years. And the financial value of retention shouldn’t be underestimated. According to Coruzant, even a 5% improvement in customer retention can increase profits by 25% or more. For me, that reinforces why taking better care of existing clients deserves just as much attention as bringing in new ones.

Over the years, I’ve learned that keeping clients isn’t only about delivering good results. It’s also about trust. Clients need to know they can rely on you, especially when something goes wrong. And once that trust is broken, it’s very hard to win back. Alpha Market Flow reports that 72% of repeat buyers say they would permanently abandon a brand after a single trust-breaking incident. That’s why I try to communicate openly, address problems early and never make promises I can’t keep.

Business impact: Focusing on existing clients gives my business more predictable revenue and reduces the constant pressure to find new projects.

One small habit that has made a big difference in my marketing work is paying attention to how customers describe their problems. I’ve learned that people rarely use the same language as the companies selling to them.

I applied this approach with an invoicing software client by studying support tickets, sales calls, live chats, reviews and internal website searches. Customers weren’t asking for an “accounts receivable automation platform.” They wanted to stop chasing late payments, avoid invoice mistakes and save time creating invoices.

I used those insights to build the brand’s narrative. On the client’s own website, I rewrote key pages around the problems customers actually described and added public pricing and customer case studies. Through digital PR campaigns, I made sure that whenever the brand was mentioned on other websites, the surrounding text explained a specific customer problem and how the software solved it. Instead of simply getting mentions, I was consistently telling the same story: This is the tool that helps you get paid on time.

Over six months, the brand earned more than 60 mentions across industry publications, comparison articles and digital PR coverage. Organic traffic increased by 25%, while organic demo requests grew by 44%.

I started using this approach long before AI search became popular, but I believe it’s even more important today. After analyzing 2 million AI citations, Discovered Labs found that content closely matching users’ questions was more likely to be cited, with stronger alignment associated with roughly 30% more citations. This reinforces something I’ve believed for years: The more consistently you connect your brand to the problems it solves, the easier it becomes for people, and now AI tools, to understand what your business offers.

Business impact: Listening to how customers describe their problems now shapes how I approach every client. When a brand is consistently connected to the problems its customers want solved, it becomes easier to find, easier to trust and easier for both people and AI tools to recommend.

One habit that has made a real difference in my business is building relationships with journalists before I have something to pitch. I’ve learned that the best media relationships develop gradually, through genuine conversations rather than requests for coverage.

I look for opportunities to connect with journalists at conferences, industry events and in private communities we’re both part of. I also try to understand what matters to them and how I might be helpful, especially when they’re looking for information, sources or expert opinions. I don’t approach every interaction with the expectation of getting something in return.

Even when I’m reading for pleasure or watching television, I often notice journalists whose work interests me. I’ll make a note of their names, look into what they cover and find a natural opportunity to introduce myself. Over time, these small interactions can turn into genuine professional relationships.

I’ve learned that it’s far better to send a relevant story to 10 or 15 journalists I’ve built relationships with than to blast the same email to 1,500 strangers. Relationships don’t guarantee coverage, but they give you something a mass email can’t: an existing conversation and a better understanding of what each journalist finds interesting.

These relationships matter to journalists, too. According to CoinFunnel, 53% of journalists consider their relationships with PR professionals important or very important to their success. That reinforces something I’ve learned through experience: Effective PR begins long before you have a story to pitch.

Business impact: Instead of starting from zero every time I have a story to share, I already know which journalists are likely to care about it. That saves time, leads to better conversations and makes it far more likely that my ideas, and my clients’ stories, actually get published.

If you want to try this yourself, you don’t necessarily have to build these habits one at a time. Many experts recommend starting with a single habit, and that’s good advice in most cases. But because these habits cover very different parts of life and work, I think it’s fine to start a few of them at once.

Taking a daily walk won’t get in the way of nurturing relationships with journalists, and working with a trainer won’t stop you from spending more time with existing clients. Pick the ones that fit your life and your business, give them a few months, and pay attention to what changes. Small habits rarely feel important in the moment, but over time, they can shape the kind of business you build.

When people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the big moves: landing a major client, launching a new service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. That’s why I’m starting with the health habits that changed how I work, before moving on to the habits tied directly to running my business.

None of these were clever strategies or big investments. They were simple habits I built into my everyday routine. On their own, each one seemed minor. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most.

#5328. Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.
